A novel topology optimization method for enhanced stress distribution using density projection and body-fitted mesh
abstract: Controlling stress distribution in structural topology optimization is crucial for preventing potential failure and reducing material usage. However, algorithms that focus solely on local stress performance while ignoring the overall stress distribution often generate structures with low overall stress levels, significantly compromising the optimization outcome. This paper presents a Density Projection Topology Optimization (DPTO) method aimed at enhancing the von Mises stress distribution in engineering structures by minimizing the weight while considering both the maximal local stress and the overall stress constraints across the whole design domain. One key innovation of this work is the combination of density projection with a linear material interpolation scheme. A metric is introduced to evaluate the greyness degree of optimized patterns, which continuously decreases as the projection parameter increases, representing the gradual elimination of greyscale from the design domain. The optimization process terminates when the greyness degree reaches a prescribed threshold. This strategy contributes to more accurate and efficient optimization processes using a body-fitted mesh, which is regenerated whenever the projection parameter changes to ensure a high-quality mesh representation. The novelty of this paper lies in the first-time integration of multiple stress constraints, density projection, and body-fitted mesh to enhance structural stress performance. The flexibility to redefine the design domain, another feature of the proposed method, results in increased design freedom and improved structural performance.

Impact of steel-to-timber joints with screws on the failure modes and reliability of a structurally indeterminate timber beam
abstract: The nonlinear behaviour of timber joints is considered in Eurocode 5 by prescribing a stiffness reduction ratio; specifically, the joint stiffness at the ultimate limit state is calculated as two-thirds of its serviceability limit state value. The system effects, i.e. how the joints interact within the global structure, are not taken into account. These simplifications may be unreliable for modern statically indeterminate structures, potentially leading to non-conservative or overly conservative designs. Steel-to-timber joints with self-tapping screws are widely used and offer high stiffness and load-carrying capacity. This study aims to assess the effects of the current design rules on the reliability of a statically indeterminate timber beam with steel-to-timber joints with self-tapping screws and subjected to a uniformly distributed load. The uncertainties in material properties, the load, and the nonlinear behaviour of joints are considered in the probabilistic model of the structure. For semi-rigid joints with laterally loaded screws, applying the code stiffness reduction ratio of 2/3 roughly doubles the probability of failure compared to the design target. Moreover, the required stiffness reduction ratio is found to be a function of relative joint-beam stiffness and the load-to-screw axis angle. The reliability-based calibrated stiffness ratio ensures that the target probability of failure is met. The framework can also be extended to other joint typologies for safer design.

Development and testing of strong-middle steel sections with enhanced buckling behaviour
abstract: This study experimentally investigates the compressive behaviour of steel tubular sections with strength heterogeneity introduced through localized Induction Heating (IH). By converting the ferrite microstructure into fine or coarse martensite through IH, the yield strength of S355 circular hollow sections (CHS) increases up to 2.4 times. These sections named Strong-Middle Sections (SMSs) exhibit higher strength at the mid-length and lower strength at the ends and are theoretically capable of achieving higher buckling loads than conventional steel sections (CSSs) due to their increased mid-span flexural resistance. To prove the concept, buckling tests were conducted on novel SMSs by varying slenderness ratio, middle-to-end material strength ratio and length of the strong middle portion. Based on test data, SMSs achieved approximately up to 40% higher buckling loads and up to 120% greater post-buckling strength than the corresponding CSSs, displaying either symmetrical or asymmetrical buckling. Digital Image Correlation (DIC) captured with high accuracy the nonlinear material behaviour of the section all the way from the elastic range of response up to complete failure of the section. Strain demands were found to be more uniformly distributed along the length of SMSs, engaging larger portions of steel section at plastic deformations, thus leading to smoother post-buckling transitions and less abrupt reduction of the post-peak strength. It was also found that EN 1993-1-1 underestimates the buckling load of SMSs and associated comparisons with test data highlighted the need for revision of the classical elastic buckling theory to account for the greater buckling resistance offered by the novel IH-treated sections.

Experimental and analytical analysis of layered concrete beams with partially stiff interfaces
abstract: The behaviour of layered flexural concrete elements is significantly influenced by the characteristics of the interface between layers. The impact of the interface must be considered during the analysis of such structural elements. This study presents an analysis of layered flexural element interface characteristics, flexural layered element behaviour and a novel analytical approach to predicting the deflection of layered concrete elements. The proposed method includes (1) a model describing the interface behaviour and (2) a deflection model for layered flexural elements. To validate the analytical models and examine the structural performance of layered concrete elements, six layered concrete beams were constructed and tested. The beams were categorized based on their interface connectors: type P beams with connectors perpendicular to the interface, and L1 and L2 beams with connectors resembling lattice girder. Additionally, each beam type was constructed with two cross-sections configurations: one with 50 mm and 200 mm layers, and another with 80 mm and 170 mm layers. Experimental results indicated that L2 beams exhibited the highest capacity before adhesive interface failure (reaching 44.3 kN and 36.2 kN load) and performed well when friction and dowel action governed the interface behaviour. Conversely, L1 beams showed the lowest adhesive resistance (reaching 25.6 kN and 25.1 kN load), while P beams demonstrated moderate performance (experiencing adhesive failure at 31.7 kN and 29.4 kN). Additionally, beams with thicker bottom layers exhibited higher flexural capacity across all behavioural stages. Moreover, different connector arrangements were the cause of different beam cracking patterns. Analytical models were used to predict the behaviour of layered beams. The analytical results were similar to the experimental results. Furthermore, differential concrete layer shrinkage was considered in the analytical calculations. The reduction in interface adhesive resistance due to differential shrinkage was found to be in the range of 0.56–0.62 MPa.

title: Development of a novel energy fuse for enhancing blast resistance in masonry infill walls
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of autoclaved aerated concrete (AAC) blocks as vertically embedded energy fuses for enhancing the blast resistance of masonry infill walls. A novel configuration is proposed, in which AAC layers act as sacrificial and replaceable elements that absorb and redistribute blast energy before it is transmitted through the wall. Validated finite element models were developed to simulate the structural behaviour of infill walls subjected to a wide range of explosive charge weights and standoff distances. Key response parameters, including support reactions, energy dissipation, displacement, velocity, and stress distribution in mortar, brick, and AAC components, were systematically evaluated. The results demonstrate that the AAC fuse system significantly improves blast performance: peak wall displacement was reduced by up to 80 %, base reaction forces by approximately 7 %, and peak stresses in mortar and brick by 59 % and over 30 %, respectively. Additionally, the presence of AAC layers reduced sensitivity to boundary conditions, highlighting its potential in retrofit applications where full anchorage is not feasible. The system also enhanced structural damping, promoted more uniform deformation patterns, and improved energy absorption over time relative to conventional masonry walls. These findings confirm that the proposed AAC energy fuse represents a practical and cost-effective strategy for improving the blast resilience of masonry infill walls, particularly in aging or vulnerable structures where traditional reinforcement methods may be difficult to implement.

Dataset of diagonally reinforced coupling beams: Axial restraint and strength design
abstract: A dataset comprising experimental results from 45 diagonally reinforced concrete (RC) coupling beams, including 21 specimens tested with some form of axial restraint conditions, were analyzed to investigate the influence of axial restraint on the seismic response of diagonally RC coupling beams. Statistical analysis revealed that the provided axial restraint significantly affected the coupling beam maximum strength, with enhanced strengths of up to three times the nominal design strength. The measured strengths were found to align closely with the flexural strength calculated based on the probable moment strength at the beam ends. In addition, a simple strength estimation method that incorporates the axial restraint effect was proposed, which provided a reasonable approximation of the experimental responses. The analyses indicated that the initial stiffness was slightly increased due to axial restraint conditions, with stiffness showing a strong correlation to the beam aspect ratio. However, the influence of axial restraint conditions on the chord rotation capacity of coupling beams was less pronounced. Furthermore, a proposed strength design procedure indicated that the diagonal reinforcement in coupling beams can be reduced by approximately 20 % compared to those determined by existing design provisions. • Axial restraint conditions enhance the strength of diagonally RC coupling beams up to three times nominal design strength. • Limited influence on stiffness and chord rotation capacity of diagonally RC coupling beams under axial restraint effects. • A proposed design approach provides an economical design for diagonally RC coupling beams in coupled wall systems.

title: Behaviour of heated steel beams with lateral and axial restraint in steel-timber hybrid structures
Buckling of viscoelastic laminated structural glass members: A novel practical approach using linear-elastic models
abstract: This study presents a methodology for estimating the critical buckling load of laminated glass plates, accounting for the time- and temperature-dependent behaviour of viscoelastic interlayers. The approach is based on a quasi-elastic approximation that allows the use of analytical expressions involving an effective stiffness. The buckling parameters required in the expressions are obtained from simplified linear-elastic finite element models of the laminated structural glass. The methodology is general and can be applied to laminated glass members with any type of viscoelastic interlayer. This paper validates the proposed methodology through comparison with layered finite element models developed in ABAQUS, showing good agreement across different boundary conditions. The proposed method significantly reduces computational effort while maintaining sufficient accuracy for engineering applications.

title: Cross-domain structural damage identification based on updated FEM and WGAN-GP: Bridging the gap between FEM simulations and actual structural responses
Bending–shear domain of Mode-V failure in hardwood dowels: Experimental tests and implications for dynamic grading
abstract: Timber joints are still built almost exclusively with steel fasteners, despite the high carbon footprint of steel production. Wooden dowels made from dense hardwoods offer a circular and renewable alternative, but current design codes do not yet cover their failure mechanisms. This study investigates the bending-shear interaction (Mode V) in rotary-cut birch and profiled beech dowels through a combination of dynamic and quasi-static testing. Ninety specimens, in two diameters and three gap-to-diameter ratios, were tested to evaluate the influence of geometry and wood directionality on strength. Free-free modal tests provided axial, bending, and shear moduli, which proved to have limited correlation with the measured shear strength, highlighting the practical limits of dynamic grading for dowel performance prediction. In contrast, quasi-static double-shear tests revealed two purely geometric parameters, the unsupported span and loading direction (radial versus tangential), that govern the shear strength of hardwood dowels. A minimalist linear model based on these parameters predicted the yield strength of birch and beech dowels with cross-validated errors below 5%. Expressed in normalised stress space, all results follow an almost linear bending-shear failure line, confirming that Mode V is a brittle shear-dominated fracture mechanism, markedly different from the curved interaction surfaces assumed for ductile steel fasteners. The study concludes by proposing a simplified design format for hardwood dowels and outlining the boundaries of applicability for dynamic grading approaches.

Experimental testing and seismic equivalency of platform CLT shear walls using galvanized nails and self-drilling screws
abstract: Cross-laminated timber (CLT) platform shear walls were first included in the U.S. seismic design standards in 2022, with specific requirements for aspect ratio, connection type, and fasteners used. These requirements limit the use of common alternatives, such as galvanized nails or equivalent strength screws, that could provide practical benefits in construction. This study investigates whether these alternatives provide equivalent seismic performance through experimental testing. The testing and analysis were guided by the seismic equivalency process outlined in FEMA P795. In total, twenty-three CLT platform frame shear walls were tested under monotonic and cyclic loading, using three different fastener types: 16D bright box nails (control group and code-approved fastener), 16D zinc-coated nails, and self-drilling #9 × 2.5″ screws. The testing followed standardized CUREE protocols, and the results were evaluated based on ultimate strength, initial stiffness, ductility, deformation, and hold-down performance. The experimental results for each alternative were compared separately using the FEMA P795 procedures. The results indicated that walls with zinc-coated nails and screws exhibited strength, deformation, and ductility values comparable to those of the reference configuration using 16D bright box nails. Overall, the testing program results support the conclusion that future code updates could broaden the types of fasteners allowed for platform CLT shear walls without detrimental effect to expected performance.

Experimental testing and comparison with analytical methods for glued-in rods in cross-laminated timber
abstract: With the advent of engineered wood products, timber has evolved into a sustainable material for modern innovative structural systems. This resurgence in the application of timber has also spurred the development of innovative connection systems. Among various timber connection methods, glued-in rods (GiRs) have emerged as a modern solution, offering superior load-carrying capacity, aesthetic integration, and suitability for concealed applications. In this study, sixteen GiR connections in cross-laminated timber (CLT) are experimentally tested to evaluate failure modes, load–displacement behavior, and strain distribution along the rod embedment length. These experimental results, combined with data from previously published studies, are used to assess the predictive accuracy and reliability of existing analytical and empirical design equations developed for the GiR connection design. The study highlights the importance of considering both the embedment length and the grain orientation when designing GiR connections in CLT. While most existing design formulations provide reasonable strength estimates, their accuracy decreases at higher embedment lengths. Moreover, variability in failure behavior across studies underscores the complexity of GiR connections. In summary, the findings of this study provide insight into the performance of current design models and contribute to the advancement of reliable methodologies for GiR connections in CLT structures.

Behavior of GFRP - SSCC - HSS composite columns under eccentric compression
abstract: A novel hybrid Glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP)-concrete-steel double-skin tubular column (DSTC) was developed to enhance the mechanical performance of traditional DSTC and promote the sustainable use of marine materials. The column comprises an outer GFRP tube filled with seawater sea-sand coral concrete (SSCC) and an inner high-strength steel (HSS) tube wrapped with GFRP. Twenty-five specimens were tested under eccentric compression to examine the effects of eccentricity ratio, GFRP layer number, filament winding angle, HSS-tube dimensions, and SSCC mix proportions. Increasing eccentricity markedly reduced capacity, while increasing GFRP layers, winding angle, or HSS-tube size, and adding silica fume improved performance and limited lateral deflection (<10 %). Mineral admixtures were also found to influence lateral dilation under confinement due to changes in particle packing structure. A predictive model for load-carrying capacity that accounts for coral aggregate strength and filament winding angle was proposed and validated against experimental results, demonstrating high accuracy. The outcomes of this study provide valuable insights for the structural design and optimization of hybrid DSTCs in marine and coastal engineering applications.

Structural behavior of RC beams strengthened with UHPFRC layers incorporating a new tension stiffening factor
abstract: This study investigated experimentally and analytically the performance of reinforced concrete (RC) beams strengthened with reinforced ultra-high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete (R-UHPFRC) layers at both ultimate and service limit states. Four large-scale beams were tested: one unstrengthened and three strengthened with R-UHPFRC layers incorporating different fiber configurations (2 % steel fibers, 2 % ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMW-PE) fibers, and a hybrid of 1 % steel + 1 % UHMW-PE fibers). Digital image correlation (DIC) was employed to monitor curvature, crack width, and crack propagation. The beam with 2 % UHMW-PE fibers demonstrated a 47 % gain in ductility and a 112 % increase in strength, while the beam with 2 % steel fibers achieved improvements of 34 % and 137 %, respectively. The beam with hybrid fibers experienced premature cover delamination. All strengthened beams exhibited substantial reductions in the average crack width at service loads (15–38 µm) compared with the control (330 µm). To capture the contribution of the R-UHPFRC layer, Bischoff’s tension stiffening factor was modified using DIC-derived data, and a simplified equation was proposed to predict average crack width. The revised factor accurately reproduced both load–deflection responses and crack widths under service conditions, confirming the validity of the proposed modification.

Investigation of the uplift load path within the gable roof of a wood-frame residential building using a full-scale wind tunnel and non-linear finite element modelling
abstract: This paper examines the vertical load path within the roof of a light-frame wood structure from full-scale wind tunnel experiments. The global roof uplift and overturning moments obtained from integrating pressure data are in good agreement with the those captured by load cells located at the roof-to-wall connections. Examination of the uplift measured in each roof truss at the critical wind angles indicates that a large proportion of roof uplift loads are transferred to the gable end truss – more than would be estimated based on tributary-area calculations using the aerodynamic measurements. The amount of load transfer to the gable end is influenced most by the number of points of connection between the bottom of the gable end truss and the top of the wall below. The archetype roof indicates little dynamic amplification or attenuation in the range of frequencies in which typical wind fluctuations occur. Therefore, a quasi-static modelling approach provides a good indication of load transfer behaviour while being more computationally efficient than time-history analysis. A three-dimensional finite element model of the test roof is developed to further investigate the load distribution behaviour observed in the tests. Toe-nailed roof-to-wall connections are modelled with non-linear withdrawal and shear behaviour, allowing for wind speeds causing roof loss to be estimated. The results from the non-linear modelling indicate that the gust wind speeds causing failure of a typical light-frame wood roof can be increased from 165 km/h to 210 km/h by providing additional nailed connections along the gable end truss roof-to-wall interface.

title: Seismic performance of steel tubes restrained laminated bamboo columns with different cross-sections
Multi-point deformation monitoring method for large-scale steel mesh hoisting based on panoramic vision and deep learning
External load crushing strength of corrugated steel-reinforced concrete pipes: Experimental testing and numerical study
Fatigue life analysis and assessment of CFRP-strengthened CHS K-joints: An LEFM -based methodology integrated with XFEM-CZM
A generalized probabilistic method for fatigue life prediction of butt-welded joints with multiple cracks based on equivalent initial flaw size distribution
Safety analysis of floating multi-module systems under connector failure
Nonlinear buckling and postbuckling of functionally graded graphene origami-enabled auxetic metamaterial cylindrical shells under combined thermo-mechanical loads
abstract: This study analytically explores the nonlinear buckling and postbuckling of functionally graded (FG) graphene origami (GOri)-enabled auxetic metamaterials (GOEAMs) cylindrical shells subjected to combined axial compression and radial pressure in thermal environment. The analysis is conducted within the Donnell shell theory, incorporates nonlinear large-deflection kinematics, and is solved via the Galerkin method. Effective material properties are derived from a micromechanical framework using a machine learning (ML)-enhanced Halpin-Tsai model, which accounts for GOri weight fraction, folding degree, and distribution pattern. Model predictions are validated against published results, demonstrating good agreement. The parametric study thoroughly examines five through-thickness dispersion patterns of GOri, along with the effects of folding degree, weight fraction, and temperature rise. The results reveal that the X-WGr distribution exhibits the highest linear and nonlinear buckling resistance. An increased GOri weight fraction significantly enhances both the linear and nonlinear critical buckling loads, while a higher folding degree reduces stability, highlighting the role of auxetic behavior. Under combined mechanical loading in thermal environment, both elevated temperature and lateral pressure are shown to degrade buckling capacity, with uniform temperature rise exerting the most pronounced effect. The results establish key design guidelines for tailoring the buckling performance of the FG-GOEAM shells through microstructural configuration and loading considerations. These findings provide useful insights for developing lightweight, high-stability shell structures in advanced engineering applications.

title: In-plane loaded medium-scale two-sided bonded glass-steel frames – Part I – An experimental study
abstract: Demands for structural efficiency, energy performance, and architectural transparency of façades are continuously growing. A novel approach to double-skin façades through the development of hybrid adhesively bonded glass-steel elements, i.e. systems with a reduced cavity width able to transfer both out-of-plane and in-plane loads, is therefore investigated. This study particularly investigates the in-plane structural performance of bonded glass-steel elements by means of experiments. Medium-scale specimens (1.2 m × 1.2 m) comprising cold-formed stainless steel frames and annealed float glass panes are assembled using two structural silicones—Sikasil® SG-500 and DowSilTM 993—and a hybrid polymer adhesive – Soudaseal 2K. During the experimental tests both bonded and non-bonded specimens are subjected to horizontal in-plane shear forces. Results show a significant increase in horizontal in-plane stiffness for bonded elements—up to 15.3 times greater than that of unbonded steel frames—highlighting the composite action between glass and steel. The hybrid polymer adhesive, in particular, demonstrates superior stiffness and composite behaviour, attributable to its reduced optimal adhesive layer thickness. These findings confirm the potential of bonded glass-steel frames to act as structural body for self-supporting double-skin façades that contribute to the building’s stabilisation system. An additional study i.e; part II, complements the experimental work with validated finite element simulations and parametric studies. This allows for the development of analytical design tools for the preliminary design of two-sided bonded glass-steel frames in the future.

title: Structural performance of CFRP-wrapped subsea buried pipeline under reverse fault movement
Experimental research on the softening effect and shear performance of planar reinforced UHPC element
In-plane loaded medium-scale two-sided bonded glass-steel frames – Part II – A numerical study
abstract: To enhance the structural and material efficiency of double-skin façades while maintaining transparency and aesthetic appeal, this study investigates bonded glass-steel frames. The system makes use of cold-formed stainless steel and structurally bonded glass panes. This investigation builds on prior experimental research, i.e. part I, in which significant gains in horizontal in-plane stiffness through the use of structural silicone and hybrid polymer adhesives was demonstrated. This paper, i.e. part II, presents a validated numerical investigation into the critical parameters influencing the in-plane load-bearing behaviour of such structural bodies. Finite element models of both semi-rigid steel frames and bonded glass-steel elements are developed and calibrated against medium-scale test data (1.2 m × 1.2 m specimens). Parameter studies reveal that section thickness, flange width, and web height are key for the in-plane stiffness of steel frames. For bonded glass-steel frames, the thickness of the adhesive layer has a dominant influence on the in-plane behaviour. Glass thickness and web height prove negligible due to the limited adhesive stiffness and the introduction of the in-plane shear load into the frame. The study highlights the enhanced composite action achievable through careful tuning of adhesive and geometric properties. It confirms the viability of bonded glass-steel frames as load-bearing components in self-supporting double-skin façades contributing to the building’s stabilisation system. The combined experimental and numerical findings can be used for the development of an analytical tool for the (preliminary) design of two-sided bonded glass-steel frames.

title: A physics-encoded recurrent neural network inspired by Bouc–Wen class models for hysteretic behavior identification and prediction of flexural-failure reinforced concrete columns
Superior impact resistance and tunable deformation behavior of plate lattice structure via networked integrated strategy

Effect of surface profile on the bond strength of lap spliced GFRP bars in concrete beams
abstract: The splice strength of new-generation GFRP bars with various surface profiles has been insufficiently studied in the literature. This paper investigates the bond between new-generation GFRP bars and concrete using the lap splice test method. The experimental program consisted of 12 full-scale reinforced concrete beams, each reinforced with spliced GFRP bars featuring ribbed, sand-coated, and grooved surface profiles, without transverse reinforcement in the splice zone. In addition to the surface profile effect, the effects of bar diameter and splice length on bond strength are assessed. Beams with No. 6 bars showed higher bond strength than those with No. 8 bars, with ratios of 1.14 and 1.07 for sand-coated and ribbed bars, indicating a greater size effect for sand-coated bars. Beams with spliced ribbed GFRP bars showed, on average, 7 % lower normalized bond strength than sand-coated and grooved bars, with minimal surface profile impact at a longer, more practical splice length. The bond strength of sand-coated and grooved bars remained identical. A dataset of 205 experimental tests was compiled to evaluate the reliability of existing bond strength equations, including those specified in ACI CODE-440.11–22 and CSA S806–12 (R2021). An equation was proposed to estimate bond strength. The proposed equation exhibited better prediction accuracy compared to existing models across all specimen categories, including the entire dataset, specimens without transverse reinforcement in the splice zone, those with transverse reinforcement, and lap splice beams. The proposed equation achieved an RMSE of 111.9 MPa on the entire dataset, outperforming ACI 440.11–22 (142.4 MPa) and CSA S806–12 (142.99 MPa). • The bond strength of new-generation GFRP bars was investigated. • Twelve full-scale beams with ribbed, sand-coated, and grooved bars were tested. • Ribbed bars showed slightly lower bond strength than sand-coated and grooved bars. • A dataset of 205 tests was compiled to assess the reliability of bond models. • Proposed equation achieved higher prediction accuracy than existing bond models.

title: Vibration serviceability assessment of footbridges: Extending the application range of current design guides
In-plane cyclic performance of damaged confined masonry walls retrofitted with steel elements and polymer-modified mortar
Experimental evaluation of mass timber composite panel connections: screw-glued, glue pressed, and SHARP metal
abstract: The current paper investigates the performance of three glue-pressed, five screw-glued, and one SHARP metal plate shear connection configurations under monotonic loading to characterize the overall behaviour and structural properties, and evaluate the suitability of these connections for use in mass timber composite (MTC) panels. Two adhesives, polyurethane (PUR), and phenol-resorcinol-formaldehyde (PRF), were used for glue-pressing and two adhesives, PL Premium Max (PL) and PUR, were used for screw-gluing. On average, the maximum shear stress for glued connections (PL, PUR, and PRF) ranged from 4.17 MPa – 5.90 MPa, while the SHARP plate configurations had an average maximum shear stress of 1.32 MPa. Screw-glued specimens with PL Premium Max exhibited the most consistent behaviour across all the configurations, indicating good repeatability and gap-filling capabilities. The average maximum shear stress for the glue-pressed specimens (PUR and PRF) was consistently above 5.0 MPa and had higher average stiffnesses than the screw-glued PL Premium Max configuration, albeit with greater stiffness variability. All screw-glued connection configurations achieved comparable average maximum shear stress (4.37 MPa – 5.20 MPa). Both screw-glued PUR configurations (150 mm and 300 mm screw spacing) had higher stiffnesses than the PL Premium Max connections; however, larger stiffness variability was also observed. Laminated veneer lumber also showed to be a promising material for the web, with an average maximum shear stress of 5.20 MPa and comparable stiffnesses to the other glue-pressed PUR and PRF configurations with glulam webs. An initial low-stiffness region (initial slip) was observed in over half of the glued specimens and was attributed to small initial movements of the specimen within the test setup. When applied to a representative 10 m long CLT-glulam ribbed panel, all connection configurations achieved near full composite action between the elements (>96 %). Overall, all the connections studied herein showed promising potential for long-span MTC panels in terms of stiffness, strength, and constructability.

Automated standardization of bridge inspection data using generative AI
abstract: This paper presents a method leveraging generative AI and natural language processing to standardize bridge inspection data, transforming it into a ready-to-use format for direct use in condition assessment, predictive modeling, and informed decision-making. This entails capturing and evaluating severity levels of reinforced concrete bridge defects from textual inspection data, such as comments provided by inspection personnel regarding type, location, and intensity of these defects. This paper employs three models: (1) a baseline generative pre-trained transformer model, which leverages OpenAI’s large language models to process textual inspection data through an optimized prompt engineering procedure; (2) a fine-tuned generative pre-trained transformer model, which builds upon the baseline by incorporating domain-specific training before being deployed to improve its performance; and (3) a newly developed natural language processing model, which employs conventional natural language processing techniques, providing a benchmark for comparison with the generative AI models. These models are implemented and validated to standardize vast amounts of inspection data extracted from 2255 inspection reports spanning five years (2018–2022) for a set of bridges in Québec, Canada. The fine-tuned model is found to outperform other models in terms of performance, stability, and reliability in detecting and standardizing the severity of different types of concrete defects in bridge decks. It achieves accuracy rates of 98.79 % for corrosion of reinforcing bars, 99.09 % for concrete delamination, and 98.64 % for cracking, scaling, and spalling of concrete. This paper demonstrates the potential for integrating generative AI into infrastructure asset management, an application that has yet to be realized.

Seismic retrofit of corner RC beam-column joints by 3D joint enlargement method: Experimental investigation
A 3D microscale modeling method for nonlinear static analysis of stone masonry walls using mathematical programming
abstract: This study uses mathematical programming for the nonlinear static analysis of masonry walls, explicitly considering their 3D microstructure. An automated procedure is developed to convert stone masonry microstructures into rigid block models, with stones represented as polyhedrons and mortar as an assembly of tetrahedrons. Interface behaviors, such as cracking, crushing, and shear failure, are formulated as inequality constraints within a standard second-order cone programming framework, incorporating force equilibrium, failure conditions, minimization of potential and complementary energy. A unified force-based formulation is derived to support both force-controlled and displacement-controlled loading protocols for pushover analysis. The proposed method is validated through simulations of interface tests on brick–mortar samples and shear-compression tests on three single-leaf masonry walls, showing good agreement with experimental crack patterns and force–displacement curves. Finally, the correlation between mechanical properties and microstructural features of rubble stone masonry walls is investigated. The results underscore the necessity of 3D geometric feature quantification and nonlinear static analysis for accurately modeling the behavior of multi-leaf stone masonry walls.

title: Statistics-driven reliability-based robust sustainability optimization of structures under material and manufacturing uncertainties
abstract: Sustainability-oriented structural design must satisfy safety requirements while reducing embodied carbon. To provide a robust framework, this research proposes statistics-driven reliability-based robust sustainability optimization for engineering structures. The material randomness and manufacturing deviations are considered. To quantify embodied carbon emissions, statistical models of embodied carbon coefficients (ECCs) for steel and concrete are established from 317 industrial records. For efficient evaluation, a newly developed Second-Order Cone Programming Extended Support Vector regression (SOCP-X-SVR) surrogate is developed. A novel kernel function is embedded to map uncertainties and design variables to structural responses and carbon metrics at low computational costs. Two case studies demonstrate that the framework achieves substantial computational savings while meeting safety targets and reducing embodied-carbon statistics. The proposed framework is extensible to additional objectives and provides a practical route to statistics-driven reliability-based robust sustainability optimization for engineering structures.

title: Mechanical behaviour of axially-loaded reinforced CGCC columns: Testing and numerical modelling
Experimental and numerical study on web crippling behaviour of high-strength aluminium alloy square and rectangular hollow sections

Structurally optimized design for adjustable joints of lightweight reconfigurable structures based on finite element analysis
Adaptive NURBS limit analysis coupled with homogenization applied to sail vaults with orthotropy induced by variable brick arrangements
abstract: It is not uncommon to observe historical masonry vaults built with portions where bricks are laid in different preferential alignments or even different textures are used. Reasons stand in building technology needs. A stability assessment is complex, because irregular orthotropy at the macro-scale is induced by stereotomy, especially in the non-linear range. In presence of double curvature vaults, assessments are carried out by combining limit analysis and finite elements, the latter being needed to reproduce correctly complex crack patterns triggering collapse. This leads to a linear programming problem, that can be similarly used to study the crack propagation in case of springing settlement. Regardless of the source of degradation, when the vault is built by assembling portions with different textures, this may generate relevant computational issues, the analyses needing several finite elements, not affordable numerical burden and high risk of premature halting. To overcome such problems, the present paper combines in series two steps: (i) homogenization performed in the rigid plastic case with (ii) adaptive NURBS limit analysis. First, a viable homogenization approach where blocks are assumed to be infinitely resistant and non-linearity is lumped on joints reduced to interfaces is proposed to deduce rapidly homogenized masonry strength domains. Then the vaults are meshed with few NURBS and rigid-plastic spline interfaces, the latter obeying the homogenized failure resistance obtained in the first step. Mesh is intentionally rough and progressively adapted in shape to enforce at the converged iteration that some of the NURBS edges coincide with the active cracks, at the same time making sure to keep unchanged the edges of contiguous patches with different textures. The proposed methodology -here applied to a historical sail vault located in Sardinia, Italy- is characterized by a huge improvement in the analysis speed, providing realistic predictions of the load carrying capacity and convincing crack patterns also in case of settlement, at a fraction of the time needed by heterogeneous approaches.

Topology optimization of structures subjected to nonstationary stochastic dynamic excitation
abstract: The most critical loads that civil structures must withstand are often stochastic, dynamic and frequently nonstationary in nature; however, this class of loading has received relatively little attention in topology optimization of structures. Existing methods that attempt to incorporate nonstationary effects are limited in scope or rely on approximations that restrict their applicability. This paper introduces a general and computationally efficient framework for topology optimization under nonstationary stochastic excitation by modeling the load as an amplitude-modulated filtered white noise. An augmented system is then obtained by combining the structural and excitation models, which allows for the calculation of the structure response covariances by solving a first-order ordinary matrix differential equation. A key contribution of this work is the derivation of closed-form sensitivities for a broad class of time-dependent objective functions, obtained through an exact adjoint formulation that avoids the approximations used in prior studies and enables large-scale topology optimization. The approach is illustrated for two benchmark buildings subjected to nonstationary ground motions, demonstrating the efficacy of the method to obtain optimized structures subjected to nonstationary stochastic excitation. Additionally, a comparison of the optimized designs for both stationary and nonstationary excitations is presented. This comparison indicates that, for typical seismic excitations, a design obtained assuming a stationary excitation is nearly identical to those obtained considering the nonstationary load.

title: Effect of surface preparation and shear links on the interface bond behaviour between ultra-high-performance and normal strength concrete
Optimized design of steel structural systems for reduced carbon footprint and enhanced resiliency in wind

Ultimate capacity assessment of reinforced concrete half-joints
abstract: Half-joints are elements widely used in bridge construction from the 1960s onwards. They are considered critical elements since they are particularly susceptible to deterioration, and their failure may cause the collapse of the entire bridge deck without guarantee any strength reserve. The aim of this paper is to analyse the different approaches to evaluate half-joint shear capacity, comparing both analytical predictions present in main design codes and the results obtained using refined non-linear finite element analyses. The accuracy of different codes’ formulations is evaluated on a dataset of experimental results collected in literature, while that of numerical models is evaluated on available experimental tests. Numerical models are capable to estimate with high accuracy the failure mode, the cracking pattern and the load-bearing capacity. Furthermore, a parametric analysis is carried out to evaluate the influence of geometrical parameters, material properties and amount and position of reinforcement on the overall capacity of the saddles. Results highlight how code formulations provide similar estimate of the capacity of the members, regardless of the failure mode involved, and are more conservative for slender half-joints. • High accuracy of NLFEA to predict half-joint ultimate capacity is achieved. • Existing code formulations underestimate half-joint capacity of 35 % in average. • Failure modes predicted by the codes do not always correspond to the effective ones. • The accuracy of code formulations depends highly on saddles geometry (deep or slender members).

A data-driven vibration response reconstruction for damping uncertainties when generalizing from the numerical model to the experimental problem
abstract: In many engineering applications, Finite Element (FE) models are calibrated in a reference structural state but must also simulate other states. For example, vibration responses of a damaged condition may be simulated using a model calibrated on the intact state. In such cases, damping changes due to damage are generally uncertain, leading to reliability issues in the simulated responses. In this work, we present a methodology that transforms vibration responses to constant damping ratios, invariant to the structural state, using data-driven reconstruction techniques. The aim is to mitigate uncertainties related to damping caused by structural changes. We find that when vibration responses are reconstructed using this methodology, more robust features can be learned from FE data, and the simulated structural conditions generalize better to the experimental domain. The reconstruction methodology, along with a sensitivity analysis and discussion of limitations, is provided. The present work can contribute to enhancing the reliability of physics-based Digital Twin (DT) models and improving cross-domain generalization between FE numerical data and experimental structures under uncertainty. • Α novel structural response reconstruction methodology. • Reliability of state estimation using FE simulation data, for DT and SHM. • Uncertainty in damping and its changes in time-response FE simulations. • Population based scheme that is not affected by damping uncertainties. • ANN trained on the numerical population enhances its generalization capability.

Seismic soil–structure interaction impacts on damage state of infilled wall structures considering in-plane and out-of-plane behaviour
abstract: This study investigates the influence of seismic soil–structure interaction (SSI) on the damage state of unreinforced masonry (URM) infill walls in reinforced concrete (RC) buildings, with particular focus on the interplay between in-plane (IP) and out-of-plane (OoP) behaviour. A series of nonlinear time-history analyses are conducted on five-, ten-, and fifteen-storey RC buildings subjected to bi-directional earthquake ground motions. The structural models incorporate nonlinear fibre-based frame elements, a simplified macro-model for infill walls capturing IP–OoP interactions, and an Equivalent Linear Spring–Damper (ELSD) model for the subsoil. An automated element removal algorithm is implemented to simulate the collapse of infill walls during seismic excitation. Comparative analyses between fixed-base and SSI models reveal that while SSI tends to reduce base shear demands, it amplifies lateral deformations, especially in taller structures. This results in increased damage levels in infill walls, including higher instances of soft-storey mechanisms and OoP failures. The findings highlight the necessity of incorporating SSI effects into seismic design for accurate structural performance assessments and improved structural resilience. • Nonlinear seismic analysis of RC frames with URM infill walls is conducted. • Effects of SSI and in-plane/out-of-plane infill interaction are studied. • IP–OoP macro-model includes collapse via automatic element removal. • Soil flexibility is modelled using an ELSD-based SSI approach. • Damage prognosois analysis of infill and structural members is carried out.

Learning multi-dimensional sensor relationships for robust marine pipeline leakage non-destructive detection via adaptive graph networks
abstract: Marine pipeline leakages pose severe environmental and economic threats, demanding accurate and robust detection systems. Sensor network-based detection faces three key challenges: highly dynamic network structures, weak leak signals with complex sensor correlations, and strong marine environmental noise. Existing methods have struggled significantly with these challenges. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel Multi-dimensional Adaptive Graph Integration Framework (MAGI). Within MAGI, an innovative Multidimensional Sensor Edge Interaction (MSEI) layer is introduced. MSEI tackles time-varying network modeling by dynamically integrating local interactions and global context, thereby generating rich multi-dimensional edge features that overcome the constraints of traditional single-weight edges. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a Feature Aggregation Network (FAN). FAN employs a parallel graph convolutional architecture and adaptive gating mechanisms, achieving noise robustness and efficient heterogeneous data integration. Experimental results validate MAGI's superior performance. It achieves up to 97 % accuracy across diverse pressures, maintains over 95 % stability in various pipeline topologies, and exceeds 90 % accuracy under extreme noise conditions. MAGI also demonstrates extremely low processing latency and excellent generalization on highly imbalanced data. With only 0.599 M parameters, 76 % fewer than state-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), MAGI is highly efficient. This work establishes a new technical paradigm for real-time marine pipeline leak monitoring and early warning.

Reliability-based assessment of knot impact and safety factor calibration for axial timber elements with knots
abstract: Several timber design codes permit, under specific restrictions, the use of structural members containing knots to promote sustainability. However, the reduction factors currently applied to strength and stiffness properties in design are not commonly calibrated through structural reliability analyses. This gap motivated the present study, whose objective was to establish additional partial safety factors based on a reliability-based framework. To this end, tensile and compressive strengths parallel to the grain were assessed through 49,000 simulations, considering variations in knot content, strength classes of timber, and loading rates. The simulations employed the finite element method, the Monte Carlo method, and selected machine learning techniques. The proposed partial safety factors were subsequently calibrated against a target reliability index Bt = 3.10. Among various machine learning techniques, Gradient Boosting Regression achieved the highest accuracy (R2 = 0.97), enabling efficient reliability assessments. Monte Carlo simulations with 125,000 samples revealed a substantial reduction in the reliability index B as knot diameter increased. Knot-free members exhibited reliability indices of Bt = 3.61 in tension and Bc = 4.03 in compression, both exceeding Bt. In contrast, the presence of knots reduced reliability by up to 21.3% and 30.5% in tension and compression, respectively. These findings guided the calibration of additional partial safety factors based on reliability analysis, with Gw,knot values ranging from 1.05 to 1.20 in tension and 1.30 to 1.55 in compression, depending on the live to dead load ratio (L/D).

abstract: This paper presents a novel interface Finite Element for the discretization of mortar in masonry walls subjected to in-plane loads. The proposed interface model accounts for the actual thickness of the joints, employing isoparametric four-node quadrilateral elements where normal stress along the joint direction is enforced to zero. A phenomenological non-linear constitutive behavior based on experimental data is also proposed for mortar, a feature which enhances the model predictivity in non-linear heterogeneous computations. Mechanical parameters for the joints are directly derived from standard tension, compression, and shear tests performed on mortar and masonry triplets, thus facilitating practical applicability in common design. A progressive elastic stiffness relaxation algorithm is implemented to handle non-linearity and softening, making the FE code particularly fast and robust. Additionally, bricks are modeled with elastic elements, with the potential for incorporating bulk-brick non-linearity through interfaces. The developed software, FEMANOLA v3.0 (Finite Element MAsonry NOn-Linear Analysis), features a user-friendly interface for mesh creation, application of loads, and post-processing inquiries. Validation is carried out through three different examples, namely a masonry triplet subjected to shear, an in-situ tested arch, and a windowed shear panel. Excellent agreement with both experimental data and previous numerical results is obtained in all cases. • Novel interface element with thickness for heterogeneous FE nonlinear analysis of masonry walls. • Phenomenological constitutive law for mortar based on tension, compression, triplet shear tests. • Explicit algorithm to deal with softening and nonlinearity based on elastic modulus relaxation. • Efficient implementation with user-friendly interface. • Validation on diverse benchmark cases (triplet test, point loaded arch, and windowed shear panel).

title: Strain characterization and off-axis damage in biaxial fatigue testing of wind turbine blades
Improving mechanical performance of weak bolted endplate beam-column connections with prefabricated cover plate components under loading

Behaviour of glulam and CLT elements reinforced with CFRP
abstract: The popularity of wood as a construction material has grown in recent decades due to considerations for sustainability as well as the increased availability of engineered wood products. To further enhance wood’s mechanical characteristics, attempts have been made to reinforce structural elements particularly on the tension side, where the failure is brittle. This study aims to investigate the impact of various retrofitting options on enhancing the overall behaviour of engineered wood products subjected to out of plane loading. An experimental program was developed to investigate the behavior of 21 timber elements, with a focus on the flexural behavior of elements with and without the effect of multi-directional FRP reinforcement. The results found that applying a tension laminate only was not effective due to premature detachment. Extending the reinforcement to the sides of the timber element in a U-shaped configuration provided a significant increase in strength. In general, the fabric consisting of bidirectional 0/90 fibers increased the peak strength, while fabric with bidirectional 45/45 enhanced the ductility of the retrofitted element. An analytical model was developed and validated, and it was shown that the model had the ability to predict the behaviour of those retrofitted beams with reasonable accuracy.

title: Lattice discrete particle model for reinforced concrete structures: A novel geometrically consistent approach
abstract: The interaction between steel and concrete is critical in the performance of Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures. Yet, the complexity of bond-slip behavior and the heterogeneous nature of concrete creates challenges for accurately predicting fracture behavior, particularly in the simulation of failure patterns. In this context, novel modifications to the Lattice Discrete Particle Model (LDPM) are proposed herein for simulating RC structures, with a particular focus on the bond-slip behavior governing the rebar-concrete interactions. A new geometrically consistent strategy is proposed to materialize steel rebar in the simulations, enabling the realistic definition of bond elements within the LDPM framework. A bond stress-strain constitutive law and a compressive behavior model for bond elements within the LDPM framework are presented. Additionally, to realistically simulate radial stresses due to rib-induced dilation, the introduction of a local rotation angle is proposed. The derived LDPM framework is extensively validated through comparisons with experimental results from pull-out tests on unconfined and confined cylinders, as well as flexural bending tests on RC beams with lap splices. The approach is shown to accurately capture important mechanical behaviors in different types of RC elements, including load-displacement responses, cracking patterns, failure mechanisms, and bond-slip behavior at the steel-concrete interface. Further validation is shown for RC beams with varying reinforcement layouts under four-point bending loads, revealing that the proposed approach can be applicable to large-scale RC structures with varying reinforcement configurations. Lastly, a parametric analysis presents the effects of key influencing factors, including the particle distribution, local rotation angle, bond strength, and critical bond strain, on the overall nonlinear response of RC structures. • A Lattice Discrete Particle Model implementation for reinforced concrete structures. • Accurate predictions of the steel-rebar interaction are demonstrated. • Rebar-rib mechanical interlock is captured via introduction of a local rotation angle. • Extensive validation is presented by means of experimental data on independent tests.

title: Elastoplastic buckling of axially compressed stepped cylindrical shells
Testing timber columns for resistance until fire burnout: Role of thermal wave, smoldering, and active suppression
abstract: This paper presents a numerical and experimental study on stability until burnout of glued-laminated timber columns in compartment fires. In a previously reported experimental study, six 3.7 m long, 280 x 280 mm² timber columns designed for 60 min of standard fire resistance failed to survive various compartment fires, with four of the six columns failing due to thermal wave penetration into the cross section during the decay phase of the fire. Here, six additional compartment fire tests are conducted, supported by numerical simulations, to investigate the design of timber columns for burnout resistance. A finite element model is used to design the size of the columns to mitigate the effect of the thermal wave. Five tests on columns up to 400 x 400 mm² show that increasing the section size at constant loading enhances fire endurance, but the columns later failed due to local smoldering. While failure in the smaller columns was driven by the thermal wave and occurred within two hours of ignition, failure in the larger columns was caused by smoldering and occurred more than 10 h after ignition. In a sixth test, on a 280 x 280 mm² column, water-based fire suppression was used 35 min after ignition. The column remained stable until burnout, showing that early fire suppression may prevent failure of timber columns by addressing both the thermal wave and smoldering mechanisms.

title: Functionally graded engineering structures: An overview
abstract: Functionally graded materials (FGMs) are engineered composites inspired by natural materials, which have been extensively investigated over the last decade as a design concept for improving the mechanical and multifunctional performances of engineering structures. By distributing material composition, density/porosity, filler content, or geometric parameters into gradient patterns, FGMs can significantly outperform traditional composites and achieve significantly enhanced mechanical, thermal, and functional properties. This review summarizes recent progress in the development of FGMs in engineering structures involving four major categories, including functionally graded concrete structures, porous structures, nanocomposite structures, and metamaterials. The effective material property models, gradient strategies, and typical structural forms are systematically discussed in these categories. The review demonstrates the advantages of FGMs in improving strength, stability, vibration performance, toughness, thermal resistance, and durability. Challenges in fabrication scalability, numerical modelling, standardization, sustainability, technological integration, and commercial adoption are identified, and future opportunities, including the integration of additive manufacturing, multiscale computational approaches, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and the adoption of sustainable raw materials, are discussed. The article concludes that FGMs provide a versatile and promising platform for the design of advanced structural systems. Further interdisciplinary research will be critical to enable their practical applications in civil, aerospace, mechanical, and energy engineering. • Gradient strategies adopted in different FGESs are summarized and classified. • A comprehensive review of typical structural forms of FGESs is presented. • Key challenges and future opportunities for multifunctional FGESs are discussed.

Percussion-based method for detecting wall tie presence in masonry walls using deep learning technique
abstract: Wall ties are critical structural components in double-leaf masonry walls, ensuring lateral stability and overall structural integrity. However, since wall ties are typically embedded within the wall, traditional inspection methods often fail to identify their condition effectively. To overcome this challenge, this study presents a non-destructive testing (NDT) and deep-learning-enabled acoustic diagnosis framework for identifying the presence and spatial distribution of wall ties based on percussion testing. Acoustic signals were collected from in-service double-leaf masonry walls and processed using segmentation and feature extraction techniques. A comprehensive comparison was conducted using multiple machine learning and deep learning models. Among them, the mel-frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC) based two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D CNN) model achieved the best performance, reaching 100 % accuracy on the test dataset and demonstrating strong generalisation on unseen wall regions (F1-score: up to 94.1 %). Moreover, heatmap visualisations were constructed to depict the predicted distribution of tie-related features across the wall surface, which revealed clear spatial correlations between acoustic responses and tie proximity. The proposed method offers a non-destructive, data-driven, and scalable solution for the structural assessment of masonry walls. • A novel percussion-based technique is proposed for detecting wall tie conditions in masonry walls. • Multiple acoustic features and classification models are systematically evaluated. • MFCC features combined with a 2D CNN model achieve superior classification performance. • The proposed model shows strong generalisation across untrained wall regions. • The method offers a low-cost, non-invasive solution for masonry structural assessment.

abstract: This paper presents the relevant results obtained in two experimental tests with real scale steel fibre reinforced concrete (SFRC) slabs supported in vertical elements representing piles. One slab was made by regular SFRC, while the other was executed with self-stressed (SS) SFRC (SFRSSC). None of the slabs included any type of conventional reinforcements. Extensive experimental programs were conducted to determine the mechanical properties of SFRC and SFRSSC, including specimens prepared at the laboratory and extracted from the slabs. The slabs were tested up to their failure, by monitoring the load versus deflection in selected points, the width and pattern of cracks, and failure modes. For a distance between supports of 3 m (L) in the loading region, the slabs with 0.15 m of thickness supported a uniform distributed load of 45.7 kN/m2 (SFRC) and 60.7 kN/m2 (SFRSSC).By performing nonlinear finite element analysis (NLFEA) with a commercial software and the design recommendations of actual Euro Code, the influence of considering the average and characteristic values of the SFRC and SFRSSC properties on the predictive performance of the adopted model is appraised. By using the estimate coefficient of variation (ECoV) method with the NLFEA, an average value of 1.0 and 0.6 was obtained for [[EQUATION]] in the SFRC and SFRSSC slab, respectively, where [[EQUATION]] and [[EQUATION]] are the predicted design load with the ECoV method and the registered experimental failure load.

A hybrid physics-informed neural network for predicting fatigue life of axially loaded grouted connections for offshore wind turbine structures
abstract: As a critical component of an offshore wind turbine foundation, grouted connections are susceptible to fatigue failure under long-term loading conditions, which makes the assessment of their fatigue behaviour essential for the overall structural integrity and maintenance. Compared to costly experimental characterization and computationally expensive numerical modelling, there is a high demand for developing a fast, efficient and accurate surrogate model to predict fatigue life. This paper develops a novel hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) model that integrates both simplified physical constraints and hidden physical laws to predict the fatigue life of axially loaded grouted connections, where the physical knowledge is the relationship between fatigue life and fatigue-related parameters. The results show that the developed hybrid PINN model achieves superior prediction accuracy compared to the current codes of practice, the conventional Deep Neural Network (DNN) model, the PINN model integrating simplified physical constraints (S-PINN), and the PINN model integrating hidden physical laws (H-PINN). To enhance the interpretability of the model, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis and physical consistency analysis are conducted to assess the contribution of each feature to the fatigue life and to investigate the distribution of predictions with respect to physical consistency. It’s found that the new hybrid PINN model produces predictions that exhibit a higher degree of physical consistency than the purely data-driven DNN model, demonstrating the reliability and robustness of the model.

Internal resonance in rotating conductive circular plate subjected to parametric excitation within coupled air–magnetic fields
abstract: This study examines internal resonance phenomena arising from parametric excitation in a conductive circular plate subjected to accelerative rotational motion within coupled air-magnetic fields. Departing from earlier work that focused solely on coupled-field multi-modal resonance, we address velocity-perturbation-driven instabilities generated by magneto-aeroelastic interactions. By incorporating geometric nonlinearities and rotational parametric disturbances, we establish precise frequency-commensurability conditions between nodal-circle vibration modes and the natural frequencies of the plate. The governing equations for multi-modal interactions under primary parametric resonance are rigorously formulated, and explicit stability criteria are obtained through eigenvalue analysis. A hybrid analytical-numerical approach reveals two distinct dynamic regimes: (1) singlemode instabilities induced by parametric-internal resonance coupling, and (2) multi-modal interactions featuring Hopf bifurcations and transient chaos. Critical thresholds for energy transfer between coupled modes are quantified, along with parameter domains governing dynamic transitions. Results show that multi-mode frequency matching can produce pronounced response amplification, while both magnetic-field intensity and rotational speed play critical roles in modulating resonance-driven destabilization. This study contributes both theoretical insights and practical value to the vibration control of high-speed rotating machinery operating under multi-field environments.

title: Novel robust formulation for manufacturing tolerant topology optimization
abstract: Accurate control of manufacturing tolerance has long been a challenge in the field of topology optimization. Within density-based frameworks, existing analytical methods tend to only provide approximated solutions, whilst numerical methods heavily rely on trial-and-error to achieve desirable manufacturing tolerance. At the same time, these strategies assume identical topology across the upper and lower tolerance bounds, which can lead to inaccurate prediction of the fabricated outcome. This paper aims to address these problems through a novel robust topology optimization scheme, termed explicit-thickness-controlled-robust, which utilizes p-norm functions as filters to produce eroded and dilated designs from a base physical design field. The exact thicknesses are prescribed by the radii of the filters, which mimic the lower and upper bounds of manufacturing tolerance. This method is notable for its ease of implementation and meeting precise thickness requirements. The formulation is integrated with the floating projection topology optimization framework, allowing the realization of smooth topologies. 2D and 3D compliance minimization case studies demonstrate the technique’s versatility and compatibility.

Out-of-plane stability design of stainless steel I-section beam-columns under moment gradients
abstract: To address the limitations of existing design specifications for laterally unrestrained stainless steel I-section beam-columns, new design rules are proposed in this study. A comprehensive parametric study was conducted using finite element modelling to investigate the member behaviour and generate benchmark member resistances, covering Class 1–3 cross-sections and considering a range of material grades, member geometries and combined loading conditions. It was observed that the numerically derived compression-bending interaction factor for out-of-plane buckling checks decreases with more pronounced bending moment gradients, indicating their beneficial influence on member resistances. Thus, calibrated against the numerical results, a new formulation of the interaction factor is proposed, covering combined compression and uniform or non-uniform bending and ensuring alignment between member buckling and cross-section resistance checks. The new proposals are shown to provide accurate and consistent member resistance predictions for all load cases, and can be applied with the partial safety factor of 1.1 as specified in EN 1993–1–4:2025. These proposals have been included in the new version of the European structural stainless steel design standard EN 1993–1–4:2025. • Out-of-plane stability and design of stainless steel beam-columns under combined compression and bending are investigated. • A comprehensive parametric study is conducted to generate benchmark member resistances and investigate member behaviour. • Interaction factors for the out-of-plane buckling check in the design of stainless steel beam-columns are proposed. • The new proposals are shown to provide accurate and consistent member resistance predictions for all load cases. • Proposals are suitable for use with the partial safety factor of γ M1 = 1.1 and have been included in EN 1993–1–4:2025.

Experimental and probabilistic analysis of masonry cavity wall ties under out-of-plane loading with application of stochastic numerical analyses
abstract: Most existing studies on wall tie material characterisation are deterministic, and the random variability of tie behaviour which arises from the tie material, mortar quality and tie installation process were not studied extensively. This study presents the results of a probabilistic characterisation of corrugated-end cavity wall ties and a spatially variable stochastic finite element analysis of one-storey cavity wall subjected to out-of-plane loading, considering variable properties for the wall ties and masonry. The tie strengths were first tested according to AS2699.1:2020, resulting in an idealised load–displacement curve capable of describing the compressive and tensile behaviour of the tie. Suitable predictive models for the characteristic points of the idealised curve were determined by considering the goodness-of-fit of a range of probabilistic distributions, allowing the random variations in the derived cavity wall tie constitutive model to be considered. The numerical results indicated that inward loading was governed by tie failure, whereas outward loading was governed by masonry tensile cracking. Further spatial stochastic simulations indicated that the mean peak load under inward loading was 2.6% lower than the deterministic baseline of 5.46 kPa, with a COV of 0.06. While the mean peak load under outward loading was 1.4% higher than the deterministic baseline of 4.96 kPa, with a COV of 0.04. The findings provide novel insights into the development of probabilistic tie constitutive model, the interaction of spatially variable components in cavity wall systems and the subtle difference in load-sharing mechanisms under different out-of-plane loading conditions, with implications for further reliability assessment and design safety. • Experimental characterisation of cavity wall ties under compression and tension. • Cavity wall tie variability was quantified to form a probabilistic material model. • Failure mode of inward loading case was governed by tie properties. • Failure mode of outward loading case was governed by masonry properties. • Subtle differences were observed between stochastic and deterministic results.

Numerical and experimental validation of a novel force correction method for hybrid simulation applied to the partitioned G-α algorithm
abstract: This paper presents the development of a novel force correction methodology integrated into the partitioned Gα algorithm for hybrid simulation (HS). The method was applied within an experimental campaign conducted at the University of Trento on steel frames equipped with energy dissipative devices, as part of the European project DISSIPABLE. The hybrid simulation technique adopted in this campaign relies on dynamic substructuring, allowing for the simulation of the nonlinear response of complex mechanical systems by coupling physical and numerical substructures. A key challenge in the implementation of HS lies in discrepancies between actuatorimposed displacements and the actual displacements of the physical substructure, which can compromise both the stability and the accuracy of the simulation. Thus, the proposed correction allows to perform tests, maintaining the internal control of actuators even in presence of axial deformability of the specimens and bolt-hole clearance. The paper details the algorithmic formulation of the correction scheme and evaluates its performance through convergence and error propagation analyses on benchmark problems. Experimental validation demonstrates that the correction strategy yields conditionally stable and first-order accurate results. The applied force corrections remained below 30% of the total force feedback, with the required correction decreasing as seismic intensity increased, reflecting the fact that bolt-hole clearance effects are more prominent at low loading levels.

Performance evaluation of damaged corrugated soil–metal bridges strengthened with CFRP patches
abstract: Many steel infrastructure systems, such as corrugated soil metal bridges (SMBs), were installed decades ago and have reached the end of their service life, primarily due to corrosion from the surrounding environment and/or mechanical abrasion. To extend their serviceability and enhance their load-bearing capacity, various rehabilitation techniques have been developed. This study investigates the structural performance of a buried arch-shaped corrugated SMB subjected to surface static loading through large-scale laboratory experiments on three configurations: intact, deteriorated, and rehabilitated bridges. A new rehabilitation technique was implemented in which carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) patches were internally applied to damaged regions of a corrugated SMB, marking one of the first full-scale investigations of CFRP use for strengthening buried corrugated SMBs under surface static loading. CFRP composites offer several advantages for repairing metal structures, including corrosion resistance, high strength-to-weight ratio, and favourable mechanical properties, which collectively improve strength, stiffness, durability, and load-bearing capacity. As an example of the observed improvements, the internal stresses at the SMB crown in the CFRP-rehabilitated configuration were reduced by approximately 29 %, accompanied by reductions of about 25 % in vertical crown deformation and 23 % in surface settlement relative to the damaged configuration. Complementary three-dimensional finite element (FE) models were developed to simulate the SMB response under static surface loading. The numerical results were validated against experimental measurements, confirming the ability of the FE models to capture the behaviour of intact, deteriorated, and rehabilitated SMBs. The validated models were then employed to study three additional damage scenarios, both before and after rehabilitation with CFRP patches, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of CFRP in mitigating performance deterioration caused by the bridge damage. • Soil-structure interaction of flexible corrugated metal bridges. • Rehabilitation of deteriorated corrugated soil metal bridges. • Large-scale laboratory experiments on three configurations: intact, deteriorated, and rehabilitated bridges. • Rehabilitation was carried out using carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) patches applied to damaged areas inside the bridge

Direct Mandrel prestraining method for shape memory couplers: Insight into mechanics of prestraining and implications on SME
abstract: Shape memory coupling technologies offer an alternative to welded, machined and bonded joints. They provide advantages such as self-locking assembly, reduced stress concentration, rapid installation, suitability for confined spaces, and in some cases cost efficiency. However, several factors influence joint performance, including the prestraining method, heat treatment, prestraining levels, activation temperature, and wall thickness, all of which affect the gripping capacity of Fe-SMA tubes. Notably, the prestraining method significantly affects the nature and distribution of stress-induced phase transformations and residual stresses, making it crucial to understand its mechanics and implications. This study provides a comprehensive characterization of the direct Mandrel prestraining method for Fe-based shape memory couplers, an essential step in their development. Specifically, the research aims to explore the mechanics of the Mandrel prestraining method through an extensive simulation-supported experimental campaign. Using validated finite element (FE) models, a quantitative assessment of deformations and residual stresses is achieved. Furthermore, the method is used for a parametric study to elucidate the relationship between the shape memory effect (SME) and various geometric and implementation factors, including heat treatment, prestraining level, wall thickness, and activation temperature.
