Experimental investigation of a dual-spar floating offshore wind farm with a shared mooring line: Extended campaign with multiple wave conditions, improved instrumentation, and reduced mooring stiffness
abstract: Shared mooring offers potential cost benefits to floating wind farms. However, it also introduces complex dynamic interactions between multiple floating structures and an interconnected mooring subsystem. From a scientific perspective, shared-mooring floating offshore wind turbines constitute strongly coupled multi-physics systems, where aero-hydrodynamic loading, mooring-line nonlinearities, and platform rigid-body dynamics interact across multiple time and length scales. Experimental investigation of such systems remains particularly challenging due to (a) the large number of variables that must be monitored over widespread areas in the laboratory, (b) the difficulty of setting up target configurations and pretensioning models appropriately, and (c) the complexity required to introduce external forcing in the form of waves, wind, and current. This paper presents an experimental study on a dual-spar floating offshore wind farm as a continuation and complement to Lopez-Olocco et al. (2023) and Liang et al. (2024). In the present paper, substantial improvements have been introduced in the experimental setup. Specifically, the use of pulleys to transmit mooring line tension has been eliminated, the tension is now measured at all fairleads, and the motions are measured on both floaters. In addition, the stiffness of the dual-spar system has been reduced by changing the characteristics of the shared line. Finally, the test matrix has been extended to include decay tests exploring coupled surge and sway modes, as well as bichromatic waves. The present and previous configurations are still comparable, but differences are large enough that they require distinct numerical modeling. In fact, the dramatic snap-slack events in the shared line found by Lopez-Olocco et al. (2023) are not found under similar wave conditions in the present reduced stiffness configuration. Also, first-order wave frequency peaks and near-zero troughs in the shared line tension PSDs have been explained here by the dynamics of relative spar motion. Overall, the results presented aim to enhance the understanding of the floaters and mooring line dynamics resulting from shared line configurations while providing benchmark data for researchers and industry. To this latter aim, multimedia of the experiments, MATLAB format figure files with all the curves in the paper, and the OrcaFlex model file with the static setup, are made available in the link https://short.upm.es/ixe17 for general use. • Scarce experimental research on shared mooring lines for floating wind turbines. • Large improvements introduced in the experimental setup wrt previous literature. • Shared line with reduced stiffness wrt previous experimental literature tested. • Dramatic snap-slack events in shared line in previous literature not existing here. • Results suggest that shared mooring can be a practical solution for cost effective mooring.

title: Seismic life cycle cost optimization of steel moment frames with/without passive damping devices: Comparative study
Nonlinear vibrations of circular cylindrical shells with different boundary conditions: Displacement field completeness
abstract: Determination of expansion terms for the displacement field discretization in energy methods, ensuring the satisfaction of all natural boundary conditions of the system, remains a significant challenge for researchers in nonlinear mechanics. This study initially outlines modeling techniques for closed circular cylindrical shells, then presents the discretization approach of the displacement field to satisfy the boundary conditions, and gives a criterion for its completeness. An energy extremization method is employed to derive the system's equations of motion. The study facilitates nonlinear dynamic analysis of shells with different boundary conditions and expansion terms, and the method is validated through commercial finite element simulations, assessing the adequacy of the expansion in satisfying natural boundary conditions. It was found that for certain boundary conditions, such as movable simply supported and also cantilevered shells, both the corresponding beam eigenfunction and its first spatial derivative must be incorporated into the displacement expansion. Conversely, for some other cases, such as immovable simply supported ends, the inclusion of terms with the first derivative of the eigenfunction is unnecessary, and the natural boundary conditions are inherently satisfied through the variational approach.

title: Research on the fire resistance performance of prefabricated angle steel lattice concrete composite beams
Pull-out performance and damage monitoring of cast SHS grouting sleeve connection for modular steel building
Advancing post-fire confinement performance of FRP jacketing with silicon-based matrix replacement
abstract: This paper investigates a silicon-based high-temperature adhesive as a matrix replacement for fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP) to serve as an alternative solution in concrete column jacketing, to address the inherent fire vulnerability of FRP composites, and enhance their suitability for structural applications. The compressive behaviour of concrete cylinders wrapped with traditional epoxy-based FRP and silicon-based matrix (SBM) FRP is examined and compared. The behaviour and effectiveness of both FRP schemes are tested after exposure to temperatures up to 800 ℃ under steady-state conditions. The enhancement of the post-heating mechanical performance of the SBM-FRP is primarily attributed to its high thermal stability and fibre-matrix compatibility, as evidenced by simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The results show that the adopted matrix replacement outperforms the traditional epoxy-based FRP, maintaining substantial strength enhancement up to 650 ℃ exposure, in conjunction with preventing fire spread (i.e., non-flammable). The superior performance of jacketed specimens with the SBM-FRP was confirmed with average compressive-strength enhancement ratios of 2.83 and 1.89 for 500 ℃ and 650 ℃ exposures, respectively. In contrast, the epoxy-based FRP–jacketed specimens first underwent matrix decomposition at 500 ℃, followed by extensive fabric oxidation at 650 ℃, resulting in an ash-like residue of the entire jacket. The feasibility of reusing the severely thermal-damaged traditional FRP jackets was examined solely for comparison with the SBM-FRP system, thereby contributing to establishing a new benchmark. In addition, the existing confinement models from the literature provide acceptable predictions for the new system at ambient temperature, leaving a certain degree of conservatism in design, indicating the adoptability of the use of SBM-FRP at ambient temperature. The results demonstrate strong prospects for the presented matrix replacement as an alternative to conventional FRP matrices used for structural confinement applications. • A silicon-based matrix was proposed to replace epoxy in FRP confinement systems. • SBM-FRP jacketing maintained effective confinement after thermal exposure up to 650 ℃. • Superior thermal stability and fibre protection of SBM-FRP were confirmed through mechanical tests and SEM analysis.

title: Fatigue performance of hybrid DSTBs with GFRP reinforcement under variable-amplitude loading
abstract: Hybrid fiber reinforced polymer (FRP)-concrete-steel double-skin tubular beams (DSTBs), featuring an outer FRP tube and an inner steel tube with concrete filling the interlayer space, have been utilized as girders and primary structural components in bridge applications where fatigue resistance is critical. To improve flexural stiffness and crack control, this study incorporates glass FRP (GFRP) bars into DSTBs and evaluates their fatigue behavior under realistic variable-amplitude (VA) traffic loading. Two sets of DSTBs, with and without GFRP bars, were tested under an overload ladder VA spectrum derived from actual vehicular loads. The results show that GFRP bars increased load-bearing capacity by 28%, enhanced effective bending stiffness by 60.2%, and reduced maximum crack widths by 54–75% across tested load levels. Specimens with GFRP bars also exhibited 9–51% longer fatigue lives compared with the unreinforced counterparts, demonstrating the ability of GFRP reinforcement to delay crack propagation and slow damage accumulation. Furthermore, VA loading produced fatigue degradation trends comparable to constant-amplitude (CA) loading within the same stress range. These findings provide essential data for fatigue-resistant design and detailing of hybrid DSTB components in bridge and precast construction. • GFRP bars reduced maximum fatigue crack widths by up to 75% under variable-amplitude overload ladder loading. • B-F specimens showed up to 51% longer fatigue life compared to unreinforced specimens. • Residual deflection and stiffness degradation progressed more slowly in GFRP-reinforced DSTBs. • VA loading induced similar fatigue life trends to CA loading.

title: Nonlinear lateral behavior of conventional and post-tensioned CLT shear walls: An analytical method based on minimum energy principle
Homogenization of interlocking brick walls under cyclic loading
abstract: Mortarless interlocking brick structures offer great potential for modern masonry construction due to their advantages in construction efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and environmental sustainability. However, their complex geometry and highly nonlinear contact interactions present significant challenges for accurate numerical simulation. To address these challenges, this study proposes an efficient computational framework that integrates the rigid-body-spring model (RBSM) with a machine-learning-based parameter identification and optimization strategy. A homogenized model that captures the geometric characteristics of a novel interlocking brick unit is developed to analyze the dynamic response of large masonry walls subjected to in-plane cyclic loading. In this framework, the multi-linear constitutive models of the interfacial springs in the RBSM are derived and simplified from the tensile–compressive behavior of concrete, with initial control-point parameters determined based on the stiffness of contact surfaces. Using these initial parameters, sample datasets are generated via Latin hypercube sampling, followed by batch dynamic simulations employing both the RBSM and finite element (FE) models. An artificial neural network (ANN) is trained to predict the error between the two models, and the RBSM parameters are subsequently optimized. Finally, the optimized RBSM is validated against experimental results of large-scale masonry walls, demonstrating excellent agreement. The proposed numerical approach effectively overcomes key limitations in the analysis of interlocking masonry systems, providing a reliable and computationally efficient tool for predicting the dynamic performance of similar structures. • A machine-learning-assisted RBSM framework enables efficient cyclic analysis of interlocking masonry. • Machine learning automates optimization of dynamic constitutive parameters in RBSM. • The optimized model accurately predicts cyclic response of full-scale interlocking walls. • A unique three-stage failure mechanism of interlocking systems is revealed.

title: Insulated concrete sandwich panels with gradient-distributed connectors: Analytical model
abstract: Insulated Concrete Sandwich Panels (ICSPs) have been widely applied in engineering due to their excellent thermal insulation, vibration isolation, and mechanical properties, where the upper and lower concrete wythes are connected by shear connectors to achieve composite action. The degree of composite action (DCA) of ICSPs is primarily governed by the shear stiffness of the connectors. Most existing studies enhance the composite action of ICSPs by increasing the usage of connectors, which in turn degrades the panels’ thermal insulation and vibration isolation performance due to the bridging effects. To address this issue, this study investigates the effectiveness of gradient-distributed connectors along the span direction to enhance composite action without increasing connector usage. An analytical model capable of considering non-uniformly distributed connector stiffness is developed to predict interlayer slip and structural deflection under bending conditions. The model is validated through both finite element (FE) simulations and comparison with existing experimental results. The FE and analytical results demonstrate excellent agreement and confirm that a gradient distributed stiffness, where stiffness increases from midspan toward the ends, significantly improves DCA. Under the test conditions, a linear gradient in connector stiffness increases the DCA by 22.35% compared to a uniform connector distribution. Parametric studies based on the analytical model further examines the effect of different parameters, including average stiffness of connectors K ave , concrete strength, the ratio of the interlayer spacing to the thickness of a single concrete wythe C ′ / t , and the length-to-width aspect ratio of the ICSPs L/b . Comparisons among linear, quadratic, and constant stiffness indicate that gradient distributions of connector stiffness consistently increases the DCA of the ICSPs. The most significant improvements are observed with low K ave , C ′ / t , and L/b , while quadratic distribution in connector stiffness gives higher DCA than linear ones. The enhancement effect diminishes as the structure approaches full composite action. The proposed analytical model offers a practical tool for optimizing connector layouts in ICSP design, enabling mechanical efficiency while maintaining insulation performance. • An analytical model for gradient-distributed connectors in ICSPs is developed to predict slip and deflection. • Replacing uniformly distributed connectors with a gradient layout increases the overall DCA by up to 22.35%. • Quadratic stiffness gradients outperform linear layouts, particularly in panels with low initial composite action.

title: Mechanical properties and constitutive model of WAAM high performance steel circular tubes at post-fire conditions
abstract: In this study, 44 coupon specimens cut from the Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) tubes were heated to different high temperature levels and then cooled down to ambient temperature inside the furnace. Subsequently, the coupon specimens were tested to evaluate their mechanical properties after being subjected to elevated temperatures in the range of 300°C to 1000°C. The WAAM tubes were fabricated by two stock wires, the high strength steel ER120 and stainless steel ER316. The fabricated tubes have nominal thickness of 2.5 mm and 4.0 mm. The coupon specimens were heated in an electric furnace to six different nominal peak temperatures, with the highest temperature of 1000 °C. Tensile coupon tests were conducted to investigate the post-fire residual mechanical properties associated with the stress-strain curves, such as Young’s modulus, 0.2% proof stress, ultimate stress, Ramberg-Osgood parameter, ultimate strain and fracture strain. The retention factors of the mechanical properties under post-fire conditions were obtained and investigated. The retention factors were compared with the predictive curves from the literature that were based on conventional high strength steel and stainless steel specimens. The findings indicated that current curves overly provided conservative predictions to those of WAAM specimens. New curves were proposed for the retention factors of mechanical properties of WAAM high performance steel (high strength steel and stainless steel) under post-fire conditions. It is shown that the proposed retention factors generally provide better predictions than those from the current curves. In addition, a constitutive model was proposed to predict the stress-strain curves of WAAM high performance steel at ambient and post-fire conditions. • WAAM high strength steel and stainless steel circular tubes fabricated. • Mechanical properties of WAAM tubes at post-fire conditions tested. • Retention factors for post-fire mechanical properties obtained. • Curves for predicting WAAM post-fire mechanical properties proposed. • Two-stage model for stress-strain curves of WAAM tubes at post-fire proposed.

title: Incipient damage localization in thick-walled hollow cylinders based on nonlinear elastic wave scattering features

Multi-scale numerical framework for effects of fiber properties on designing composite wind turbine blades
abstract: This study presents a multi-scale numerical framework accounting for microscopic failure phenomena for the aero-structural design of a 10MW offshore wind turbine with 90 m-span blades that are made of glass-fiber or carbon-fiber reinforced plastics: GFRP (Silenka E-Glass 1200tex®) or CFRP (Torayca T700S®, T800S®, or T1100G®). Using static aeroelastic analysis combined with structural sizing and failure analysis, the structural thickness of spar caps, leading and trailing panels, and webs were estimated. Starting with the evaluation of aerodynamic force by computational fluid dynamics, the structural thickness was then updated in an iterative manner until the margin of safety for all failure modes, including matrix-dominant failure and shear/compression buckling, satisfied the requirements. The results showed that the matrix-dominant failure was observed only in the GFRP model, whereas shear buckling was more prevalent in the CFRP models. Owing to matrix-dominant failure, the leading panel of the GFRP model had the greatest thickness among all the models. Additionally, it was shown that using stiffer fiber in the CFRP materials decreases the thickness of the components, and the T1100G model exhibited the lightest structure among all the models. This study is the first attempt to quantitatively assess the impact of the material characteristics of carbon-fiber on their application in the blade structure of a 10MW-class offshore wind turbine. The proposed aero-structural design framework improves the efficiency of the digital design of wind turbine blades. • Multiscale framework bridges micro-failure and structural sizing for wind turbine. • FSI analysis by RANS for rotating blades was performed with structural sizing. • Matrix-dominant failure occurs in GFRP; shear buckling governs thinner CFRP blades. • High-stiffness T1100G CFRP achieved a 56.6% weight reduction compared to GFRP.

abstract: This study aims to investigate the influence of integrated multilayer configurations and innovative corrugated core geometries (butterfly and square) on the low-velocity impact performance of composite sandwich panels. The panels, including skins and cores, were fabricated from woven glass fiber and ML-506 epoxy resin with HA-11 hardener using the Vacuum-Assisted Resin Transfer Molding (VARTM) technique. Low-velocity impact tests were conducted using hemispherical cylindrical indenters with diameters of 10 mm and 20 mm to examine the effect of impactor size on structural response. Key parameters analyzed included contact force, total and specific energy absorption, global bending deformation, and fracture patterns, for both foam-filled and non-foam-filled panels. The results indicate that, without foam, butterfly-shaped cores achieved higher peak load (up to 1239.5 N), greater energy absorption (up to 13.429 J) and specific energy absorption (up to 0.417 J/g), and failure displacement compared to square cores. Additionally, the 10 mm indenter primarily caused perforation, whereas the 20 mm indenter induced crushing failure. These findings highlight the critical role of core geometry and impactor size in determining the impact resistance and energy absorption efficiency of multilayer composite sandwich panels.

State-of-the-art on the flexural-torsional buckling of arches
abstract: A state-of-the-art is presented in the form of a literature review of over 100 papers which describe research on the flexural-torsional buckling of arches. Early research on the flexural-torsional buckling of arches mainly focused on elastic theoretical solutions and testing with more recent research focusing on finite element analysis, ultimate strength and design equations. This paper firstly presents research on the elastic flexural-torsional buckling of arches, including the effects of temperature, pre-buckling deflections and restraints. This is followed by finite element methods for the elastic flexural-torsional buckling of arches. Inelastic flexural-torsional buckling of arches and non-linear finite element analysis are described next, followed by research on testing of arches. Finally, proposed equations for the design of arches are presented. Closed form solutions for the elastic flexural-torsional buckling of arches are generally only possible for arches subjected to equal and opposite end moments (uniform bending) and to uniformly distributed radial loads (uniform compression). For other types of loading, the finite element method employing a linear buckling analysis can be used. The ultimate load capacity for arches can be determined from testing or by non-linear finite element analysis. The conclusions summarise each topic in detail and recommendations for future research are also presented.

title: Hierarchical surrogate modeling for fragility analysis with dual-layer active learning and prior knowledge-informed data reuse
Influence of pile and soil parameters on the seismic performance of RC bridge piers: From global fragility to local damage
Design and modelling of grouted corrugated duct connections in precast GFRP-reinforced concrete structures
abstract: The design of grouted corrugated duct connections (GCDCs) in precast concrete structures requires adequate length of corrugated duct and embedded bar. Both parameters have been extensively studied for conventional steel-reinforced concrete (RC). While equations for corrugated duct length may be adapted to other reinforcement types, bar embedded equations cannot be directly applied to glass-fibre reinforced polymer (GFRP) bars due to their different characters. Nevertheless, studies on GCDCs in GFRP-RC remain limited. To address this gap, this study investigates the behaviour and design of GCDCs in GFRP-reinforced precast concrete and proposes appropriate design equations and procedures. A finite element (FE) model was developed and verified against experimental tests of column-footing assemblies. Several bond models were also evaluated to identify the most appropriate representation of GFRP-grout bond-slip behaviour. The verified FE model was subsequently adopted in a parametric study to examine the effects of bar embedded length, bar diameter, and grout strength. The results highlight the combined influence of these parameters on column performance, including lateral capacity and bar stress development. The findings demonstrate that the predictive equation for the minimum required embedded length developed for steel bars is not applicable to GFRP bars. Based on the FE results, a refined equation was therefore proposed to estimate the minimum required embedded length of grouted GFRP bars. This equation considers the GFRP bar diameter, grout strength and stress of the bar. The refined equation reliably predicts the minimum embedded length required to prevent bar pull-out.

Conductor forces on end transmission towers subjected to downbursts
abstract: Most weather-related transmission line failures are caused by High Intensity Wind (HIW) events such as downbursts. A crucial element of transmission lines’ structural integrity is the end towers, which should contain the incidents of cascading failure. The most challenging part in modelling and designing transmission lines is the conductors’ reactions since the conductors possess highly nonlinear structural behaviour. The aim of the current study is to provide simplified practical methods to estimate both the longitudinal and transverse reactions of the conductors on an end tower. Firstly, the critical downburst configurations that cause maximum longitudinal and transverse reactions on an end tower are determined through a parametric study of different downburst configurations. Then, the effects of different conductors’ parameters on their longitudinal reactions are studied. As a result, two methods are developed taking into account practical ranges of different parameters governing the conductors’ behaviour. The first method features the use of three-dimensional linear interpolation through a set of eight charts. The second method utilizes multiple regression analysis to develop a simple and accurate equation. Finally, equivalent uniform velocity factors are presented in order to calculate the transverse reaction acting on the end tower.

title: A modular assembly fabrication approach to tensegrity prism domes
Proposed new hysteresis model for dowel-type connections of timber lateral load resisting systems
abstract: The load–deformation behaviour of dowel-type connections plays a critical role in governing the seismic performance of timber lateral load-resisting systems (LLRS) such as timber braced frames (TBF). Despite numerous experimental investigations on dowel-type connections, little research has focused on developing hysteretic models capable of accurately simulating their monotonic and cyclic behaviour. This study introduces a new model, GVDHysteretic, capable of simulating monotonic and cyclic characteristics of dowel-type connections, using relatively few parameters as inputs. The model was implemented in OpenSees and validated with published experimental test results of various LLRSs. Comparative analyses were conducted alongside currently available hysteretic model, whereby the proposed model achieved closer agreement with experimental test results, particularly in simulating initial slack, loading/unloading and reloading stiffness, strength, cyclic degradation, and pinching behaviour. The seismic performance of full-scale archetypes with TBF was evaluated using the proposed model and available hysteresis models. The results of the seismic collapse assessment demonstrated that the choice of the hysteretic model and modelling methodology can significantly affect the results of the analyses at system-level. The implications of not accurately capturing the intricacies exhibited in LLRS involving dowel-type connections may cause unconservative designs being given a satisfactory outcome, as well as unrepresentative predictions of system-level behaviour during seismic events.

Experimental and analytical investigation of wind-induced response in a lighting tower
abstract: This paper presents the results of a long-term monitoring campaign on a 16.6 m steel lighting tower located at the Harbor of La Spezia, Italy. More than 5000 h of wind velocity, strain, and acceleration data were collected from which structural displacements were derived under varying wind conditions. The experimental evidence provides a robust benchmark for validating analytical gust-response models and for systematically addressing input uncertainties. The novelty of this research lies in: (i) the long-term full-scale monitoring data of a slender monopole under real environmental conditions; (ii) the combined use of strain- and acceleration-based techniques for displacement estimation; (iii) the quantification of parameter uncertainties by means of a three-level framework, ranging from code-based assumptions to site-specific measurements; and (iv) the explicit separation and quantification of model bias versus parameter bias in the dynamic response analytical estimation. Results highlight the sensitivity of the adopted analytical prediction to parameter accuracy and underscore the need for field data to support reliable assessment of wind-induced response of slender vertical structures.

title: Proposed modifications to EN1993-1-8 for resistance and yielding patterns of unstiffened T-stubs
abstract: This paper presents the results of a comprehensive experimental study on 64 unstiffened T-stubs. All three failure modes defined in Eurocode EN 1993-1-8 were systematically examined by varying key parameters such as flange plate thickness, bolt-to-stem distance, edge distance, bolt diameter, and bolt grade. The experimental findings revealed average test-to-predicted strength ratios of 1.35 and 1.21 for Method 1 and Method 2 of EN 1993-1-8, respectively. For more than 15 specimens, however, the existing design model failed to accurately predict the failure mode. Classical double-curvature yielding was observed in the majority of specimens. However, some specimens displayed a distinct yield pattern, characterized by single-curvature yielding with corner yielding—behavior not explicitly addressed in the Eurocode. To resolve these discrepancies, the study proposes modifications to geometric parameters and introduces an additional yield pattern that incorporates the observed single-curvature yielding with corner yielding. These adjustments reduced the average test-to-predicted strength ratio to 1.06 and significantly improved the accuracy of both failure mode and yield pattern predictions. As part of the investigation, both ultimate and plastic resistances were evaluated. The average ratio of ultimate to plastic resistance was found to be 2.49, indicating a substantial reserve strength beyond the plastic limit. The proposed yield pattern was also validated through finite element analyses.

title: In-plane cyclic performance and analytical assessment of conventional mortar masonry, dry-stacked ICEB, and EMM-reinforced ICEB infill walls
abstract: The seismic performance of masonry infill in reinforced concrete (RC) frames is critical for resilience in earthquake-prone regions. Although economical, unreinforced infills often fail in a brittle manner, showing signs of diagonal cracking or out-of-plane collapse. An innovative and cost-effective way to reinforce interlocking compacted earth block (ICEB) infill walls is explored in this study using expanded metal mesh (EMM). A mortar-bonded conventional infill wall, an ICEB wall that is dry-stacked, and an ICEB wall that is reinforced with EMM are the three full-scale specimens that are studied under quasi-static cyclic loading. The EMM-reinforced ICEB wall exhibited 1.56 times, 2.1 times, and 1.51 times the lateral strength, ductility, and cumulative energy dissipation of the dry-stacked ICEB wall, respectively, and 1.31 times, 2.38 times, and 1.23 times those of the mortar-bonded conventional infill wall. A strut-based analytical model is developed and calibrated using nonlinear masonry prism data to accurately predict lateral shear capacity. Its close agreement with experimental trends confirms its reliability for seismic assessment of EMM-reinforced ICEB-infilled RC frames.

title: Evaluation of time-varying dynamic properties of base-isolated high-rise building during lateral extension using monitored data
abstract: Understanding how building dynamics evolve during structural modifications is a critical challenge in structural engineering. Among such modifications, horizontal expansions can significantly alter the dynamic characteristics of a building. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a case study detailing the continuous structural health monitoring of a 20-story base-isolated building during a 16-month lateral extension project. Ambient vibration data were analyzed using the Frequency Domain Decomposition method to track the time-varying changes in the building’s characteristics. The analysis yielded several key findings. A significant shift in the torsional center was observed to be closely associated with construction events, and the real-time dynamic coupling of the two linked structures was captured through a second-mode transition. The study also indicated a correlation between the variations of the dynamic properties, including natural frequency and damping ratio, and the specific construction stages. Finally, distinct evolutionary paths were noted for the translational and torsional damping ratios, suggesting their different sensitivities to physical mechanisms, as reflected by their distinct reaction timings during the construction processes.

Eccentric compressive performance of CFST columns reinforced with annular stiffeners
abstract: A concrete-filled steel tube (CFST) column reinforced with annular stiffeners is a novel composite member that exhibits enhanced axial compressive and flexural performance owing to improved confinement. The annular stiffeners consist of curved steel connected by circular plates. This study investigates the eccentric compressive performance of such composite columns. Eccentric compression tests were first conducted, followed by the development of a refined finite element model to explore the underlying mechanical mechanisms. A comprehensive parametric analysis was then performed to examine the effects of design parameters. The applicability of existing design codes or theoretical models was also assessed through comparative evaluation. Based on the experimental and analytical findings, design formulas for the normalized load–bending moment ( N / N u – M / M u ) interaction curve were developed to predict the ultimate eccentric bearing capacity of this composite member. The results reveal that the annular stiffeners provide strong confinement to the core concrete under eccentric compression, resulting in higher stress levels in the core concrete than in the extreme compression-fiber concrete at the ultimate state. An increase in concrete strength elevates the balanced failure point of the interaction curve, causing it to approach that of reinforced concrete columns. In contrast, increasing the strength and thickness of the outer steel tube, as well as the strength, thickness, and distribution angle of the curved steel, or increasing the slenderness ratio, reduces the balanced failure point and shifts the interaction curve toward that of steel members. Comparisons with experimental results confirm the high predictive accuracy of the proposed design formulas.

title: Multi-stage energy absorption of 3D hollow auxetic metamaterials at extremely low relative density
Seismic design and response of inverted-V CBFs compliant with European and Canadian Standards
abstract: This paper describes the main findings of a research activity devoted to investigating the influence of the design rules provided in the second generation of Eurocode 8 (EN 1998–1–1, EN 1998–1–2) and Canadian steel design standard (CSA S16) on the seismic performance of chevron or inverted-V CBFs. With this aim, a parametric numerical study was carried out on a set of inverted-V CBFs alternatively designed in accordance with the above-mentioned codes, varying (i) the rigidity of beam-to-column connections in the braced bays (either pinned or moment-resisting), (ii) different levels of the design seismic intensity. Nonlinear static and dynamic analyses were carried out to investigate the local and global responses of the examined structures. Based on the obtained results, both EC8 and CSA S16 compliant CBFs exhibited a satisfactory seismic response in terms of interstorey drift and brace ductility demand distributions. The EC8-compliant CBFs with fixed beam-to-column connections showed a greater loss of lateral strength due to large P -Δ effects. On the other hand, the Canadian frames experienced more pronounced drift and damage concentration. The flexural demand in the columns can be significantly greater than the assumed design values, eventually leading to column plastic hinging phenomena as observed for EC8-compliant CBFs with fixed beam-to-column connections. Moreover, in the case of the braced spans equipped with moment-resisting joints, the columns exhibit double-curvature bending moment distributions, which is beneficial for their stability compared to the cases with pinned joints, where mostly single-curvature flexural demand occurs at the lower levels. Potential margins of improvement were identified and discussed for both EC8 and CSA S16 standards.

title: Over-height vehicle impact severity assessment for through-plate girder railroad bridges
abstract: Abstract Low clearance railroad bridges in the United States are prone to frequent impacts from over-height vehicles, which can lead to structural damage and disruptions in railroad bridge service. Current practice mandates the closure of bridges after an impact is reported. However, this approach results in traffic delays and loss of revenue for railroad owners in cases of minor impacts, which occur far more frequently than major ones. While researchers have developed approaches to detect such impacts using acceleration responses obtained from sensors mounted on the bridge, the severity is generally difficult to ascertain. Therefore, there is a need for a reliable method to assess both the occurrence and severity of impacts. Although previous studies have used permanent displacement thresholds to rate impact severity, measuring permanent displacement is challenging and too expensive to be scalable. To address these challenges, this study proposes the use of an artificial neural network model to assess impact severity based on the impact impulse, peak acceleration, and spectral energy of detected impacts. The performance of the model is further validated using both simulated and field-collected impact data from a through-plate girder railroad bridge in northern Illinois. The results demonstrate that the developed approach reliably detects and determines the severity of impacts. This solution allows railroad owners to better prioritize the allocation of limited resources towards the inspection of bridges after major impacts.

Design variables influencing the seismic performance of buckling-restrained braced frame building archetypes and simplified tools to estimate their demands
abstract: This study examines and quantifies the influence of key design variables like drift limit, brace configuration, brace angle, etc. on the seismic performance of buckling-restrained braced frame (BRBF) buildings. The effect of these design variables on peak storey drift ratio (PSDR), peak floor acceleration (PFA), mean annual frequency of collapse ( λ c ), and expected annual loss (EAL) is characterised using 25 BRBF building archetypes. Measures that increase structural stiffness, such as designing to lower drift limits and using moment-resisting beam–column connections, are shown to mitigate collapse risk and economic losses. Most of the buildings designed to drift limits above 2.0 % following conventional practice failed to meet the collapse performance objective of λ c < 1 0 − 4 prescribed by the New Zealand seismic design standard. Even fewer buildings met the loss target of EAL < 0.1 % prescribed by the NZ low-damage seismic design guidelines. Finally, simplified PSDR and PFA prediction tools are developed to enable demand-targeted BRBF structural and non-structural design for enhanced seismic resilience. These tools achieve R 2 = 0 . 95 and prediction errors below 10 %. When compared to existing demand prediction methods found in the New Zealand design code and FEMA P-58, the developed PSDR prediction model is comparable in accuracy and precision but simpler to use. The PFA prediction models, however, are more accurate and precise.

title: Conditional probability of wind and seismic hazards with applications to structural building reliability
Tensile performance of rebar welded joints jacketed with SCC and UHPC for repair applications
abstract: The replacement of longitudinal rebars through welded joints is a technique used to restore the structural performance of bridge piers damaged by earthquakes or corrosion. In such repairs, the welded joints between new and existing rebars are typically embedded in newly cast concrete. However, the influence of this surrounding concrete on the tensile performance of the welded joints has not been thoroughly investigated. This study explores this effect by testing specimens with welded rebar joints embedded in self-compacting concrete (SCC) and ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC). A series of uniaxial tensile tests were conducted. Two practical splice geometries were investigated: (i), named R4V*, an indirect butt weld supported by two short lap bars welded on one side of the joint with auxiliary direct butt welding, and (ii), named R6V*, an indirect butt weld executed against a V-angle backing with auxiliary direct butt welding, each tested at different weld lengths and bar diameters (d). Results showed that for weld lengths of 1.0d, only the R4V* weld satisfied the failure criterion of fracture occurring in the base metal. At 1.5d, both weld types met this criterion. Tests with SCC and UHPC jackets revealed that fibre-reinforced concrete sustained load-sharing even after initial cracking, delaying the failure of the embedded joint. Three mechanical models were evaluated to predict the tensile-yield capacity of the specimens: (1) Rebar-only model, which assumes the welded rebar alone carries the load. (1) Rebar + full-jacket model, which adds the contribution of the entire concrete jacket in tension. (3) Rebar + UHPC-ring model, which augments the steel capacity with the tensile resistance of a calibrated UHPC annulus; calibration showed that an annular thickness of three bar-diameters yields the best overall fit.

Bonding behaviour of steel-FRP composite bars and ultra-high performance concrete: Test, meso-scale modelling and theoretical analysis
abstract: This study integrates pull-out testing, meso-scale finite element (FE) analysis, and theoretical modeling to explore the interfacial bonding mechanism between steel-FRP composite bars (SFCBs) and ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC). Eight groups of pull-out specimens were fabricated, incorporating two matrix types—normal-strength concrete (NSC) and UHPC—and three types of reinforcement. A two-dimensional meso-scale FE model was developed, and 75 sets of parametric analyses were performed. The results show that the interfacial bond failure between SFCBs and UHPC is predominantly governed by progressive shear failure of FRP ribs, exhibiting notable ductile behavior. Compared with NSC, UHPC markedly increases both the peak bond stress and bond stiffness of SFCBs. Increasing the steel fiber volume fraction in UHPC from 0% to 2% improves the bond strength by 42%; however, a further increase to 3% leads to a pronounced reduction in the enhancement, suggesting a threshold effect of steel fiber reinforcement. As the steel ratio in the SFCB reinforcement cross-section increases, the secondary stiffness ratio decreases, the initial bond stiffness improves, and the peak bond stress correspondingly declines. Based on the parametric analysis results, a bond strength prediction model incorporating the reduction effect of the steel ratio was proposed, demonstrating good agreement with experimental results. In addition, a fundamental anchorage length model was established, determining the SFCB-UHPC bond coefficient as 0.06. Finally, a modified four-stage bond-slip constitutive model was developed, which effectively reproduces the stress fluctuations arising from the periodic detachment and re-engagement between FRP ribs of SFCBs and the concrete interface during the residual stage, as well as the gradual decay of residual stress. To facilitate practical engineering applications, an open-source, Python-based intelligent fitting tool was correspondingly developed to enable automatic stage identification and accurate parameter extraction for the proposed model.

Study on shrinkage and creep characteristics of composite bridge deck with top-mounted longitudinal ribs in steel truss girder
abstract: The shrinkage and creep of concrete in steel-concrete composite decks directly affect the structural forces and alignment during bridge construction, with this influence becoming more pronounced as the span increases. This study aims to investigate the shrinkage and creep characteristics of concrete in steel-concrete composite bridge decks with top-mounted longitudinal ribs, as well as its influence on the girder alignment during construction of long-span steel truss girder cable-stayed bridges. The on-site model tests were conducted using the Xinshi Jinsha River Bridge on the Sichuan Yanjiang Expressway, which has a main span of 680 m, as the engineering case study. Based on 215 days of strain and deformation monitoring results, the time-dependent characteristics of shrinkage and creep were analyzed. Hyperbolic power functions were developed to model the shrinkage equivalent temperature and creep coefficient for direct application in construction alignment control. The results indicate that the measured strains in both the model concrete and steel plates, as well as the model deflection, all followed an exponential growth pattern over time, increasing rapidly within the first 30 days and then gradually slowing down. A uniform cooling mode was found to match the shrinkage effect best. The maximum shrinkage equivalent temperature approached –32 °C for C40 concrete and –28 °C for C50 concrete, both of which are higher than the values suggested by design codes. The maximum creep strains of the concrete were 414 µε and 425 µε, respectively—a significant magnitude that cannot be neglected in bridge structural analysis. Girder deformations were calculated using the shrinkage and creep coefficients fitted to the ACI 209 model and compared with those based on code values. For three key stages—maximum cantilever, mid-span closure, and 10 years post-completion—the differences reached 2.6 cm, 2.4 cm, and 4.9 cm, respectively. After the mid-span closure, the maximum differences between the measured deck elevations and the calculated results based on the experimental and code-specified coefficients were 6.6 cm and 11.5 cm, respectively. This demonstrates that using the experimental shrinkage and creep coefficients enables better control of the bridge construction elevation.

title: Investigation of force-transfer mechanisms in reinforced concrete walls with construction joints using high-fidelity simulations
abstract: This study investigates the cyclic response and force-transfer mechanisms of reinforced concrete (RC) walls with construction joints using experimentally validated high-fidelity numerical simulations. Four wall specimens with varying aspect ratios, material strengths, and reinforcement details, including the presence or absence of dowel reinforcement across the construction joint, are analyzed and compared with test results. The simulations closely reproduce the observed hysteretic responses, damage evolution, and sliding behavior. For specimens with limited sliding deformation, peak lateral strength is governed by flexural yielding, and the measured strength is well predicted by the shear corresponding to the development of nominal flexural strength at the wall base. In contrast, specimens with lower aspect ratio exhibit apparent sliding shear deformation following tensile yielding of the longitudinal reinforcement, suggesting that the strut-and-tie force-transfer mechanism may not be appropriate for estimating their peak strength. Large sliding deformation concentrated within a narrow width along the construction joint activates significant reinforcement dowel action, which is the key contributor to the specimen’s residual strength and possibly produces a secondary strength peak. Both experimental and analytical results further show that providing additional dowel reinforcement may shift the critical sliding plane above the dowel reinforcement, reducing the effective aspect ratio of the upper wall segment and accelerating diagonal tension cracking, thereby limiting deformation capacity. For specimens with apparent sliding deformation, shear-friction-based models fail to adequately explain post-peak strength retention. A dowel-action-based sliding-shear model provides a more realistic representation of the sliding-induced force-transfer mechanism, resulting in an improved predictions of the maximum sliding strength.

Probabilistic system failure assessment of transmission tower lines in a changing climate
abstract: This paper presents a probabilistic framework for modelling cascading structural failures in electric power transmission tower lines subjected to wind hazard events in a changing climate. Recognizing the limitations of treating towers as isolated components, the study incorporates interdependencies among towers due to mechanical connectivity through conductors. The proposed model captures both the randomness of initial tower failures caused by wind and the subsequent correlation and clustering of tower failures resulting from structural imbalances. System-level fragility functions are derived from finite element simulations and fitted using probabilistic distributions. The transmission line system is modelled as a sequence of regular towers, with initial failures occurring independently. The failure patterns segment the system into intervals, where cascading is modelled as a stochastic process influenced by proximity to failed towers and load redistribution. An advanced virtual modelling technique combined with analytical expressions are proposed to analyse the probability distributions and generating functions of clustering of tower failures. Such that for different transmission tower line systems, the total potential failed towers and probabilities can be predicted directly under strong wind hazards. Outcomes are used for assessment on climate change risks and impacts for a large-scale transmission tower line network, which provides the foundation of decision support for climate change adaptation planning.

title: Three-dimensional finite element modelling for failure analysis of an H-rotor vertical axis wind turbine blade
abstract: The structural vulnerability of the blade component is considered a major barrier to the widespread development of vertical-axis wind turbines. To address a key challenge in the literature, a three-dimensional finite element model was developed to investigate the structural behaviour of a straight blade. In the first phase, the properties of the base materials were obtained using analytical, experimental, and meso-scale numerical techniques. Based on ASTM standards, test coupons were fabricated, tested, and digital image correlation was then used to measure elastic properties. In the second phase, the blade geometry was generated in Ansys SpaceClaim and analysed in Ansys under extreme wind and operational load cases in IEC 61400–1 standard. After validation, three model variants (I, II, and III) were compared to confirm the significance of three-dimensional modelling. The detailed model (III) was used for failure analysis for which a macro was employed to track the Tsai–Wu failure index. The macro was capable of identifying various failure modes using maximum stress and Hashin failure criteria. The three models predicted the blade deformation with < 10% difference but showed > 20% variation in von-Mises stress predictions. Under both load cases, the blade structure remained safe with a maximum failure index of ∼0.18. Close to the blade end region, von-Mises stress was maximised within the spar caps whereas Tsai-Wu index showed the shear web as the most critical component, mainly loaded with structural torsion. The failure criteria showed potential for various failure modes across different regions of the blade.

Experimental evaluation of effects of geometry and reinforcement on bearing capacity of concrete bearing pads representing substructures under spherical sliding bearings
abstract: This study examines the bearing strength of concrete pads used beneath spherical sliding bearings (SSBs) through a total of 62 tests conducted on 1/5- and 1/2-scale specimens, focusing on the effects of specimen geometry, boundary conditions, and reinforcement. The dimensional ratio H p / d , defined as the ratio of the concrete pad height ( H p ) to the characteristic length of the concrete surrounding the loading area ( d ), was found to be a key parameter, and results indicate that a minimum value of 0.6 is required for concrete pads to achieve sufficient confinement and reach their intended bearing capacity. To evaluate pads with various geometries, a new evaluation method, the Pseudo Area Method, was proposed, limiting the effective bearing area based on H p / d = 0.6. Foundation-type specimens exhibited significantly higher capacities than column-type specimens, demonstrating the structural advantage of installing pads on foundations, particularly under sudden seismic-induced axial force increases. Reinforcement was effective only when a threshold of H p / d ≥ 0.5 was satisfied. A regression-based increment factor, α r = (2.65 ρ (max ( H p / d − 0.5, 0)) + 1), was integrated into the AIJ (2022) bearing-stress formula, showing good agreement with experimental results. The findings confirm the necessity of a threshold for H p / d in pad design and support the proposed evaluation method for practical SSB applications.

Stability and load capacity of cylindrical tensegrity modules considering geometrical and material nonlinear behavior
abstract: Cylindrical tensegrity modules are lightweight self-stabilizing systems that derive their structural integrity from a balance of tensile forces in cables and compressive forces in struts. This study investigates their stability and load capacity, accounting for geometric and material nonlinearity. A nonlinear finite element model is developed to conduct a detailed parametric nonlinear analysis considering large displacements and rotations and the possible asymmetric response of the system. The deformation kinematics under vertical loading, which identifies a characteristic screw-like motion that critically influences its stiffness, post-buckling stability and load capacity. The proposed framework enables a comprehensive quantification of how topological, geometric, and material parameters govern the system’s ultimate load capacity and stability, thereby providing clear guidelines for the optimal design and reliable application of cylindrical tensegrity modules.

Through-thickness residual stress distribution in welded cruciform specimens
abstract: Tensile and compressive residual stresses induced by the welding process can lead to premature buckling and reduce the ultimate resistance of slender structural members subjected to compression or bending. The effect of residual stresses on a member’s ultimate resistance has been incorporated into current design provisions for steel structures based on the assumption of a uniform through-thickness distribution, with residual stresses equal to the average value of two surfaces. To evaluate the validity of this assumption, the present study employs a non-destructive neutron diffraction method to measure through-thickness residual stresses in welded cruciform specimens. The measurement includes three fillet-welded specimens with varying weld sizes and one butt-welded specimen. The results of the longitudinal and transverse residual stresses for the region near the weld toe reveal non-uniform, symmetric through-thickness distributions about the mid-thickness, with the maximum stresses occurring at the surface and the minimum stresses at the mid-thickness.To further investigate the residual stress distribution in welded sections, validated thermomechanical elastic-plastic finite element models were developed to predict through-thickness residual stress variations in regions beyond the weld zone of the welded cruciform specimens. Additionally, a thermomechanical elastic-plastic finite element analysis was conducted for a T-joint specimen, where the residual stress distributions in the flange and web are similar to those of a welded I-section. Notably, both the web and flange showed non-uniform through-thickness residual stress distributions in areas with tensile residual stresses at the surface, highlighting the need to reconsider the conventional assumption of uniform through-thickness residual stress in structural design.

title: Corrigendum to “On the use of 6C seismic station for bending-to-shear and torsional building response assessment at TAIPEI 101” [Eng Struct 361 (2026) 122782]
Machine learning-based residual strength prediction for quasi-statically damaged aluminum honeycomb sandwich structures
abstract: Aluminum honeycomb sandwich panels serve as primary load-bearing members in aerospace and satellite structures, but their susceptibility to localised damage from tool drops, ground handling, and runway debris remains a recurring concern for damage-tolerance assessment. Most published compression-after-impact studies address single-impact damage; the influence of multiple, spatially distributed dents on the residual edgewise compressive strength has received limited attention. In the present work, AA6061-T6/AA5056 honeycomb panels with 1–4 hemispherical indents (viz. 5, 10, and 15 mm diameter at 30 mm centre-to-centre spacing) were tested under quasi-static indentation followed by edgewise compression after indentation (CAI). A cohesive-zone finite-element model reproduced the experimental load–displacement response to within 4.7% mean peak-load error, and a six-feature physical descriptor set was used to train Ridge and Gaussian-process surrogates which interpolate within the tested envelope. The undamaged CAI strength was 329 MPa; specimens damaged with 5 mm indenters retained over 91% of this baseline regardless of the number of dents, while four 15 mm indents reduced the strength by 29.5%. A change in degradation rate was identified at approximately 17 J of total absorbed energy, separating a regime which retained over 85% of baseline from one governed by debond-driven face-sheet buckling. Under grouped leave-one-out cross-validation, in which both the held-out experimental sample and its finite-element twin are excluded from training, Ridge regression predicted CAI strength with R 2 = 0 . 92 and RMSE = 7.2 MPa; a simple lookup baseline collapsed from R 2 = 0 . 99 to R 2 = − 0 . 17 between the two protocols, owing to the FEA-twin leak which inflates the originally reported scores. The validated surrogate enables rapid CAI-strength estimation within the tested envelope of 5–15 mm indenter diameter, 1–4 indents per panel, 30 mm centre-to-centre spacing, and quasi-static loading at room temperature.

title: T-section stiffeners for enhanced ductility of flat-sided FRP-confined double-skin tubular columns: Concept and demonstration

Mechanical performance of segmental beams with staggered joints: Experiment and simulation
abstract: Segmental precast assembly is crucial for industrialized bridge construction. However, joints in such structures pose a safety challenge. Discontinuity of longitudinal reinforcement at joints weakens structural capacity in shear and flexure. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces a novel staggered joint configuration, which miniaturizes large joints, disperses small joints, and conceals transverse joints. This design breaks down a single large joint into two smaller ones. It transforms a completely unreinforced section into one with partial continuity of reinforcement. Additionally, vertical prestress is applied near the neutral axis. To evaluate performance of the new joint, nine T-shaped test beams are designed and tested under combined bending and shear. The influence of four key parameters: joint type (staggered vs. vertical), location, step geometry, and vertical prestress level, are analyzed. Compared to the brittle diagonal compression failure of beams with conventional joints, the beams with staggered joints exhibited ductile shear-compression failure. Their ultimate load increased by up to 24.4%, and their deformation capacity enhanced significantly. The stress increment in internal prestressing tendons is higher than that in external tendons, and the prestress variation curve shows a typical "bi-linear" characteristic, consistent with the stiffness degradation law after joint cracking. A finite element model is established that comprehensively considers concrete shear softening, unbonded prestressing effects, and joint interface behavior. The simulation results agree well with the experimental results in terms of failure modes and load-displacement relationships. A formula for the shear capacity of staggered joint beams is proposed based on the truss-arch model theory. This formula explicitly quantifies the contributions of the joint type (distinguished by the equivalent rib width coefficient of the arch), shear-span ratio, and prestressing. Verified against experimental values and literature data, the formula provides conservative predictions (with an average ratio of calculated to experimental value of 0.84), offering a direct theoretical basis for the engineering design of this new type of structure.

Extended analytical model for shear-loaded steel-to-timber connections with screws and profiled nails
abstract: This study introduces an extended analytical model based on Yield Theory to predict the load-bearing capacity of steel-to-timber connections with screws and profiled nails under shear loading. The model considers the deformed state of fasteners, incorporating four distinct failure mechanisms that explicitly account for the rope effect. Unlike the European Yield Model (EYM), where the rope effect is empirically defined and attributed to friction between the steel plate and timber at the shear plane, the Extended Model directly integrates the axial forces acting along the fastener into the analytical formulation of each failure mechanism. The proposed model was validated against experimental results from connection tests using profiled nails and screws with various geometries and configurations. The findings reveal that the Extended Model provides a significantly improved prediction of load-bearing capacity compared with the traditional EYM adopted in Eurocode 5 and its revised version.

title: Data-efficient memory-augmented autoencoder for real-time daily anomaly detection in bridge health monitoring
abstract: Daily anomaly detection in bridge structural health monitoring (SHM) demands models that can operate under limited labeled data, severe class imbalance, and strict real‑time constraints. This paper presents a data‑efficient memory‑augmented autoencoder (AE) framework designed for real‑time daily anomaly detection in operational SHM environments. The method employs an AE to extract compact latent features from raw sensor data, applies synthetic minority oversampling in latent space to address imbalance, and integrates a simplified memory‑augmented classifier capable of rapid adaptation from few samples. An adaptive daily update loop incorporates relabeled misclassified instances for retraining, enabling same‑day deployment. Evaluations on the IPC−2020 Sutong Bridge dataset and a newly labeled Yonghe Bridge dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach matches or exceeds the accuracy of state‑of‑the‑art baselines while reducing daily update time to under 40 s. By combining smart sensing, efficient learning, and scalable deployment, the framework supports resilient SHM systems capable of timely fault detection and continuous infrastructure safety assessment.

title: Ensemble machine learning with Bayesian optimization for vehicle–bridge pier impact force prediction from structural responses
Study on flexural behavior and bearing capacity calculation method of concrete-filled double-skin steel tubes
Evaluation of load-carrying capacity of horizontal joints in concrete wind turbine towers
abstract: Concrete wind turbine towers are typically subjected to complex combined loading, including compression, bending, shear, and torsion, due to wind actions and prestressing forces. However, current design methodologies are inadequate for accurately assessing the load-carrying capacity of horizontal joints under such multi-axial stress conditions. To accurately evaluate the load-carrying capacity of horizontal joints in concrete wind turbine towers subjected to combined compression, bending, shear, and torsion, three scaled-down concrete tower specimens were tested under representative multi-axial loading conditions. The failure modes, load-displacement responses, and other key parameters were measured and analysed. The results demonstrated that the torsional and shear resistance of the horizontal joint regions was primarily governed by the frictional force developed at the joint interface as a result of prestressing. While higher prestress level enhanced the ultimate load-carrying capacity, they also led to a reduction in the ductility of the specimens. A refined finite element (FE) model was subsequently developed in ABAQUS and calibrated against the experimental results. Building upon established calculation methods for evaluating the torsional and flexural capacities of horizontal joints in concrete towers, and based on the fundamental form of the interaction equation for structural load-carrying capacity under combined loads, a new analytical framework was established to evaluate the load-carrying capacity of horizontal joints under combined loading conditions. Based on the refined FE model, a series of parametric numerical analyses were performed. Subsequently, the coefficients in the proposed evaluation equations were calibrated using the numerical simulation results, leading to the development of a comprehensive method for evaluating the load-carrying capacity of horizontal joints.

title: Seismic performance-based design of shear pins in double spherical surface isolation bearings for railway bridges
DIC analysis of unreinforced masonry panels under diagonal compression using virtual gauges and damage indicators
abstract: Masonry walls subjected to seismic events experience in-plane loadings, primarily inducing diagonal forces. The ASTM-standardized diagonal compression test replicates these conditions on square masonry panels to investigate failure mechanisms and determine the diagonal tensile strength. Conventional methods measure strains along the diagonals but lack accuracy in representing damage mechanisms in heterogeneous materials like masonry due to their localized nature. To overcome this limitation, Digital Image Correlation (DIC) has emerged as a robust, contactless technique for full-field measurement of surface displacements. This method provides rich insights into strain fields and crack propagation across the specimen. In this study, DIC data are processed through an adapted methodology to quantify mesoscopic damage distinguishing mortar and blocks, providing deeper insights into the heterogeneous masonry behavior under diagonal compression.

title: Experimental and numerical investigation of shear buckling behaviour of friction stir welded 6013-T6 aluminium H-shaped beams
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) facilitates the fabrication of aluminium alloy H-shaped beams, with thin webs for lightweight bridge and building structures, however, the shear buckling behaviour of such members and appropriate design rules remain insufficiently characterized. Six FSW 6013-T6 aluminium alloy H-shaped beams were tested under shear-dominated loading, with variations in weld configuration and end restraint conditions. The shear buckling modes, tension-field development, load-displacement responses and ultimate shear buckling bearing capacities were comprehensively recorded. The refined finite element (FE) models, incorporating FSW softening, residual stresses and initial geometric imperfections, were developed and validated against experimental results. A parametric study involving 798 models was then performed to quantify the effects of web slenderness, web aspect ratio, weld properties (strength, width and location) and end restraint on post-buckling shear resistances. The combined test and numerical database were used to evaluate the shear design provisions in EN 1999–1–1:2023 and ADM 2020, which were found to yield conservative predictions by over 26.6–42.2%, with increasing scatter at higher web slenderness. To improve design accuracy while retaining the existing code framework, modified shear design formulations were proposed for both EN 1999–1–1 and ADM 2020, and a dedicated shear design curve was developed within the direct strength method (DSM) framework. The modified test/FE-to-prediction ratios concentrated within the range of 1.002–1.202, with COVs of 0.05–0.18, providing a rational basis for the design and potential codification of FSW 6 × ×× -series aluminium alloy structural members.

title: Experimental investigation on the hysteretic behavior of concrete-filled steel tubes with defects representing local corrosion
From constitutive models to shear capacity prediction: A comparative review of international design provisions for ultra high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete beams
Performance of self-tapping screw connections under moisture content change
abstract: Self-tapping screws are widely used in timber connections due to their ease of installation and reliable mechanical performance. However, moisture variations during construction can significantly affect the performance of these connections. Changes in moisture content in steel-to-wood connections may induce additional stress on self-tapping screws, potentially compromising structural integrity. This study investigates the short-term performance of self-tapping screw in steel-to-glulam connections, focusing on the effects of installation torque and moisture-induced dimensional changes in glulam. Experiments were conducted to quantify the axial load generated by torque and to assess the additional load induced by wood swelling due to moisture content increase. During wood shrinkage in drying condition, however, a reduction in axial load was observed, and no screw failure occurred in any test scenarios. Additionally, a finite element model was developed to simulate the connection response to moisture content change. The simulation successfully captured the development of stress in the screws caused by torque and moisture content increase. The results indicate that the combination of torque and swelling can increase axial stresses up to 60% of the ultimate tensile capacity of the screw.

title: Field measurements of the structural response of a linked twin-tower super-tall building during two typhoons
A novel voice coil actuator for active mass damping systems: Design, mechanism, and compensation

Experimental investigation of a novel SMA-friction self-centering brace with adjustable mechanical characteristics
abstract: To achieve an optimal balance between self-centering capability and energy dissipation performance, this study proposes and experimentally evaluates an adjustable SMA-Friction Self-Centering Brace (SFSCB), comprising NiTi shape memory alloy (SMA) cables arranged in parallel with frictional components. The working mechanism of the SFSCB is introduced, and its adjustable advantages over conventional SMA cable bracing are discussed. A series of cyclic loading tests were conducted under various conditions to investigate the effects of adjustable pre-pressure in frictional components, initial pre-tension in SMA cables, as well as loading frequency and loading displacement on the SFSCB behavior. The SFSCB exhibited flag-shaped hysteresis loops, excellent self-centering ability, stable energy dissipation, and minimal residual deformation. Increasing frictional force significantly enhanced the energy dissipation capacity with minimal impact on the self-centering behavior. The pre-tension in SMA cables contributed to reduced residual deformation and improved transition stiffness, while its influence on peak strength was limited. The SFSCB was found to be insensitive to frequency effects, achieving a maximum strain of 12.4% and a peak strength of 172.4 kN. Fatigue tests further demonstrated that, despite progressive degradation of SMA cables, stable frictional dissipation provides pronounced energy dissipation redundancy, ensuring sustained seismic performance. The findings highlight the SFSCB’s suitability for seismic-resilient structures by showing that its hybrid mechanism enables precisely controllable energy dissipation and a recentering capacity that can be tuned from partial to full self-centering.

Cyclic drift capacity and modeling of slab-column connections with and without shear reinforcement
A method for devising omnidirectional inelastic response models from uniaxial behavior
abstract: There is a wide variety of nonlinear hysteretic numerical models for simulating the mechanical responses of structural and geotechnical components or subsystems. A large subset of these models is constructed to offer only uniaxial responses and is typically packaged as zero-length macroelements. When multi-axial responses are required, these uniaxial elements are attached orthogonally to the host structural model and offer uncoupled reactions. In nonlinear loading regimes, this approach yields inaccurate estimates of both the directions and magnitudes of the reaction forces, with the latter occasionally exceeding the intrinsic capacity/strength of the modeled medium or component. A framework based on multi-surface plasticity is offered herein to address the problem. Specifically, omnidirectional macroelement models are proposed, and examples are implemented in ABAQUS for p-y models used in pile-soil interaction analyses and triple friction pendulum (TFP) bearings. The developed p-y model is verified against three-dimensional continuum finite element simulations of a laterally loaded pile embedded in sand, and the omnidirectional TFP model is validated against laboratory test data. The proposed approach can be applied to other similar problems by recalibrating the yield surfaces and hardening rules to match the uniaxial backbone curve and by adjusting the unloading-reloading rules.

title: Joint estimation of railway ballasted track irregularities and stiffness using dual Kalman filter strategy and dynamic vehicle-track model
abstract: Track irregularities and support stiffness are key parameters for running safety and structural health monitoring (SHM) of ballasted railway lines. Most existing approaches focus on track irregularity identification, however, the measured response is typically coupled with stiffness variations (e.g., ballast or support degradation, track defects), leading to biased irregularity estimates. To address this, this paper presents a Kalman filter (KF)-based framework that jointly estimates vertical track geometry and support stiffness from on-board measurements on ballasted tracks. The method is built on the KF framework with a multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) vehicle–track observation model, using wheelset accelerations (ABA) and bogie motions as measurement inputs. The stiffness parameter is updated through a frequency-domain indicator extracted from the ABA response in the KF framework. Numerical validations show that the filter achieves stable identification of both track geometry and stiffness across a wide range of noise levels. In practical on-board measurements, the available sampling frequency is often lower than that required to run the MDOF model. Interpolation is therefore employed to reconstruct the measurement signals at a resolution compatible with the model. The analysis follows a procedure involving down-sampling, noise contamination, and subsequent interpolation of the measured signals. Four different interpolation methods are applied and compared. The results show that spectrum zero padding achieves the most accurate stiffness estimation, as it preserves the frequency content around the observed resonance, and the effect of interpolation on the irregularity estimation is limited. These findings suggest that the proposed dual KF framework provides a feasible model-based approach for simultaneous geometry and stiffness estimation, and can be potentially extended to field applications with appropriate tuning of the dynamic model and process noise.

title: Nonparametric and deep learning methods for long-term monitoring of Strain Influence Lines under environmental and damage effects
Experimental dynamic out-of-plane response of masonry buildings: mechanism activation, progression, and collapse
abstract: Many uncertainties are related to the seismic out-of-plane (OOP) response of unreinforced masonry (URM) structures. Challenges include the prediction of the triggering acceleration, velocity, and their role on the final collapse mechanism. To date, shake-table tests have investigated limited boundary condition scenarios, and the common unrestrained wall-to-wall and wall-to-diaphragm connections lack investigation. These conditions lead to hybrid two-way bending, a response featuring simultaneous rocking and horizontal bending, so far observed only in a static environment. This paper discusses an extensive shake-table campaign comprising 211 tests to observe the OOP response of URM specimens with no top horizontal connection subjected to structural and input variations. A novel methodology combining dynamic testing and Digital Image Correlation (DIC) techniques is proposed. Mechanism interaction is addressed in three instances, namely activation, progression, and near-collapse. Results demonstrate the existence of hybrid two-way bending, characterised by sustained horizontal one-way bending cycles, and short, sudden rocking events. Five distinct collapse mechanisms are observed, thereby strengthening the literature on the issue. The campaign has generated a robust experimental dataset, which supports validation of analytical and numerical models, as well as further probabilistic analyses (i.e., fragility analysis).

Comparison between homogeneous beech and hybrid beech-silver fir glulam beams made with short supply chain timber
abstract: The growing request of timber for high performance constructions coupled with the depletion of conifer resources due to the ecosystem modification caused by global warming, makes it necessary to explore alternative supply sources. Additionally, the increased emphasis on sustainability within the supply chain has strongly influenced the worldwide relaunch of small local businesses, aiming to provide regionally sourced materials while reducing environmental impact and fostering economic resilience. This study investigates the mechanical properties and bonding quality of homogeneous beech and hybrid beech-silver fir glulam beams produced using short supply chain timber from Southern Italy. This research aims at demonstrating the feasibility of a local production using underused hardwood species as beech. Mechanical characterization included bending and shear tests, as well as evaluations of finger joint and glue line performance. The achieved evidence demonstrated the goodness of both configurations that meet or exceed the standards for structural timber. In particular, the hybrid configuration proved to have comparable mechanical properties for homogeneous and hybrid beams while being lighter and more material-efficient.
