Bonding quality assessments revealed that finger joints performed satisfactorily for both species, with values exceeding the characteristic strength of the respective timber grades. Glue line strength was comparable to other literature results, though homogeneous beech beams faced challenges in delamination resistance, highlighting the need for further adhesive optimization. Conversely, hybrid beams exhibited superior bonding durability, effectively addressing hardwood gluing challenges. This research proved the potential of hardwood use for the realization of engineered products for structural applications; it also highlights the potential of hybrid configurations in optimizing material performance to realize high-performance structural components while supporting local timber supply chain. Future research should refine bonding techniques for hardwood glulam and explore alternative adhesives to further improve durability and performance.

title: Innovative V-shaped buckle-based in-situ joint reinforcement technology for the transmission tower: Mechanistic synergy and quantitative tensile capacity enhancement
Deformation mechanisms and quasi-static energy absorption of three-directional elliptical re-entrant lattice structures
Constraint-based regulation of dynamic characteristics for aerospace pipes with complex shapes
Research on the constitutive bond-slip model and design methods of steel plate-rebar lap splices
Seismic response reconstruction of high-speed railway bridges using wavelet neural operators with multi-head attention based on sparse measurement data
Toward a general and reliable application of overstrength in timber engineering
abstract: Capacity design is fundamental to achieve ductile structural behaviour, yet its implementation in timber engineering remains challenging due to the material’s inherent variability and brittleness. Existing definitions of the overstrength factor – whether based on the load-and-resistance factor design (LRFD) framework or derived from component-level structural reliability analysis – often fail to ensure the intended failure hierarchy or result in uneconomic designs. This paper revisits the concept of overstrength, focusing on the unique characteristics of timber structures, where ductility is typically provided by steel connectors with negligibly varying properties while properties of timber components exhibit significantly greater stochastic variability. A new system-based reliability concept is introduced that simultaneously accounts for interactions between actions, ductile capacities, and brittle capacities. By linking target failure probabilities for ductile and non-ductile components, the proposed definition ensures that brittle failure remains consistently less likely than ductile yielding, even in cases where the variability of the brittle, non-ductile components is much higher than of the ductile component, as common in timber engineering. A comprehensive parametric study involving 60 cases evaluates the influence of load ratios, model uncertainty, and variability in actions and capacities within structural reliability analyses. The outcome from the structural reliability-based overstrength formulation was converted into overstrength factors applicable within the LRFD framework. Results show that current overstrength provisions may be insufficient or conservative, whereas the proposed approach provides a more reliable, transparent, and adaptable basis for future code development.

title: Experimental investigation on connection response of frameless cold-formed steel corrugated walls
Experimental investigation of ultimate lateral resistance of superstructure–steel pipe pile foundation–soil systems considering local buckling–induced strength deterioration of pile members
abstract: Steel pipe piles supporting buildings may lose lateral resistance during strong earthquakes because local buckling at pile heads degrades member strength under high axial force. Although the lateral resistance of single piles and pile groups has been widely studied, a rational framework for evaluating the ultimate lateral resistance of superstructure–pile foundation–soil systems while accounting for local buckling–induced strength deterioration is still lacking. This study proposes such a framework by integrating experimentally identified collapse mechanisms, finite element evaluation of degraded pile bending resistance, and virtual-work-based system analysis. Centrifuge lateral loading tests on two-pile foundations embedded in sand revealed that the ultimate state is governed by a two-hinge mechanism in each pile and that system collapse is triggered by hinge formation in the embedded portion of the back pile after progressive axial force redistribution and pile-head local buckling. Based on these observations, finite element analyses were used to quantify the degraded bending moment after local buckling through a plasticity-ratio-based procedure, and the system ultimate lateral resistance was then evaluated by accounting for the internal work of both piles and soil, including group pile effects. The study demonstrates that local buckling–induced deterioration is a decisive factor in the maximum lateral resistance of steel pipe pile foundation systems and provides a mechanics-based basis for performance-based design of building pile foundations.

title: Bridge influence line identification using convex programming from Bridge Weigh-in-Motion strain signals
abstract: The influence line for a point on a structure shows how shear force or bending moment, or typical strain components, at that point changes as a unit load moves along the structure. The bridge influence line can be used in Bridge Weigh-in-Motion (BWIM) systems and Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) systems. Influence line identification from measurement data is a possible alternative to Finite Element Method-based solutions since measurement-based approaches do not need model validation, and expertise in numerical modelling. A novel convex programming-based influence line identification method is introduced in this paper. Its comparison with previous methods is also executed showing that this novel method results in 0.46% lower Over Relative Errors, while the Amplitude Relative Errors increase by 0.06% in different scenarios compared to the best state-of-the-art methods. The decrement in Overall Relative Error is even higher (0.82%) under high noise level conditions while the Amplitude Relative Error increment (0.09%) is kept low. Robustness tests are also conducted by introducing varying levels of noise to axle loads, vehicle location, and strain signals. Finally, the proposed method is also evaluated experimentally.

title: A latent diffusion model based generative AI framework for the inverse design of additive manufactured lattice structures
Development and mechanical evaluation of stress-line inspired ribbed timber slabs with stay-in-place formwork
Interlayer cracking-induced crushing performance degradation and anisotropy in FDM-printed TPMS lattices
Mainshock-aftershock fragility and risk analysis for RC frame structures based on Bayesian networks
Damage quantification of RC beam-column joints under beam-end impact: A criterion based on deformation
Interaction of the rocking steel interconnection with intra-connections in a moment resisting modular joint
abstract: The structural behaviour of modular joints in prefabricated prefinished volumetric construction (PPVC) can be highly influenced by the interactions between interconnections (module-to-module) and intra-connections (beam-to-column). A joint featuring a novel Rocking Steel Interconnection (RSI) has recently been developed, and experimental investigations of its interaction with a single intra-connection have shown promising results. However, the behaviour of the RSI when engaged with two intra-connections has not yet been investigated. To address this, the present study conducted a full-scale cyclic test on a specimen incorporating an RSI and two intra-connections. Subsequently, a numerical model was developed to assess the effects of key parameters governing this interaction, including beam size, axial load, and beam length. The experimental results revealed a wide hysteretic response attributed to plastic hinge formation at the intra-connections. The presence of the ceiling beam redistributes the moment, reducing the demand on the RSI. The FE parametric analysis further demonstrated that the ratio of floor beam to ceiling beam sizes in a joint plays a critical role in distributing moments among the connections. The axial load also improves the joint performance till it does not exceed the column compressive buckling capacity. Nevertheless, using shorter beams could alter the sequence of failure modes and interfere with the axial load efficiency.

title: Axial compressive behavior of CFRP-confined Scrimber column
abstract: The limited availability of high-quality natural timber has stimulated the development of engineered wood products for structural applications. Scrimber, a veneer-based composite manufactured from fast-growing timber, exhibits high strength and dimensional stability but remains prone to brittle splitting under compression. This study experimentally investigates the axial compression behavior of circular and square Poplar Scrimber columns confined with carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP). Test results show that CFRP confinement significantly enhances the peak compressive stress, deformation capacity, and post-peak stability of Scrimber columns, while altering the failure mode from tensile splitting and delamination to shear-dominated failure and localized compression crushing. Circular columns exhibit greater confinement efficiency than square columns due to more uniform confinement effectiveness in square sections. Increasing CFRP thickness improves axial performance up to an optimal level; further increases lead to pronounced out-of-plane deformation prior to peak stress, limiting additional enhancement and reflecting a competition between strength gain and stability loss. Based on the experimental results, an empirical model is proposed to predict the peak compressive stress of CFRP-confined Scrimber columns, incorporating nonlinear confinement efficiency, strain effectiveness, and sectional shape effects. The model shows good agreement with test data and provides a rational basis for the analysis and preliminary design of CFRP-confined Scrimber columns.

title: SeisCFM: Conditional flow matching for three-component ground motions with engineering fragility validation
Experimental and theoretical study on flexural behavior of SCC-UHTCC composite beams
Flexural behavior and interfacial debonding of RC beams strengthened with CFRP-reinforced Engineered Geopolymer Composites (EGC)
Post-fire compressive behavior and validated thermal elastic-plastic modeling of SBHS500 girder-end components subjected to localized thermal histories
abstract: Localized bridge fires create steep thermal gradients near girder ends where compressive stability can govern post-fire decisions. This study investigates welded SBHS500 (Steels for Bridge High-performance Structures; yield strength of 500 N/mm 2 ) cruciform components subjected to localized thermal histories and develops a validated sequential thermal elastic-plastic finite element (FE) framework for post-fire assessment. Eight specimens were heated over the lower quarter to 600 or 900 °C and then water- or air-cooled. Permanent out-of-plane deformations, residual stresses, and monotonic compressive responses were measured; complementary tensile tests quantified cooling-dependent retained properties for regions heated above the A1 transformation temperature. Heating to 600 °C followed by water cooling caused negligible changes (-1.4% stiffness and −1.0% peak load). Severe exposure at 900 °C reduced peak resistance by 12.0% after water cooling and 25.5% after air cooling and produced pronounced local imperfections. Relative to the intact tensile-test means, retained yield strength increased by 24.7% after 900 °C water cooling but decreased by 43.9% after 900 °C air cooling, confirming the need for cooling-dependent property updates. The FE framework incorporating welding, prescribed temperature histories, geometric nonlinearity and spatially varying retained properties predicted stiffness within 1.0–1.6% and peak resistance within 3.0–7.6%. Parametric analyses show that neglecting retained-property updates can overestimate resistance by 6.8–42.3%, whereas residual stress effects remain below 5%. This work fills a gap by providing component-level post-fire stability evidence for SBHS500 under localized thermal histories.

title: Predictability of numerical models for reciprocal structures
abstract: Scientific literature shows that the actual behaviour of metallic reciprocal structures can differ significantly from that predicted by numerical models. This discrepancy is mainly due to the connections, whose complex designs generally exhibit nonlinear behaviour, including friction, locking effects, and semi-rigid responses. When the connections are perfectly rigid, as in welded beams, the structure is referred to as a gridshell, which is not the subject of this paper. Conversely, a reciprocal structure is theoretically composed of stacked beams and therefore features perfectly hinged (pinned) connections. In this article, we demonstrate that hinged connections enable a reliable numerical model. We develop a connection consisting of a spherical hinge assembled to rods attached to the ends of the bars, and we propose a methodology for integrating this connection into a numerical model to obtain reliable computational results. To achieve this, large-scale steel structural prototypes equipped with such a connection were constructed and tested. The results show a strong similarity between the numerical and experimental values of displacements and stresses. The experimental measurements were performed using a redundant measurement system, notably a motion capture system, which is highly effective for measuring threedimensional displacements and had never previously been used for reciprocal structures.

title: Machine learning-based optimization on CFRP repairs for earthquake-damaged round-ended hollow piers in a high-speed railway bridge
Generalization assessment of data-driven hydroelastic models for flexible offshore structures across distinct sea states
abstract: Fast and reliable prediction of hydroelastic responses is essential for the design and monitoring of flexible offshore structures, yet conventional simulation tools struggle to capture nonlinear and stochastic wave effects efficiently. This study develops a data-driven surrogate based on long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to predict hydroelastic responses of a top-fixed flexible cylinder in irregular seas. Using two sea states with similar spectral characteristics but different nonlinearity levels, we conduct a systematic, experimentally validated assessment of model generalization through within-sea-state validation and cross-sea-state transfer assessment. Results show that while the surrogate performs accurately within its training sea state, its ability to generalize depends strongly on the nonlinear characteristics of the training data. A model trained on the more nonlinear sea state transfers effectively to the milder one, whereas the reverse leads to significant underprediction of peak responses. The findings demonstrate the importance of nonlinear exposure in training datasets and provide practical insight for constructing robust, fast surrogate models for hydroelastic prediction in offshore engineering applications.

title: Negative stiffness-based retrofit strategy for bridges accounting for soil–structure–interaction effects
abstract: This study presents a soil-consistent seismic retrofit strategy for seismically isolated bridges based on the implementation of extended KDampers (EKDs) installed in parallel with the isolation bearings. A three-span isolated bridge is modeled through an SSI-consistent dynamic formulation incorporating sway–rocking foundation behavior, enabling explicit representation of soil flexibility and its interaction with supplemental vibration control devices. The EKD is designed through a constrained optimization performed independently for EC8 soil types A, B, C and D. The excitation input used during optimization consists of soil-specific sets of spectrum-compatible artificial accelerograms. Engineering performance criteria, stability requirements associated with the negative stiffness element, and manufacturing limitations are enforced within the optimization loop. The optimized retrofit configurations are subsequently assessed using both artificial accelerogram sets and soil-adjusted real earthquake records. The performance of the proposed EKD system is comparatively evaluated against conventional lead rubber bearings (LRB) and tuned mass dampers (TMD). Numerical results demonstrate that the EKD consistently provides superior mitigation of deck displacements and accelerations across all soil conditions considered.

title: Experimental study on the seismic behavior of innovative hybrid FRP-steel reinforced self-centering shear wall under different axial compression ratios
Blast response of lunar regolith-GUHPC arch structures under propellant explosion
Seismic performance of light timber frame structures with sheathing and cladding: Experimental shake table tests
abstract: This paper presents dynamic and seismic tests on a two-storey light timber frame structure with OSB sheathing and additional gypsum fibre board cladding on a biaxial shake table. The work is part of the HELEPOLIS research project on the influence of fire protective cladding on the lateral load-carrying behaviour of light timber-framed walls. The test specimen was investigated with sheathing only and with additional cladding. The experimental programme comprised white-noise and impulse excitations to identify dynamic properties, as well as increasing seismic excitations up to structural failure for the cladded setup. The main objectives were: (i) quantifying the amplitude dependence of the dynamic properties; (ii) identifying the influence of cladding on stiffness and resistance; (iii) characterising the nonlinear response and failure mode of the cladded structure; and (iv) assessing vibration-based indicators for damage detection. The results show that the natural frequencies decrease with increasing amplitudes while damping ratios increase significantly. The additional cladding increases the stiffness of the structure significantly. At the same time, it can lead to higher base shear and hold-down forces, which may critically affect the design of non-ductile elements. The experimental data underline the need to explicitly consider claddings in the seismic design of light timber frame structures. Under seismic excitations incrementally scaled up to a peak ground acceleration of 0.98 g, the failure of the 2nd storey is governed by ductile failure of the stapled sheathing-to-framing connection. The failure is preceded by a marked reduction of natural frequencies. In addition, a comprehensive dataset is provided.

title: Investigation of the oblique impact and ricochet behavior and dynamic response characteristics of long-rod kinetic energy projectiles against concrete targets
Axial-flexural mechanism and design method of grouted connection for high-rise modular steel structures: Numerical and theoretical analysis
Transfer learning-based prediction of impact force-time histories for larger-scale RC beams
Effect of fiber type on pull-out and shear strengths of various cast-in connectors in thin UHPFRC panels of different thicknesses
abstract: Ultra-High Performance Fiber-Reinforced Concrete (UHPFRC) enables a reduction in the overall volume of concrete required to satisfy structural requirements, leading to lightweight thin structural elements suitable for a variety of applications. This paper investigates the pull-out ( P u ) and shear strength ( V u ) of 48 cast-in connectors in ultra-thin UHPFRC panels ranging from 15 to 38 mm in thickness and reinforced with 2% steel fibers. Results were compared with counterparts reinforced with 2% polyoxymethylene (POM) fibers, which could be advantageous in terms of fire resistance and reduction in concrete spalling in building wall applications due to the increase in gas permeability under higher temperatures reaching up to 600 ℃ ℃ . The study examined three types of connectors, namely headed and L -shape bolts and headed inserts. It was shown that pull-out and shear strengths of cast-in connectors in panels with steel fibers range from 2.1 to 2.4 times those with POM fibers. Head diameter of the connector directly affects pull-out strength but not shear strength. As edge distance increased from 2.6 to 6.7 times the connector diameter, the shear capacity increased by 69%. Panel thickness directly affects pull-out and shear strengths of connectors that are fully embedded. For example, a 50% increase in panel thickness increased pull-out and shear strengths by 135% and 49%, respectively. New design equations have been developed for cast-in connectors in thin UHPFRC panels with steel fibers.

title: Effect of multiple wind barriers on wind characteristics of the vehicle-train-bridge system of a single-deck rail-cum-road bridge
Experimental and numerical study on eccentrically compression-loaded stainless-clad bimetallic steel cold-formed square hollow section stub columns
Seismic behavior of the modular corrugated plate sidewalls with large length-to-height ratios
The influence of soil-structure interaction on the seismic performance of prefabricated assembly monolithic underground frame structures
Failure mode identification of reticulated shells with BC joints considering member buckling and joint failure
From divergence to synergy: A multi-hazard framework for structural design under winds and earthquakes
abstract: Structural design for wind and earthquake resistance has historically evolved along separate tracks, reflecting differences in loading characteristics and performance objectives emphasized in practice. Wind demands are typically long-duration and dominated by mean and turbulent pressures, while the responses of wind-sensitive structures are often governed by low-frequency dynamic behavior and serviceability criteria such as drift and acceleration. Earthquake demands are transient base excitations that generate inertial forces throughout the structure, which have traditionally driven ductility-based strategies to achieve life safety under rare but severe events. This work examines how these contrasting traditions shaped prescriptive, hazard-by-hazard workflows and discusses why a “governing hazard” mindset can be risk-inconsistent in dual-hazard settings, particularly when sequential hazards and lifecycle consequences are considered. The paper then synthesizes recent progress toward a unified multi-hazard framework through Performance-Based Engineering, where common performance objectives and risk metrics (e.g., expected annual loss) enable consistent comparison and decision-making across hazards. In this context, emerging developments in performance-based wind engineering, including increased use of nonlinear analysis and controlled inelastic mechanisms under extreme winds, illustrate the growing methodological convergence between the two fields. The review concludes by identifying critical research gaps and future directions to support implementable, risk-consistent multi-hazard design.

title: Compression and shear stability capacity design for a composite wall combining concrete-filled steel tubes and corrugated steel plates
abstract: This paper proposes a novel composite wall system integrating concrete-filled steel tubes (CFSTs) and corrugated steel plates (CSPs), where CFSTs sustain vertical compression and CSPs resist horizontal loads. To establish a robust stability design methodology under compression, shear, and combined loading, an integrated approach combining theoretical derivation and numerical simulation is employed. Key findings include the characterization of elastic shear buckling modes and the formulation of a theoretical shear stability equation based on CFST-CSP interaction. Furthermore, the axial compressive stability is evaluated, alongside a critical assessment of major international design codes. Numerical analyses of load-displacement curves and stress distributions further elucidate the interaction mechanisms, revealing that the CFST-CSPCW system exhibits superior compression-shear performance: as the axial load ratio increases from 0 to 0.6, the reduction in shear-bearing capacity remains within 10%. Finally, a comprehensive compression-shear interaction model is established. Validation results show that the proposed design framework is highly reliable, with prediction errors for stability capacity consistently below 10%. This methodology provides a solid foundation for the engineering application of CFST-CSPCWs.

title: A spring-suspended sectional model system with actively tunable damping: Concept, design, and performance validation
ULiteCrackNet: An ultra-lightweight crack segmentation model balancing accuracy and efficiency with stable diffusion–enhanced transfer learning
Experimental investigation and design approach on reinforced alkali-activated slag-based concrete columns under eccentric loading
abstract: Alkali-activated slag-based concrete (AASC) has emerged as a promising engineering material that can significantly reduce the environmental impact of concrete production while utilizing industrial by-products. Although the material-level properties of AASC have been extensively studied, there is limited research available on the structural performance of reinforced AASC (R-AASC) columns. Furthermore, current design standards lack specific guidelines for the design of R-AASC columns under eccentric loading. Therefore, this paper attempts to develop a design approach for R-AASC columns through experimental investigation and theoretical analysis. A series of eccentric compression tests was conducted on fourteen R-AASC columns and five reinforced Portland cement-based concrete (R-PCC) columns. The experimental variables comprised concrete type, concrete compressive strength, eccentricity ratio, slenderness ratio, and longitudinal reinforcement ratio. The test results demonstrated comparable failure modes, load-carrying capacities, and ductility factors between R-AASC and R-PCC columns. The load-carrying capacity of the R-AASC columns was reduced by increases in both the eccentricity and slenderness ratios, whereas it was enhanced by higher concrete compressive strength and longitudinal reinforcement ratio. Furthermore, the ductility factors of these columns, ranging from 1.46 to 1.58, were comparable to the range of 1.49–1.58 observed for R-PCC columns. Subsequently, the second-order effect in R-AASC columns was evaluated using the moment magnification factor specified in the existing standards. The predictions obtained from various design models showed that the American standard was more consistent with the experimental results. Based on this, a design approach was proposed to predict the load-carrying capacity of R-AASC columns under eccentric loading. Finally, the proposed approach was validated by comparing its predictions with experimental results from the present study and the literature.

title: Wind–vehicle–bridge interaction and driving safety reliability under skew winds
abstract: Wind-induced vehicle accidents on bridges depend not only on mean wind speed but also on turbulence and pavement roughness. Existing wind–vehicle–bridge interaction (W-VBI) studies typically rely on a limited number of stochastic wind and pavement realisations, restricting the quantification of record-to-record variability in driving safety. This study proposes a W-VBI framework that explicitly embeds this variability into the driving safety assessment. Applied to a twin box-girder bridge, the methodology combines stochastic simulations of turbulent wind and pavement profiles with aerodynamic coefficients obtained from wind-tunnel tests, which are used to define wind loads in the coupled W-VBI analysis. Over 85,000 nonlinear simulations are conducted for 11 wind angles, five gust levels, two high-sided vehicles, and speeds from 15–130 km/h. Vehicle overturning, side-slipping, and yawing probabilities are calculated, using bootstrapping techniques to evaluate the statistical stability of the simulations. Results show that wind and pavement randomness induce significant record-to-record variability in vehicle safety, while bootstrapping enables estimation of the minimum number of stochastic records required for statistically stable reliability assessments.

title: Experimental investigations on corrosion-fatigue coupling behavior of rib-to-deck welded joints in orthotropic steel decks
abstract: As a critical detail in orthotropic steel decks of long-span bridges, rib-to-deck (RD) welded joints are susceptible to corrosion-fatigue cracking under long-term cyclic traffic loads in corrosive environments. However, their corrosion-fatigue behavior remains largely unexplored, as realistic component-level reproduction of corrosion-fatigue interaction is challenging for such complex welded details. To address this gap, this study experimentally investigates the corrosion-fatigue coupling behavior of full-scale truncated RD joints of a long-span bridge, using a custom-fabricated laboratory setup. Impressed-current accelerated electrochemical corrosion and cyclic mechanical loading were applied simultaneously in a time-compatible manner. Twelve specimens were tested under three fatigue load amplitudes and three corrosion levels, with three pure-fatigue cases as references. The dominant cracking mode—cracking at the U-rib weld toe—in the pure-fatigue case remained unchanged under coupled corrosion-fatigue conditions, indicating no crack-mode transition. The hot spot stress analysis demonstrates that corrosion-fatigue interaction significantly degrades fatigue performance by accelerating crack initiation and thereby reducing overall fatigue life. S-N curves show that fatigue lives decrease by 16.42%, 37.93%, and 59.01% under low, moderate, and high corrosion currents, respectively, compared to the no-corrosion case. The corrosion characteristic analysis and fracture morphology observations further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in capturing the representative corrosion-fatigue interaction. This work provides component-level experimental evidence and mechanistic insights into corrosion-fatigue coupling in RD welded joints, facilitating improved fatigue design and durability evaluation of orthotropic steel decks.

title: Experimental investigation on prestressed concrete beams with localized strand damage: Tilt-based deflection mapping and damage indicators
abstract: This study investigates the structural response of prestressed concrete beams with localized strand damage under both serviceability and ultimate loading conditions. Seven simply supported beams, with a clear span of L = 7.0 m, were cast as scaled bridge girders representing different damage scenarios. Inspection windows were created at L /2, L /3, and L /4 to simulate corrosion-induced defects by selectively severing prestressing strands in a controlled manner, thereby reducing the effective prestressing steel area. The beams were tested under combined dead load and increasing midspan live load, applied through loading-unloading cycles from service levels up to failure. A dense network of MEMS tiltmeters was used to measure spanwise rotations, which were converted into deflection profiles using a straightforward slope-integration procedure that preserved support compatibility and was cross-validated against independent laser targets and LVDTs. Based on the reconstructed deflected shapes under incremental quasi-static cycles at serviceability load levels, two complementary sets of damage indicators were defined. The first set, DI₁ (loading), includes the absolute peak deflection during the load plateau (DI 1- u ) and its position (DI 1- x ). The second set, DI₂ (residual), includes the peak residual deflection after unloading (DI 2- u ) and its location (DI 2- x ). The u components reflect damage severity, while the x components provide damage localization. These indicators consistently identified the damaged regions and scaled with the number and position of severed strands, in agreement with force–displacement responses, moment–curvature relationships from sectional analysis and observed failure modes. The results demonstrate that rapid static testing combining tilt-based deflection mapping and local crack-opening measurements provides a practical and reliable approach for detecting, ranking, and localizing tendon damage in prestressed concrete girders.

title: Improved Rigid Body Spring Model for quasi-static large deformation analysis of RC beam-column sub-assemblage under column removal
Experimental shear failure of reinforced concrete beams in fire conditions
abstract: This paper presents the results of a test campaign of twelve reinforced concrete beams without transverse reinforcements under four-point bending and thermal loading in order to achieve their shear failure in fire conditions. Midspan deflection, temperature, shear strength and crack angle of the beams were measured throughout the campaign. Furthermore, the experimental shear strength of the beams at ambient temperature was compared to predictions from ACI Code-318–25 and EN 1992–1–1. Then, the experimental shear strength of the beams in fire conditions was compared to predictions from EN 1992–1–2 and those derived from a design model based on the upper bound kinematic approach of the yield design theory. Such comparisons were made using different values of the effectiveness factor applied to the compressive strength of concrete, available in the literature, making it possible to show the influence of such a factor on the comparative results.

title: Post-earthquake residual vertical load-carrying capacity (VLCC) of Y-shaped bridge piers: Experimental studies and numerical simulations
Rocking behavior of prestressed concrete-filled steel tubular lattice towers under compression-bending-torsion loading
Machine learning-based multiscale surrogate model for local fatigue analysis in railway bridges
abstract: Fatigue analysis of railway bridges typically relies on global methods based on catalogued S-N curves for nominal stresses, which may not accurately represent the actual load transfer mechanisms at critical details. Local fatigue methods can overcome this limitation, but their adoption has been hindered by the computational burden of global-local Finite Element (FE) analyses. This work proposes a hierarchical surrogate-based approach to derive multiscale models that efficiently relate global-scale structural responses to the input parameters of a local fatigue method, enabling fatigue predictions consistent with the physical scale of the phenomenon. The surrogate model is based on a supervised learning framework combining a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and regression models, trained on FE simulations but capable of incorporating experimental data when available. Its performance is demonstrated through a case study based on validated FE models, in which local von Mises stresses at the critical hotspot are predicted from responses evaluated at only two selected global-scale locations. R 2 values exceeding 0.9934 are achieved for unseen train loading events, while computation time is reduced from several days per load case to approximately 3–6 s, enabling integration into digital twins for infrastructure asset management.

title: Full-scale experimental and numerical study on hydrogen explosion and RC wall response: Confinement effect
Development of a novel laminated bamboo-rubber seismic isolator for rural buildings
Stiffness-based failure of low-strength shallow masonry vaulted floor slabs
Proposed seismic performance factors for linked column frame systems using FEMA-P695 methodology
abstract: The Linked Column Frame (LCF) system is a relatively recent lateral force-resisting system designed to reduce repair costs and downtime after earthquakes through replaceable links while satisfying conventional life safety performance objectives under design-level seismic demands. However, existing studies primarily adopt seismic performance factors from Special Moment Resisting Frame (SMRF) systems without a systematic evaluation specific to LCF behavior. This study develops seismic performance factors for LCF systems using the FEMA P695 methodology. Thirty-one archetype buildings (3-, 6-, and 9-story) were designed with standard W-shapes and built-up section (BUS) short and intermediate links. Various combinations of the response modification factor (R) and displacement amplification factor (Cd) were investigated. Nonlinear time history analyses were conducted in OpenSees using 44 ground motion records. Structural performance was evaluated based on link rotation, interstory drift, and residual drift under Design Basis, Maximum Considered, and Collapse-Level earthquakes. Results indicate that the Cd/R ratio is a key parameter governing the strength and stiffness of LCF systems, while interstory drift is the controlling performance criterion compared to link rotation and residual drift. Maximum interstory drift demands decreased with increasing building height, identifying 3-story LCF systems as the most vulnerable. An optimal combination of R= 8 and Cd= 3 provides reliable seismic performance while reducing structural weight and construction cost relative to SMRF-based designs. These findings establish a consistent, performance-based basis for selecting seismic design factors for LCF systems and support their broader application in earthquake-resistant design.

title: Editorial Board
Adaptive multi-point reliability-based topology optimization for deteriorating structures with design-dependent critical time tracking
abstract: This paper presents an adaptive multi-point constraint formulation for time-dependent reliability-based topology optimization (TD-RBTO) of deteriorating structures. Under inspection-based management protocols, load rating revisions and posting interventions create non-monotonic demand trajectories, so that maximum structural vulnerability may occur at interior service-life instants rather than at the terminus. Single-point or prescribed fixed-time assessment can therefore permit reliability violations during substantial portions of the operational life, a phenomenon termed regime exploitation . A stress-norm aggregation measure, established in stress-constrained topology optimization, is adapted to characterize the design-dependent fatigue demand governing degradation kinetics. By emphasizing highly stressed members rather than averaging over the structural volume, this aggregation creates a physically motivated coupling between topology decisions and degradation rates, and consequently between design configuration and the temporal location of peak vulnerability. The performance measure approach (PMA) is supplemented with a second-order reliability correction that inflates the search-sphere radius to compensate for limit-state curvature at the most probable point, mitigating systematic non-conservatism inherent in the first-order approximation at modest additional cost. The proposed framework is referred to as Adaptive Multi-Point TD-RBTO. At prescribed update iterations, the PMA constraint is evaluated over candidate service-life times to identify the current critical time and nearby active reliability constraints. The active time set is then updated only when the governing time region shifts. This adaptive critical-time tracking prevents regime exploitation without changing the PMA framework into a reliability-index approach. Complete sensitivity analysis captures the dependency chain from design variables through the characteristic stress field to degradation rates and structural response, with correlated non-Gaussian random variables handled through the Nataf transformation. The methodology is demonstrated on planar and spatial ground-structure examples, both solved to convergence. Monte Carlo (MC) validation confirms that the adaptive designs meet the target reliability within MC confidence intervals over the evaluated service-life validation times, whereas prescribed fixed-time formulations can permit reliability violations at shifted critical times and first-order-only formulations incur a systematic deficit across the service life.

title: A consistent force-based prestressed beam model with curvilinear tendons and bond–slip
abstract: This study proposes a unified force-based formulation for three-dimensional Timoshenko beam elements that includes the classical fiber-section approach, the bond–slip effects in arbitrarily curved or draped prestressing tendons, the multiple construction stages and the time dependent losses such as concrete creep, shrinkage, and steel relaxation. The concrete fibers follow a three-dimensional damage-plasticity law, and the tendon-concrete interaction evolves through internal variables that reflect the grouting sequence. Even though different mixed formulations can be used, this paper presents the force-based formulation, that provides the best approximation of the bond behavior. All the mentioned aspects are coupled in a framework within the same element state determination problem. Validation against representative experimental tests shows that the proposed formulation reproduces full nonlinear load–displacement curves, tendon bond–slip profiles, and failure modes that conventional flexure-only, perfectly bonded models cannot capture. Both in the bonded and unbonded tests, the response is reproduced with only three beam elements, while in the CFRP-strengthened beam tests, peak load and initial stiffness are predicted within 10% of the experiments’ results. The proposed element can simulate the nonlinear response of prestressed concrete beams, incorporating time-dependent losses, arbitrary tendon geometries, segmental construction, staged prestressing, and bond conditions ranging from fully bonded to fully unbonded.

title: Bond–slip behaviour and constitutive modelling of screwed-in threaded rods in glulam joints
abstract: Steel screwed-in threaded rods (STRs) can form high strength connections in glued laminated timber (glulam) structures. However, the bond–slip behaviour of STRs embedded in glulam is not well understood and detailed constitutive models to describe this behaviour are lacking. This study addresses that knowledge gap through an extensive experimental programme comprising 280 pull-out tests on 16 and 20 mm diameter STRs under monotonic loading with STR-to-grain angles ranging from 0°–90°. Key bond–slip properties, including withdrawal strength, bond stiffness, slip at peak stress, maximum slip, and fracture energy, are quantified in terms of both the mean and 5th-percentile values. The results show that withdrawal strength increases with STR-to-grain angle up to 30° and then remains approximately constant, while bond stiffness decreases and both slip at peak stress and maximum slip increase with angle. A larger rod diameter generally increases withdrawal strength, maximum slip, and fracture energy, and reduces scatter, indicating reduced sensitivity to local defects. Mechanics-informed regression models are developed for the mean and characteristic bond–slip properties as functions of glulam density, rod diameter, and inclination angle. A new constitutive model is proposed that captures the full nonlinear bond–slip response of STRs in glulam. The model shows strong agreement with experimental results and provides length-independent parameters suitable for analytical design methods and interface-based numerical simulations.

title: Experimental and analysis on seismic performance of precast concrete frame with internal hinged substructure
Ultimate and repairability performance of steel eccentrically braced frames designed according to the 2nd generation of Eurocode 8: A parametric study for medium-rise buildings
abstract: In the present work, the structural performance of steel eccentrically braced frames (EBFs) designed according to the 2nd generation of Eurocode 8 is parametrically investigated via both static and dynamic non-linear analyses. For this purpose, an archetypal medium-rise building has been selected as a case study. Seismic design is performed considering different i ) ductility classes (medium/high), ii ) levels of seismic hazard (S δ = 0.66 g /0.76 g ) and iii ) link configurations (short/long). The impact of new design rules for medium- and high-ductile steel EBFs is first discussed in terms of material consumption and ultimate performance. A peculiar focus is hence given to after-earthquake repairability (AER), which is addressed via a probabilistic approach based on FEMA P-58 indications. In light of the obtained results, it is concluded that new Eurocode 8 can result in slightly lighter structures (up to –12% in terms of weight per single EBF) without altering their overall seismic performance in terms of collapse mechanisms, relevant resistance and lateral stiffness. AER proves to be very satisfactory, with only limited after-earthquake damage (residual inter-storey drift ≤ 0.5%) occurring also in medium-ductile EBF structures, i.e., for which seismic design rules have been strongly simplified.

title: An accurate and unconditionally stable elastoplastic dynamic analysis of 3D-frames using mathematical programming
Timber connections with increased friction in the shear plane: Experimental and analytical investigations into strength and stiffness
abstract: Timber connections with increased friction in the shear plane are studied, focusing on experimental and analytical approaches to enhance load-carrying capacity and stiffness. Conventional aluminium connectors, while structurally adequate, pose environmental and fire-resistance limitations. As an alternative, densified veneer wood (DVW) was introduced for system connectors, offering superior sustainability and fire performance. The research explores surface modifications to improve frictional behaviour, thereby optimizing strength and stiffness. Short-term push-out tests examined various surface treatments and screw configurations, revealing that pronounced surface structuring significantly increases ultimate load capacity, while flat, uniform surfaces better maintain stiffness. Long-term duration-of-load tests confirmed that frictional performance remains stable over time, with creep factors for inclined screws significantly lower than those for other dowel-type fasteners. An analytical model was developed to predict load-carrying capacity and stiffness, incorporating friction effects and deformation perpendicular to the grain. The mechanical model proposed in the new generation of EC5 overestimates the stiffness when used for connections with connector plates and inclined screws, because it neglects deformations perpendicular to the grain beneath the connector plate. In contrast, the herein presented spring model incorporates compression behaviour perpendicular to the grain, thus, predicting load-carrying capacity and stiffness accurately for a range of timber components, including CLT and GLT reinforced with fully threaded screws. The results demonstrate that DVW connectors with appropriately modified surfaces can achieve high ultimate loads and reliable long-term performance, thereby supporting their adoption in sustainable timber construction.

title: A review of structural simulation of reinforced ultra-high performance concrete and high-performance fiber-reinforced cement-based composite members
abstract: Ultra-high performance concrete (UHPC) and high-performance fiber-reinforced cementitious composites (HPFRCC) are a class of material that are gaining popularity due to their enhanced performance and damage tolerance which make them promising for seismic applications where energy dissipation is crucial. Extensive experimental and numerical studies have been carried out to understand the performance of UHPC and HPFRCC structural components as well as to recognize the influence from different parameters such as matrix tensile strengths, reinforcement ratios, and loading conditions. This review paper intends to provide a comprehensive summary of numerical simulation works performed to simulate structural response for seismic applications and other structural engineering uses. The simulation works are categorized based on their computational complexity. The paper concludes with key points such as the use of computationally efficient concentrated plasticity models to capture global component responses such as peak loads, initial stiffness, energy dissipation, pinching, and opting for detailed modeling approaches such as continuum models when local responses such as reinforcement strains or failure mechanism are required to perform parametric analysis. Suggestions for future work includes the integration of shear–flexure interaction in fiber-based models, developing steel models that account for necking, and incorporation of initial flaws in continuum models.

title: In-situ 3D deformation monitoring of subsea pipelines using a novel rigid-flex shape sensing array
Experimental and numerical analysis of hybrid SMA-Steel wire mesh reinforced ECC for synergistic resilient infrastructure
In-plane buckling behaviour and mechanical properties of low-pressure inflatable arches: Experimental investigation and numerical simulations
Cold-formed shear walls with burring holes for the seismic strengthening of existing reinforced concrete buildings
abstract: Decarbonization is a key priority in the global effort to promote sustainable development and mitigate climate change. A significant contribution can be made by renovating the existing European building stock, which is largely characterized by low energy efficiency and inadequate structural performance. To address this challenge, integrated and sustainable renovation strategies based on Life Cycle Thinking principles have been proposed, aiming to enhance both structural safety and energy performance. In this paper, cold-formed steel panels with burring holes are proposed as earthquake-resistant elements for the integrated renovation of existing reinforced concrete (RC) buildings. These shear walls are used in Japan as lateral force-resistant systems for new lightweight buildings. The proposed retrofit solution offers key advantages, including lightness, ease of installation, and the possibility of disassembly and component reuse, thereby enhancing overall sustainability. Three finite element modelling strategies with varying levels of complexity are presented to capture the behaviour observed in previous experimental campaigns. A design methodology for a retrofit solution for RC buildings is developed, incorporating the stringer-panel model to derive forces in individual elements. Finally, both the modelling approach and design method are validated through application to a reference case study building representative of existing RC structures not designed according to earthquake-resistant provisions. Vulnerability analyses have been performed, demonstrating the effectiveness of the designed retrofit solution involving perforated metal panels.

title: Population-based structural health monitoring of historical masonry bridges using spaceborne InSAR measurements
abstract: Italy’s railway network includes nearly 10,000 masonry arch bridges, many of which now carry loads far exceeding their original design while undergoing material degradation, posing a major infrastructure management challenge. Conventional structural health monitoring relies on costly on-site instrumentation that cannot be deployed at this scale. This paper proposes a population-based SHM framework that identifies anomalous deformation in masonry arch bridges from satellite interferometric (InSAR) measurements, while keeping physically meaningful, engineering-interpretable indicators. For each bridge, Sentinel-1 line-of-sight displacements and environmental variables (air temperature and soil moisture) are condensed into compact statistical features describing the global displacement distribution, independent of the uncertain position of individual InSAR scatterers. Subspace alignment, a feature-based domain adaptation technique, is used to harmonize the baseline feature distributions across structures with different geometry. To overcome the scarcity of labeled anomalies, a simplified parametric bridge model is used to generate a population of synthetic bridges with imposed anomaly scenarios, on which a bidirectional long short-term memory regression network is trained. Through simulation-to-real transfer, the network is then applied to real data. The model outputs two physically interpretable descriptors, namely anomaly intensity and spatial extent. Validation is carried out on eight masonry arch railway bridges in Liguria, Italy. A persistent localized settlement identified on one structure is consistent with independent velocity maps. The framework offers a scalable, non-invasive tool for regional-scale screening and inspection prioritization of heritage bridge stocks.

title: Nonlinear buckling responses of a confined liner reinforced by functionally graded graphene with atom vacancy defects under thermal-mechanical loading
A displacement-control finite element framework for thermal buckling and post-buckling analysis of continuous welded rail
Digital twin-driven intelligent structural fault diagnosis and decision-making for earth-rock dams using large language models
Multi-directional quasi-static testing of unbonded post-tensioned precast segmental bridge piers: Effects of loading-path geometry, variable axial load, and direction-dependent boundary conditions
SS2SF-GAN: A cGAN-based model for reconstructing stress field from sparse strain measurements in perforated grillage structures
Vibration suppression of irregularly shaped composite curvature shells in thermal environment: Modeling and experiment
Probabilistic prediction of bridge-tower temperature fields in high-altitude cold environments using Monte Carlo dropout neural networks
Experimental study on seismic behavior of pre-stressed disc spring self-centering beam-column joint with rotational friction energy-dissipating device
Flexural behavior of CFS composite truss: Test, simulation, and theoretical calculation
Influence of textile layout on the flexural behavior of TRECC-strengthened reinforced concrete beam by hybrid anchoring technique
Probabilistic serviceability assessment of footbridges subjected to crowd-induced lateral vibrations
abstract: Lightweight and flexible footbridges are increasingly susceptible to large pedestrian-induced lateral excitations. Current research typically relies on deterministic estimates of critical crowd sizes, which often neglect behavioral uncertainties and utilize simplified single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) models. To address these limitations, this study proposes a probabilistic framework to estimate the likelihood of exceeding lateral serviceability limit states. The methodology employs an equivalent beam model to account for spatial variations as pedestrians traverse the span, avoiding the limitations of fixed-point oscillating load models. A novel foot-force model based on gait stability is developed and validated against experimental data. Monte Carlo simulations are then used to propagate parametric uncertainties and generate fragility curves and surfaces. Case studies on various bridges reveal that serviceability performance is significantly more sensitive to bridge frequency than damping, particularly when the bridge frequency avoids the mean pedestrian gait frequency. Additionally, a procedure for estimating maximum occupancy limits is introduced to ensure operational reliability. This work introduces a formal reliability-analysis procedure, providing designers with essential tools to probabilistically assess performance objectives and ensure compliance with serviceability requirements.

title: Freeze-thaw behavior and frost susceptibility of variable-cross-section high-speed railway subgrades in cold regions
Experimental and numerical study on out-of-plane mechanical performance of rectangular steel tube border-reinforced foam ceramic with mortar layer composite wall
Physics-constrained Gaussian process regression for probabilistic shear strength prediction of RC shear walls
Inverse design of metaconcrete surface wave barriers via response surface method and genetic algorithm for broadband vibration isolation
Numerical investigation on collapse-induced impact among reinforced concrete frame structures based on DEM
Resistance of SMB ceiling-floor system in edge column loss: Test and parametric analysis
Structural design optimization of concrete slabs: A systematic review
abstract: Structural design optimization (SDO) has long promised to revolutionize structural design, yet its impact on everyday engineering remains limited. This review synthesizes 25 years of research on SDO of concrete slabs in buildings. Increasingly volatile and conflicting objectives, and the rise of non-standard, material-efficient slab systems, challenge established design methods. SDO can address such problems by formulating them as mathematical optimization problems (OPs). Following PRISMA 2020, we identified 63 relevant publications from 906 records, comprising 151 OPs across eight slab types. We analyze OP formulations, analysis and optimization methods, and design insights. Flat, solid, and ribbed slabs account for more than 85% of OPs, while non-standard slab systems remain rare. OP complexity ranges from 1 to > 100,000 variables and 0–49 constraints, yet no recurring formulation defines a standard OP for any slab type. Metaheuristics dominate algorithm choice, although cross-class benchmarks provide limited support for this dominance. Many studies provide design insights, only 10% address real projects, and no optimized design is reported as built or issued for construction. Heterogeneous OP formulations, inconsistent reporting, weak baselines, and insufficient cross-class algorithm benchmarking hinder comparability and prevent study-specific insights from becoming transferable design guidance. Key research gaps include representative cross-class benchmarking suites, further work on analysis and solution-mapping surrogates, expanded case studies on non-standard slab systems, and multi-objective optimization under objective-input uncertainty.

title: Energy transfer mechanism of floating wind turbines under the combined effects of typhoons, waves, currents, and their coupling
Variability-weighted damage identification method considering the competition between sensitivity and uncertainty
Scaling behavior and mechanism of shear-failure reinforced concrete beams under impact loading
abstract: The scale effect of reinforced concrete (RC) beams under impact is critical for extrapolating prototype behavior from scaled tests; however, for shear-dominated members, the coupling between strain-rate sensitivity and geometric scaling remains inadequately characterized. This study develops and validates a high-fidelity finite element model in ABAQUS/Explicit to investigate the effects of the shear span-to-depth ratio a/h0 and geometric scale factor λ on the impact behavior of RC beams. The results show that decreasing a/h0 from 3.5 to 1.5 changes the governing mechanism from flexure-dominated to shear-dominated behavior, accompanied by a more direct load-transfer path and more localized shear damage within the shear span. For geometrically similar beams with a/h0 = 1.5, significant scale effects are observed: as λ increases from 1.0 to 3.0, the failure mode evolves from distributed multi-crack damage to a dominant diagonal shear crack, the normalized peak mid-span deflection and residual displacement increase by 24.8% and 26.1%, respectively, and the normalized peak impact force decreases by 36.9%. The scale effect is closely related to the non-uniform scaling of strain-rate magnitude and spatial distribution, which leads to a mismatch in dynamic strength between prototype and scaled beams. In addition, a peak displacement prediction formula considering the coupling of strain rate and shear span-to-depth ratio was proposed and validated. These findings provide support for evaluating the impact resistance of full-scale shear-failure RC beams based on scaled test results.

title: Configuration design and self-deployment performance of kirigami-inspired thick panel origami
abstract: Abstract Origami has been widely applied in the design of deployable spacecraft structures. This paper investigates the configuration design and self-deployment performance of a kirigami-inspired thick panel origami mechanism with a single degree of freedom(single-DOF). Firstly, the unit design is based on both intra-leaf and extra-leaf folding patterns, resulting in three unit types with varying leaf angles. Meanwhile, the merge and relace typological connected methods was employed to construct a single-DOF cell. Using the spatial mechanism theory, the kinematic parameters were analyzed, and the constraint equations for the closed-loop mechanism were derived. Moreover, mock-up folding sequences were produced offering a potential solution for spacecraft deployable structures. Finally, the self-deployment performance were explored under varying number and position of driven elements, and the influencing factors in deployment were investigated. The results demonstrate that that both the number and position of the driven elements significantly influence the self-deployment state. Additionally, thicker panels, fewer panels, and higher-quality hinges contribute to easier and more effective unfolding of the model.

title: Effect of sustained loading on the deflection and post-unloading flexural performance of geopolymer concrete slabs
Testing and design analysis of WAAM high strength steel square hollow sections in compression
An auxetic trampoline metamaterial with tunable bandgap under prestrain
Axial compression behavior of circular CFDST stub columns with localized corrosion: Testing, numerical modeling and design
A novel wet joint featuring ultra-high-performance concrete and U-shaped thermoplastic GFRP bars: Shear behavior and strength model
Surrogate model-based reliability assessment of long span suspension bridges considering multiple failure-modes and random fields
Quasi-static cyclic tests of innovative prefabricated CFST bridge piers with replaceable components
Seismic ductility of precast round-ended hollow columns with UHPC shallow socket connections: Tests and design method
abstract: Socket connections offer a promising structural solution for precast assembled columns in high-seismicity mountainous regions. However, their application is limited by the large minimum embedment depth required by current designs. This constraint is particularly problematic for precast round-ended hollow columns (REHCs) with variable cross-sections used in railway bridges in such regions. To address this gap, a novel ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) shallow-socket connection was proposed in this study. Using this new connection, the minimum embedment depth is reduced to 0.28 times the maximum cross-sectional dimension while maintaining ductility comparable to cast-in-place columns. Quasi-static tests were firstly conducted on five precast REHC specimens with variable cross-sections to evaluate their damage evolution, hysteretic behavior, and ductility. The results showed that the proposed connection delivers seismic performance comparable to cast-in-place columns under both strong-axis and weak-axis loading. The tests identified two previously underexplored phenomena. First, the yield curvature varies nonuniformly along the column height due to the combined effects of cross-sectional stiffness gradients and a bottom solid segment. Second, differences in load-bearing capacity between the strong and weak axes of the round-ended cross-section induce asymmetric tension shift of the longitudinal reinforcement between orthogonal directions. Therefore, an equivalent linear yield curvature distribution model for REHCs with variable cross-sections was developed. A ductility-based design approach was formulated that incorporates bending gradients, longitudinal reinforcement tension shift, strain penetration, and shear. Additionally, a unified equivalent plastic hinge length model was proposed that accounts for directional differences in tension shift. Experimental validation indicated that the proposed design approach achieves a mean prediction error of approximately 8% for the displacement ductility ratio. The findings provide critical technical and theoretical support for industrialized construction and ductility-based seismic design of railway bridges in high-seismicity regions.

title: High-degree-of-freedom shape optimization of bridge main girder sections based on deep reinforcement learning: A co-design approach for static wind load and sectional stiffness
Axial compression behaviour and design of high-strength steel tube-confined steel-reinforced concrete columns
Behavior of monopile-supported offshore wind turbines under normal operational and extreme-parked conditions in loose sand
abstract: Enhancing the performance and ensuring the long-time reliability of Offshore Wind Turbines (OWTs) requires a comprehensive understanding of OWT system response and interactions between OWT system components under realistic loading conditions. This paper presents Real-Time Hybrid Simulation (RTHS) results for a monopile-supported OWT under normal and extreme loading scenarios, which include aero-hydro-mechanical-geotechnical-structural component interactions. RTHS divides the OWT into analytical and experimental substructures, with dynamic equilibrium and compatibility maintained at the interfaces between substructures. The analytical substructures model the superstructure of the OWT above the mudline, along with the applied wave and wind loads, and the effects of the power-take-off unit using well-established numerical models, while the experimental substructure is the soil-monopile system that is physically tested in the laboratory. The RTHS results reveal that the OWT exhibits a ratcheting response due to a progressive accumulation of the monopile displacement under cyclic and dynamic loads. In addition, the stiffness and damping characteristics of the soil-monopile system change significantly, where the lateral stiffness increased by more than 100% and the damping ratio decreased by 76% relative to initial values during the RTHS. The results show that the OWT system response is dominated by wave loading and influenced by the soil-monopile response. The 1st fore-aft tower-monopile mode frequency was reduced by about 10% relative to a reference case without soil-monopile effects. The study shows that the soil-monopile response must be considered to accurately simulate the response of OWTs to various loading conditions.

title: Shaking table tests on a three-storey precast RC frame structure assembled with energy-dissipating self-centering rebar couplers
Bending-dominated chiral metastructures with tunable thermal expansion: Planar-to-cylindrical design and dual-mechanism modeling
Ductile design of reinforced concrete members constructed from brittle concrete
A physics–data co-driven spatio-temporal graph attention network for full-field structural response reconstruction and dynamic parameter identification
Aerodynamic shape optimization of bridge towers based on a hybrid Softplus-Kriging surrogate model: Reducing aerodynamic interference on adjacent hangers
Conch shell–inspired thin-walled structure with enhanced energy absorption and impact resistance
Physics-informed probabilistic neural network for reliable condition assessment and failure prognosis of substructures in floating offshore wind turbines
abstract: The structural integrity of substructures in Floating Offshore Wind Turbine (FOWTs) is critical importance and efficient and reliable health condition assessment methods are essential to ensure their long-term reliability and safety. Modern intelligent prognostic approaches based on deep neural networks are generally developed by learning the mapping between theoretical health condition with the monitoring observations. However, their performance can deteriorate significantly when failure data are limited or unavailable. To address these challenges, this study proposes a reliable intelligent prognostic framework capable of predicting failures even in the absence of direct failure observations. The proposed framework consists of three main modules: (i) a robust health indicator construction module for extracting representative degradation information from monitoring data; (ii) a Physics-Informed Dual Decoder prognostic module, which incorporates physics-informed inductive bias to constrain latent fatigue-evolution dynamics and predict future health states; and (iii) a reliability assessment module for quantifying structural reliability based on the prognostic results. The framework's effectiveness is validated through fatigue degradation analysis on three typical FOWT substructures. The results show that, as structural fatigue degradation progresses, degradation-related dynamic response changes can be effectively captured by the proposed TDA-VMD-based health indicator construction method, leading to more robust health assessment features. Furthermore, by introducing physics-informed inductive bias to constrain the latent dynamics of fatigue evolution, the proposed PIDualDecoder model enables more physically consistent and reliable fatigue prognosis, particularly for long-term prediction. These improved prognosis results further provide more confident support for reliability assessment, thereby contributing to safer and more cost-effective operation and maintenance of FOWTs.

title: A load-independent constraint framework for structural life prediction of creep–fatigue crack growth in mismatched welded joints
Seismic performance assessment of power systems considering dual correlation of seismic demand and component capacity
A compact isolator for multi-directionally coupled vibration
Zero-shot temporal learning for prediction of thermal load in composite bridge decks using sparse temperature measurements
Design of assembled quasi-zero-stiffness metastructures with nonlinear stiffness coupling
A multi-wedge ratchet device for tension-only dampers: Prototype test and demonstrative application
Behavior and modeling of FRP-confined silica-fume-modified steel slag concrete
A knowledge distillation-based transfer learning framework for peak seismic response prediction of urban building clusters
Post-fire mechanical behaviour of wire-laser additively manufactured high-strength steel plates
Automated finite element mesh generation of damaged concrete structures using semantic point clouds
Design method and reliability analysis of three-dimensional basalt fabric reinforced concrete slabs
High-speed railway track void monitoring under sensor failures: A physics-guided robust mixture-of-experts approach
MAGIC-Frame: Multi-agent GRPO-based intelligent code-compliant optimization for irregular steel frame structures
Editorial Board
Uncertainty-aware detection of early damage in a full-scale steel railway bridge
abstract: Reliable detection of early structural damage is essential for safe and efficient management of existing bridges, yet validation of unsupervised damage detection methods is often limited by the scarcity of validation data, particularly for early damage. Recent developments in uncertainty-aware vibration-based damage detection show that autoregressive coefficients and their estimator covariances can enable a reliable computation of Mahalanobis squared distances, even in high-dimensional settings. This paper, which builds on these developments, evaluates the capability of detecting damage states representing early damage. To this end, a new experimental measurement campaign has been conducted in which 22 gradual damage states, representing different progressions of four realistic damage types, were imposed on a full-scale steel truss bridge under controlled excitation and moderate environmental variability. The results show clear separation between undamaged and damaged conditions across all damage states, including the earliest damage progressions. Near-perfect classification is achieved using the uncertainty-aware Mahalanobis distance, with balanced accuracies above 99%. Moreover, the damage-index distributions exhibit low dispersion and consistent behavior across temperature regimes. These findings demonstrate that subtle damage-related changes in the structural response of steel bridges can be detected supporting potential integration of such work into real-world SHM systems after further validation under operational conditions.

title: Flexural behavior and crack resistance of joints in hot-rolled section steel-UHPC composite deck under negative bending: Experiments and analysis
Towards a physically based design framework for rocking structures
abstract: A methodology is presented for the seismic assessment of overturning safety of rocking structures, including single blocks, multi-block columns, and arches. The proposed methodology does not require nonlinear dynamic analysis, and it can enable the development of an efficient, prescriptive design procedure for rocking structures. The rocking behavior under earthquake excitations is analyzed both analytically and numerically, and fundamental, physics-based relationships between natural records and analytically-derived single- and double-pulse excitations are highlighted through the introduction of two key parameters: the impulse duration and the impulse-moment duration. Using these rocking parameters, the simplified overturning acceleration response spectrum (OAS) is defined, where overturning safety is expressed through a limit to the normalized peak ground acceleration as a function of the frequency parameter ( p ) that characterizes the structure. The OAS can be approximated through the envelope of a uniform minimum threshold and two curves proportional to 1 / p and 1 / p 2 . The accuracy of the simplified OAS curves is illustrated using a set of 100 ground motion records that include time histories from both near-field and far-field events. When location-specific design curves are determined, engineers may assess rocking structures using only the block characteristics, eliminating the need for time–history analyses. The analogy between this approach and conventional response spectrum analysis for elastic–plastic structures is also demonstrated.

title: Force-configuration mapping for cable force identification: Incorporating bending stiffness while bypassing unknown boundary restraint stiffness
Experimental and numerical investigation on flexural performance of ultra-high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete (UHP-FRC) hollow panels with different longitudinal reinforcements
abstract: Prefabricated hollow panels with ultra-high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete (UHP-FRC) offer an efficient approach of reducing dead load by removing low-stress concrete while maintaining flexural efficiency. However, the interaction between different UHP-FRC and longitudinal reinforcements remains inadequately understood. This study addresses this gap through a combined experimental and numerical investigation on flexural performance of 18 hollow panels fabricated with ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC), ultra-high-strength engineered cementitious composite (UHS-ECC), and lightweight high-strength ECC (LW-ECC), reinforced with steel bars, carbon FRP (CFRP) bars, or steel-FRP composite (SFC) bars. A stiffness-equivalent reinforcement design enabled meaningful cross-comparison among reinforcement types. Results reveal a strength-deformability trade-off governed by reinforcement selection. SFC-reinforced panels achieved the highest flexural capacities in all concrete groups, reaching 75.2 kN (UHPC), 79.5 kN (UHS-ECC), and 64.6 kN (LW-ECC), representing 52–77% increases over steel-reinforced counterparts and exhibited smoother post-peak softening than CFRP-reinforced panels due to ductility from the steel core. Steel-reinforced ECC panels demonstrated exceptional deformation capacity, with peak deflections of 34.2 mm (UHS-ECC) and 44.3 mm (LW-ECC) and stable post-peak load retention. A nonlinear finite element model, calibrated against experimental results (errors <10% for key response points), was employed for parametric studies on void size and reinforcement ratio for CFRP reinforced LW-ECC panels.

title: Unsupervised learning driven graded monitoring diagnosis of bridge tension-compression bearing degradation
abstract: Under external loading, the alternating transition of bearing between tensile and compressive states leads to the degradation of its tensile performance, which poses a threat to the overall safety of bridge structures. However, due to the lack of a clear understanding of the tensile degradation mechanism, existing studies have difficulty performing graded diagnosis of bearing degradation, thereby limiting the development of differentiated maintenance strategies for varying degradation conditions. To address this issue, this study proposed a graded diagnosis method of bearing tensile performance degradation through structural health monitoring driven by unsupervised learning algorithm. First, the working mechanism of the tension-compression bearing was analyzed. Based on the Rayleigh method, the mapping relationship between the bearing tensile stiffness and the bridge structure frequency under different working conditions was established. Then, an unsupervised learning algorithm combining manifold learning and Gaussian mixture model (GMM) was proposed to separate environmental effects from unlabeled frequency data. Using statistical characteristics of the diagnostic indicators under the normal and partial fracture conditions of the bearing, an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) control chart was employed to diagnose different degrees of degradation of the bearing tensile. Finally, the proposed method was verified through the monitoring data of a real cable-stayed bridge. The results demonstrated that the proposed method can achieve the graded diagnosis of the bearing tensile degradation and offer a guidance for the tension-compression bearing maintenance.

title: Experimental and numerical study of diaphragm in-plane stiffness on the seismic performance of building structures with DCPCF
Toward robust detection of interfacial debonding in CFRP-strengthened concrete: A GMM-Bayesian fusion approach
Risk-based decision support for maintenance and repairability of corroded RC columns under seismic loading
Research on the wind-induced internal and net pressure with openings on the cylindrical roof based on the covariance integration method
Integrated fire-structural analysis of glulam reticulated shells: Fire response and post-fire performance
