Acceleration Prediction-Truncated Compensation Neural Network for dynamic modeling of multi-degree-of-freedom coupled systems
Longitudinal forces induced by transit loads: Field testing and modeling
Ultimate load performance of tubular composite joints under various loading conditions
abstract: This research investigates non-welded tubular composite joints, highlighting theirpotential for offshore structures, such as wind turbine supporting jackets. These jointsface complex loading from wind, waves, and tides. These forces generate axial forcesand bending moments in the joints. tubular composite joints leverage the interfacialbonding between the composite and Circular Hollow Section (CHS) members forefficient load transfer. A critical failure mode is interfacial debonding. This paperfocuses on the characterisation and resistance of interfacial debonding in tubularcomposite joints through monotonic experiments. X90-joints are subjected to axialtension, axial compression, axial tension with out-of-plane bending (Nx+Mop), axialcompression with out-of-plane bending (-Nx+Mop), axial tension with in-plane bending(Nx+Mip), and axial tension + out-of-plane bending + in-plane bending (Nx+Mop+Mip).Experiments are performed on joints scaled to 1/4th of the real size found in typicaljacket designs. Numerical models employ cohesive zone modeling (CZM) to predictdebonding failure modes. Results from the experiments reveal that debonding failure isthe predominant mode under different loading conditions. Combined loading influencesthe sequence and extent of debonding propagation, although not affecting the primaryfailure mechanism.

title: Seismic performance of self-centering rocking bridge piers with external energy dissipation device considering pile-soil interaction
Multi-mode vibration control of long cables using lateral and rotational dampers
Influence of record-to-record variability on the assessment of unreinforced masonry buildings
abstract: A major source of uncertainty in the seismic assessment of existing masonry buildings lies in the definition of the seismic action. While nonlinear quasi-static or dynamic analyses typically address epistemic uncertainties, record-to-record variability can significantly influence the statistical distribution of structural response. This study investigates the impact of record-to-record variability on the seismic assessment of unreinforced masonry (URM) buildings representative of pre-code construction in seismic-prone urban regions. The building stock is modelled in OpenSees using a three-dimensional macroelement approach capable of reproducing both in-plane and out-of-plane wall behaviour, and simplified nonlinear material laws for interface elements. The seismic action is defined based on pre-defined seismological scenarios for multiple soil types. The combination of building archetypes (varying in plan configuration and number of storeys) and seismic intensity levels resulted in approximately 45,000 nonlinear response-history analyses executed via cloud computing. From these simulations, capacity curves and empirical distributions of engineering demand parameters (EDPs) and intensity measures (IMs) are derived across multiple damage states. Fragility functions are developed, and a bootstrap-based framework is implemented to quantify ( i ) the number of records required for stabilisation of median and dispersion estimates under different convergence thresholds, and ( ii ) the minimum number of analyses needed to capture a target seismic demand with prescribed probability levels. The results provide quantitative guidance on ground motion suite size for nonlinear dynamic assessment of existing URM buildings, supporting a rational balance between statistical reliability and computational efficiency.

title: Cyclic tests of precast concrete double beam-to-column connections with emulative joint details
Axial compression behaviors of laminated bamboo columns with steel-encased bonded connections: Experimental and theoretical investigations
Geometric assessment of precast concrete components using structurally informed semantic point clouds
Steel exoskeleton systems for seismic retrofit: Connection design and performance
abstract: Steel exoskeletons are widely investigated in literature since they can strengthen the as-built structure without interrupting the activity within the existing structure. However, only few studies investigate the influence and the design procedure to define the connection between the existing structure and this strengthening solution. The main aim of the present work is to introduce a general design procedure for these connection systems as well as evaluate their influence on the global reinforced structural behaviour. Therefore, a real case-study steel school building was selected, and both the orthogonal exoskeleton and the connection system were properly designed. The local connection system performance in terms of capacity, stiffness and ductility was investigated by means of refined numerical analyses. A non-linear spring was then calibrated on the connection system response, and its performance was accounted for in the global analyses. The results showed that the design procedure introduced allows for obtaining a good connection system able to resist in the elastic range up to the design demand and to exhibit a ductile behaviour for larger values of imposed displacements. From a global perspective, it was underlined that only if the connection system capacity results in being stiff and resistant, its presence could be disregarded within the global analyses.

title: Experimental assessment of strengthening strategies for enhancing the seismic response of URM walls with arch-type openings
A geometrically nonlinear analysis of tensegrity structures using physics-informed neural networks
Bond-splitting behavior and development length of post-installed reinforcing bars for low-invasive RC bridge slab widening
Light frame wood sheathing-to-rafter connections: Experimental capacity and cyclic behavior analysis
abstract: Tornadoes and hurricanes create high suction pressures on roofs, making the roof sheathing-to-rafter connection a critical part of the structural load path in light-frame wood (LFW). Past studies have characterized the uplift capacity of fastened roof sheathing connections; however, the connection’s cyclic characterization has garnered little research attention and is necessary for robust finite element analysis of LFW structures. Long-duration hurricane winds can induce cyclic loads on roof sheathing, which may weaken fastened connections over time and increase the risk of progressive damage. The present study addresses this gap by investigating the cyclic behavior of twelve variations of LFW sheathing-to-rafter connections, including variations of sheathing type and fastener type and count. Monotonic and cyclic test results are compared and evaluated against empirical capacity estimates calculated using specified design equations. Key cyclic parameters, such as ductility, initial stiffness, energy dissipation, strength degradation, and equivalent viscous damping, are analyzed to capture both the elastic response and progressive deterioration under repeated loading. The results show that the peak capacity under cyclic loading was reduced by approximately 14 – 33% from monotonic loading for nailed connections, with statistically significant reductions observed for the plywood-nail P-N-1F and P-EN-2F configurations. A parametric sensitivity analysis showed that fastener type was the dominant variable affecting cyclic peak capacity, while sheathing type was not statistically significant. Furthermore, nailed connections, particularly with oriented strand board sheathing, exhibit reduced capacities compared to empirical estimates, with measured-to-calculated ratios as low as 68%. These results suggest that current design standards, which primarily rely on monotonic testing, may overestimate actual performance under high-wind conditions. These findings can inform updates to building codes and design standards, guide construction best practices, and enhance the structural resilience of LFW structures in high-wind regions.

title: Shear strength of reinforced concrete columns retrofitted using mini-hybrid-wall technique
abstract: This research developed the shear-resisting mechanism for reinforced concrete (RC) columns retrofitted by casting two concrete walls on both sides, sandwiched by two parallel steel plates and tightened by high-strength steel bars. This is an extension of thick hybrid wall (THW) technique, a technique that increases lateral strength while preserving deformation capacity. Compared with the THW technique, distinct differences were observed in the shear-resisting mechanism of columns retrofitted with two additional walls. Therefore, this extended configuration is termed to as the mini-hybrid wall (MHW) technique to address the observed differences. Previous studies showed that the THW technique transforms the soft-story mechanism of piloti-type buildings and the shear failure of unreinforced masonry wall (URM)-infilled RC frames to the flexural mode. Thus, the MHW technique was investigated as a unified technique for both types of mentioned buildings. Practically, THW cannot be applied on the inner columns of URM-infilled RC frames owing to the existence of masonry walls on both sides of inner columns; hence, addressing this limitation and testing the shear strength of the MHW technique were the main research objectives. Cyclic loading tests were conducted on six retrofitted specimens subjected to axial force. Two specimens represented the application of the MHW technique to piloti-type buildings, two to URM-infilled RC frames, and the remaining two represented THW application to URM-infilled RC frames. Consequently, the shear-resisting mechanism for the MHW technique was developed. This study showed that the MHW technique significantly improves the shear strength of both URM-infilled and piloti-type RC buildings.

title: 3D simulation of masonry bridges under earthquake loading using an enhanced macroscale masonry model with embedded discontinuities
abstract: This paper investigates the 3D response of masonry arch bridges under earthquake loading, focusing on the interaction between the masonry components and the backfill under static and dynamic loading up to collapse. An advanced 3D modelling strategy is employed, in which masonry arches, piers, and spandrel walls are represented by an efficient continuum macroscale model that accurately captures masonry anisotropy through practical calibration of material parameters. Furthermore, zero-thickness plastic-damage interface elements are employed to simulate the interaction between masonry and backfill, which is modelled as a continuum elastoplastic frictional-cohesive material. Two realistic single and multi-span brick-masonry multi-ring arch bridges are investigated. Numerical predictions obtained by the proposed macroscale strategy are compared with detailed, yet more computationally expensive, mesoscale simulations. The results shed light on the complex response of masonry bridges under earthquake loading, confirming the accuracy of the developed macroscale modelling approach, which significantly reduces the computational cost while enabling detailed 3D nonlinear static and dynamic analysis of realistic bridges.

title: Bayesian optimization-based calibration of 3D discrete element models from shake table test data
abstract: Discrete Element (DE) models effectively capture the dynamic behaviour of blocky structures, yet calibrating their parameters remains challenging. This paper presents a Bayesian optimization-based method to calibrate DE models using measured data. The approach is applied to a scaled prototype of a Roman Obelisk tested on a shake table. Stiffness and friction angle of non-linear springs at contacts, and mass-proportional Rayleigh damping, were calibrated to match experimental displacements and frequencies. The method efficiently derived mechanical parameters for the structural model, which accurately predicted the seismic response of the obelisk tested in the laboratory. Results highlight the potential for expanding this technique to field applications, where periodically updated digital twins could support targeted inspection and assessment.

title: Impact responses of circular steel tubes at elevated temperatures: Experimental and numerical studies
Material-based modelling of CLT shear walls considering compression and connection zones
abstract: This study addresses a critical gap in modelling the seismic response of Crosslaminated timber (CLT) shear walls: the lack of a unified approach that simultaneously captures compressiontoe crushing, contact evolution, and connectionzone biaxial/rotational effects for both platform and balloon configurations under cyclic loading. A materialbased FE framework that combines an explicit compressiontoe representation with multiple nonlinear connector elements for connections, e.g., holddowns, implemented using WoodST to model orthotropic damage–plasticity. Eight fullscale balloontype walls (aspect ratios 4:1 and 6:1) were tested under monotonic and cyclic protocols and used to validate the models without parameter calibration. The framework reproduces global load-displacement response, compressionzone migration/length, uplift distribution, and connectionlevel force paths. A simplified model—using elastoplastic CLT, single multiDOF connector per holddown, and M–N–V coupling—achieves close agreement with advanced FE and tests while enabling efficient nonlinear responsehistory analysis. The results provide a practical, scalable path to accurate and computationally efficient seismic analysis and design of masstimber systems.

title: Dynamic response and plastic damage of stiffened steel plates with initial crack subjected to repeated ice impacts
A unified IGA-parameterized level set framework for non-probabilistic reliability-based topology optimization and fast CAD model regeneration
Interval prediction for multi-point displacement of high arch dams based on graph embedding clustering and iTransformer-psLSTM
Rotation capacity of cold-formed hollow columns under cyclic biaxial bending
Fatigue behavior and life prediction of frost-damaged reinforced concrete beams under water submersion: Experimental and numerical study
abstract: Reinforced concrete (RC) bridge deck slabs in cold regions are frequently subjected to both fatigue loading and freeze–thaw cycles (FTC), leading to progressive deterioration. However, current design approaches typically treat these mechanisms independently, which may result in non-conservative service life predictions. To elucidate the influence of FTC on fatigue performance, three-point bending fatigue tests were conducted on RC beams under dry, submerged, and combined FTC and submersion conditions. Under severe frost damage, fatigue life is reduced by 80% relative to wet fatigue and by up to 98.3% relative to dry fatigue. A finite element model was developed and calibrated within a multi-scale computational framework to quantitatively analyze the fatigue behavior of frost-damaged RC beams. Based on numerical and experimental results, an empirical prediction formula was proposed for the reduction factor for wet fatigue life ( R F ) from the relative dynamic modulus of elasticity (RDME).

title: Experimental study on active local flexural strengthening of reinforced concrete beams using near-surface-mounted NiTiNb shape memory alloy wires for wet-joint repair
Coupled bending-shear-torsion behaviors of U-shaped composite girders with corrugated steel webs
abstract: U-shaped composite girders with corrugated steel webs (U-CSW) exhibit considerable promise for widespread implementation in urban rail transit viaducts, owing to their superior prestressing efficiency, excellent shear resistance and effective mitigation of cracking. During service, eccentric loading subjects U-CSW members to coupled bending–shear–torsion interactions, yet the underlying interaction mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. This study systematically investigates the mechanical behavior and failure mechanisms of U-CSW under combined bending–shear–torsion loading, and proposes a predictive approach for determining the ultimate bearing capacity associated with distinct failure modes. Finite element models of U-CSW are developed and validated against available experimental data, followed by comprehensive parametric analyses incorporating key parameters such as the bending-to-torsion ratio, web thickness-to-height ratio, span-to-height ratio, width-to-height ratio, and boundary conditions. The findings indicate that the dominant failure mode of U-CSW shifts from flexural failure to bottom slab shear failure as the bending-to-torsion ratio decreases. Simply supported U-CSW with shorter spans are particularly susceptible to bottom slab shear failure, whereas smaller web thickness-to-height ratios (e.g., 1:250, 1:167, 1:147) promote shear buckling failure in the corrugated steel plates. Through theoretical derivation and numerical simulations, interaction relationships among bending, shear, and torsion are established. These research outcomes offer valuable theoretical support and practical design guidance for the application of U-CSW under eccentric loading scenarios.

title: Progressive collapse resistance of steel modular beam-column substructures enhanced by vertical connections between double beams
Smart structural health monitoring using multi-camera computer vision and edge computing for long-span bridge mode shape identification
abstract: Accurate displacement measurement is critical for reliable structural health monitoring (SHM) and modal identification of large-scale structures. Computer vision–based displacement measurement provides the advantages of long-distance monitoring, non-contact sensing, and easy deployment, making it well suited for civil infrastructure SHM. Nevertheless, its large-scale use remains constrained by the substantial data volume generated from high-frame-rate video and the difficulty of achieving precise synchronization among multiple cameras, which hinder continuous multi-point monitoring on large structures. This study develops and validates an advanced multi-camera edge-computing vision-based 2D displacement measurement system (EdgeCVDMS-II) for synchronized, real-time multi-point displacement tracking and mode shape identification. The system integrates six high-resolution IMX477 cameras with adjustable zoom lens and an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge device, enabling low-latency GPU-accelerated template matching with subpixel refinement. Laboratory validation on a 4 m long simply-supported bridge model demonstrates the displacement measurement accuracy of 0.15 pixel, with a normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) of 1.45% relative to laser displacement sensors and excellent agreement with accelerometer-based modal parameters. Field deployment on a 280 m long span cable-stayed bridge confirms the system’s capability to capture spatially dense low-frequency dynamic displacement responses under ambient excitation at over 100 m stand-off distance. The identified fundamental mode shape achieved strong correlation with accelerometer-derived results (MAC = 0.9724), demonstrating robustness low-order modal identification and serviceability-level structural assessment under real-world conditions. The proposed EdgeCVDMS-II overcomes key limitations of existing vision-based methods by providing synchronized, distributed, and real-time video processing and displacement measurements, extending the applicability of computer vision–based SHM to continuous monitoring of large-scale civil infrastructure.

title: Structural behavior and failure mode of bolted steel moment connections under localized fire: Comparison of conventional and fire-resistant steel
Multi-scale optimization method for metamaterial plates with compression-torsion coupling inertial amplification
Novel self-centering steel beam-to-column connection with shape memory alloy-based web hourglass pins
A low-exponent nonlinear fluid inerter-based damper for structural vibration control: Experiment and numerical investigation
Experimental characterization of sliding and shear mechanisms in EPS-insulated foundations for seismic loading conditions
abstract: Thermally insulated foundation systems with expanded polystyrene (EPS) layers placed beneath reinforced concrete slabs are increasingly used in practice. However, their mechanical behavior under combined normal and cyclic shear loading is not sufficiently documented for structural and seismic analyses. This study presents an experimental investigation of the frictional, shear, and compressive response of EPS-insulated foundation assemblies. Monotonic and cyclic shear tests were performed on single-layer and double-layer EPS configurations, including button–groove connections. The specimens were placed over a waterproofing membrane either freely or bonded with adhesive. The results showed that sliding at the EPS–waterproofing interface governs the response of the assembly. The shear capacity of button–groove connections (approximately 80–100 kPa) and of homogeneous EPS layers (approximately 170 kPa) exceeded the shear stress at sliding initiation. This indicates that failure within EPS material or at the interlayer connection is not expected prior to interface sliding. Static and kinetic friction coefficients were determined as 0.61 and 0.58 for freely placed insulation, and 0.96 and 0.65 for bonded insulation. Limited cyclic tests provided qualitative information on the hysteretic response of the interface. The results suggest that the envelope response may be approximated by a simple elasto-plastic relationship. Compressive tests confirmed that EPS400 panels reached strengths between 440 and 487 kPa at 10% strain and exhibiting progressive densification without brittle failure.

title: Spatial multi-modal vibration suppression using distributed dynamic vibration absorbers: Modeling, optimization and implementation
Seismic damage-state classification of prefabricated steel pipe pile–supported wharves using a global lateral stiffness reduction indicator
Shape-finding for a triple-tower spatial double-cable suspension bridge with upper hangers
Bayesian-based lifetime seismic fragility estimation of tall steel buildings with a time-varying capacity model degraded by wind-induced fatigue damage
Experimental and numerical investigation of CFRP bar-reinforced UHPC columns under eccentric compression
Automation framework for fiber-based modeling and optimization of large-span spatial steel structures
LES simulations of downburst-ABL wind interactions and their impact on building aerodynamic loads
abstract: Downbursts generate localized and non-stationary outflows that differ fundamentally from the quasi-stationary atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) winds used in design standards. However, the combined effects of downburst outflows and background ABL winds on building aerodynamics and loads remain insufficiently characterized. This study employs large-eddy simulation (LES) to investigate the interaction between a downburst-like impinging jet (DB), an ABL wind, and a mid-rise benchmark building. A two-stage validation of the ABL wind-building and isolated DB cases confirmed adequate resolution of turbulent kinetic energy and correct inertial subrange behavior, with good agreement against wind-tunnel data. Combined ABL-DB simulations revealed two dominant flow features: a near-surface accelerating wall jet and an overlying velocity-deficit layer. Above the wall jet, the strong downdraft blocks the background ABL flow from penetrating the high-momentum jet core, producing a marked velocity deficit aloft. The ABL wind breaks the symmetry of the outflow, deflecting the wall jet downstream, shifting stagnation, intensifying near-ground velocities, and elongating the wake. At lower elevations, the peak ABL-DB velocity is approximately 33% higher than the mean ABL-DB value (plateau), highlighting the severe impact of downburst pulse on near-ground wind loading and wind–structure interactions. The building further modifies this compound flow through aerodynamic effects such as edge separation, roof-corner vortices, and downstream recirculation. An energy-based metric, the available dynamic pressure ratio (ADPR), showed strong near-ground energy concentration, with values substantially higher than ABL wind baseline. Surface pressure and integrated force analyses demonstrated that peak lateral loads under ABL-DB wind can exceed windward streamwise loads by up to 1.5 times. The results show that transient ABL-DB interactions fundamentally alter the building loading hierarchy, with lateral facades often governing, and must be explicitly considered in performance-based wind design.

title: Experimental study of wind loads on circularly perforated thin porous structures
Shaking table tests on seismic response of prefabricated subway station with tenon-bolted connecting joints
Experimental and numerical full-scale investigation of a large triangular laminated insulating glass unit in bending under quasi-static loading
abstract: Large laminated insulating glass units (IGUs) with thin glass panes are increasingly used in lightweight structures, while experimental data under high uniform loads remain limited. This paper presents a case study on full-scale tests and nonlinear Finite Element (FE) simulations of large triangular IGUs subjected to quasi-static hydrostatic pressure. Three IGUs with an area of 4.26 m 2 and defined boundary conditions were tested to failure. Each unit consisted of two laminated panes of 6-mm-thick fully tempered glass with 1.52-mm-thick PVB interlayers and a 15-mm-thick cavity Water pressure, cavity pressure, pane deflections, and surface strains were measured. A nonlinear FE model including geometric nonlinearity, shear transfer, and load sharing between the panes was constructed and experimentally validated. The results show that nonlinear effects occur at relatively low load levels and become dominant with increasing deflection. At the maximum load, the average ultimate pressure was 74.5 kPa and the maximum deflection was 81 mm, corresponding to a deflection-to-thickness ratio of ∼ 6.8 based on the 12-mm total glass thickness of one laminated pane. At maximum load, the cavity pressure reached up to 45% of the applied load. The FE model predicted center deflections within ∼ 5% of the measured values and reached good overall stress agreement. The results indicate that linear approaches significantly underestimate the response of such large IGUs under increasing loads, highlighting the need for nonlinear FE analysis in similar configurations.

Synergy between ultra-high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete (UHP-FRC) and longitudinal bars in thin panels under flexure
abstract: Ultra-high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete offers high strength, ductility, and durability, making it attractive for lightweight modular and marine structures. However, the optimal reinforcement strategy for advanced concrete remains unclear, particularly when considering thin-section applications and corrosion-resistant alternatives to steel. This study investigates the flexural behavior of thin structural panels made with ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC), ultra-high-strength engineered cementitious composites (ECC), or lightweight ECC. The longitudinal reinforcements include steel, carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP), and hybrid steel-FRP composite (SFC) bars, while a stiffness-equivalent design was adopted to ensure comparable axial stiffness. Four-point bending tests were conducted to evaluate cracking performance, deflection capacity, failure mode, and energy absorption. Results showed that concrete ductility and bar type strongly influence the flexural performance. Steel-reinforced panels yielded in a ductile manner but had relatively low peak loads. CFRP-reinforced panels showed significantly higher peak loads (up to ~30 kN, nearly double that of steel case) but failed in a brittle manner. SFC-reinforced panels achieved high strength while maintaining ductility via a bi-linear response. Notably, ECC panels exhibited multiple fine cracks (<0.2 mm even near peak load) and large deformability, and showed significantly higher toughness and deformation capacity than UHPC panels. These findings highlight that combining lightweight, ductile ECC with corrosion-resistant bars yields thin structural panels with excellent flexural capacity, ductility, crack control, and weight efficiency, suited for modular construction and marine environments.

Experimental out-of-plane seismic response of URM gables: Role of roof flexibility and differential input
abstract: Low-rise masonry buildings around the world often include unreinforced masonry (URM) walls combined with pitched roofs that are supported or enclosed by masonry gables. Such buildings constitute a significant portion of the built environment in several earthquake-prone regions, affected by either natural or induced seismicity. Masonry gables in these structures have repeatedly shown high seismic vulnerability to out-of-plane excitations, as documented in post-earthquake survey studies. This paper presents the main outcomes of an experimental campaign carried out within the ERIES-SUPREME project to increase the understanding in URM gable out-of-plane seismic response. Three full-scale, densely instrumented gable specimens were tested using a dual shake-table configuration and subjected to incremental dynamic excitations up to collapse, simulating both induced and tectonic earthquake scenarios. The experimental tests examined the influence of differential motions between the top and base of the gable wall, either linearly amplified or both amplified and out-of-phase, implemented by the two tables to reproduce the interaction with three distinct roof diaphragm configurations. Experimental results are discussed in terms of observed failure mechanisms, hysteretic force-displacement behaviour, as well as acceleration and displacement capacities. In particular, increasing roof diaphragm flexibility leads to earlier activation of the out-of-plane failure mechanism and to a marked reduction in collapse acceleration at the gable base, while the acceleration at ridge level provides a more consistent representation of the effective seismic demand acting on the gables.

Experimental investigation on seismic performance of a new precast segmental self-centering bridge column with varying-strength external dissipators
abstract: Precast segmental self-centering (PSS) bridge columns offer damage-controllable seismic performance, but current designs of PSS columns employing uniform-strength or base-only energy dissipator configurations exhibit concentrated gap-opening deformation and limited efficiency. This study proposes a new PSS column with varying-strength dissipator arrangement and evaluates its effectiveness through six full-scale quasi-static tests. The results indicated that the PSS columns with multi-joint dissipator configurations substantially outperform those with base-only arrangements. Among multi-joint dissipator specimens, the proposed varying-strength configuration maintains comparable strength to uniformly strong dissipators while providing significant advantages in other aspects. It transforms the deformation pattern from concentrated opening at a single joint to balanced distribution across multiple interfaces, reducing maximum joint opening distance by half. This balanced behavior results in higher equivalent damping ratio and controlled prestress loss. For the PSS columns with base-only dissipator configurations, the seismic performance proves less satisfactory. Their mechanical performance and energy dissipation capacity show limited improvement over the benchmark specimen without dissipators. Dissipator strength in these columns requires careful selection, as excessive strength instead degrades the energy dissipation efficiency and increases the risk of tendon yielding. Remarkably, simply adding a small-strength dissipator at the second joint from the base substantially improves the seismic performance. Moreover, practical design recommendations for the proposed multi-segment PSS bridge columns are suggested based on the experimental findings.

Efficacy of external guy-wires in reducing wind-induced response of super-tall towers: Experimental and PBWE analyses
abstract: Performance-based wind engineering (PBWE) has garnered recognition as a critical approach for the design and analysis of high-rise buildings, which are particularly vulnerable to wind-induced loads. This study proposes to examine the PBWE methodology for a unique structural system, a super-tall building tower supported by external guy-wires. Two reduced-scale models (rigid and aeroelastic) are tested in two wind tunnels to quantify experimental errors and inter-laboratory discrepancies. The aeroelastic model test results are compared against numerical predictions (at model scale) using, as generalized wind loads, the measurements carried out on the rigid model. The numerical predictions of the building rooftop lateral dynamic displacement standard deviations align reasonably well with the experimental measurements, found in the aeroelastic test. Some discrepancies are observed between experimental across-wind displacement standard deviations and numerical results; they are attributed to different laboratory and turbulence conditions. Finally, the PBWE analysis is employed to predict the structural fragility functions of the peak lateral rooftop displacements on an archetypic full-scale super-tall structure, equipped with external guy-wires.

Reliability-based seismic performance assessment of single-pier hybrid coupled walls with hinged base and corner components
abstract: This study concerns single-pier hybrid coupled walls (SP-HCWs), a recently proposed alternative to conventional hybrid coupled walls (HCWs), the latter consisting of two reinforced concrete (RC) walls coupled by steel links. In SP-HCWs, a single RC wall is coupled to two steel side columns through steel links. This configuration simplifies the RC wall response under horizontal actions and reduces the amount of concrete in favour of steel, enabling faster erection, easier post-earthquake repair, and improved disassembly at the end of service life. To further enhance seismic performance, an alternative base detail for the RC wall was introduced, i.e., a hinged wall–foundation connection combined with vertical steel corner components. Previous numerical investigations based on nonlinear static (pushover) analyses highlighted the potential of SP-HCWs proportioned according to a specifically developed design approach, for both cases of fixed and hinged bases. The present study advances the assessment of SP-HCWs and their design method by moving from static to nonlinear time-history analyses, explicitly accounting for uncertainties in the seismic input. The resulting response dataset is exploited to perform seismic reliability analyses to evaluate the ability of the proposed design method to maintain the probability of failure under satisfactory levels as well as to derive behaviour (q) factors. The outcomes provide a deeper understanding of the seismic performance of SP-HCWs, fostering possible future real-world applications.

Large-scale long-term transient topology optimization method based on improved Duhamel integral
abstract: While transient topology optimization is essential for dynamic engineering applications, large-scale long-term problems remain computationally prohibitive due to the iterative nature of conventional time-integration schemes like the Newmark-β method. To improve design efficiency and accuracy, we propose an efficient optimization framework based on the Duhamel integral to solve large-scale problems with high degrees of freedom (DOFs) under prolonged loading. By integrating modal reduction to transform large-scale systems into decoupled single-degree-of-freedom problems, we derive an efficient recursive transient responses and utilize the Modal Acceleration Method (MAM) to ensure accuracy against high-order mode truncation. Unlike traditional numerical integration, this analytical approach ensures unconditional stability even with larger time steps and enables direct sensitivity analysis through explicit formulations. Numerical examples involving millions of DOFs and long durations demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational cost, making large-scale transient topology optimization practically tractable.

A novel TMD parameter design method for multiple-mode vortex-induced vibration control of bridges characterized by closely spaced modes
abstract: In recent years, as bridge spans continuously increase, the number of bridges characterized by closely spaced modes has grown rapidly, making multiple-mode vortex-induced-vibration (VIV) control increasingly challenging. Classical tuned mass damper (TMD) parameter design approaches are typically based on the mode-by-mode design method, which performs well for bridges characterized by widely spaced modes. However, for bridges characterized by closely spaced modes, the commonly used assumption of simplifying the bridge-TMD system into a two-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) model becomes invalid. This study first demonstrates that mode coupling commonly exists in bridge-TMD systems and that it can be effectively eliminated through an appropriate selection of TMD installation locations. It is further revealed that mode coupling exerts a pronounced influence on the VIV response of the bridge, the optimal TMD parameters, and the resulting control efficiency. Therefore, for a bridge characterized by closely spaced modes, it is essential to analyze the bridge-TMD system using a multiple-mode method that accounts for both resonance and non-resonance modes. Based on the above findings, a novel TMD parameter design method is proposed for multiple-mode VIV control of bridges characterized by closely spaced modes, and its effectiveness is verified through numerical analyses on several continuous girder bridges. The results demonstrate that the TMD designed using the proposed method achieves significantly higher control efficiency than that designed by the classical mode-by-mode design method.

title: Collaborative mechanism of multi-cavity-column steel frame–SPSW structures and energy-based seismic damage analysis

Tensile stress-strain models for quenched and tempered high-strength structural steels after fire exposure
abstract: Quenched and tempered (QT) high-strength structural steels (nominal yield stresses 690−960 MPa) have tempered martensitic microstructures that provide high strength but also make them susceptible to degradation under fire exposure compared with conventional mild steels. This deterioration affects their post-fire mechanical behaviour. Although extensive experimental data on the residual properties of QT steels after exposure to elevated temperatures are available, unified stress–strain models covering different grades are still lacking because of the complex influence of multiple parameters. In this study, 209 post-fire stress–strain curves were collected from published studies, together with results from 16 additional tests by the authors, to examine the effects of exposure temperature, heat soak time, cooling rate and steel grade on residual mechanical performance. A criterion was established to distinguish between discontinuous yielding (with a yield plateau) and continuous yielding (without a plateau) in the post-fire stress–strain behaviour. Two corresponding stress–strain models were formulated to predict the residual mechanical response of QT steels after fire exposure. The proposed models show close agreement with experimental data and can be used for the post-fire evaluation and rehabilitation of QT steel structures.

Three-dimensional damage visualization of civil structures via Gaussian Splatting-enabled digital twins
abstract: Recent advancements in civil infrastructure inspections underscore the need for precise three-dimensional (3D) damage visualization on digital twins, transcending traditional 2D image-based damage identifications. Compared to conventional photogrammetric 3D reconstruction techniques, modern approaches such as Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and Gaussian Splatting (GS) excel in scene representation, rendering quality, and handling featureless regions. Among them, GS stands out for its efficiency, leveraging discrete anisotropic 3D Gaussians to represent radiance fields, unlike NeRF's continuous implicit model. This study introduces a GS-enabled digital twin method tailored for effective 3D damage visualization. The method's key contributions include: 1) utilizing GS-based 3D reconstruction to visualize 2D damage segmentation results while reducing segmentation errors; 2) developing a multi-scale reconstruction strategy to balance efficiency and damage detail; 3) enabling digital twin updates as damage evolves over time. Demonstrated on an open-source synthetic dataset for post-earthquake inspections, the proposed approach offers a promising solution for comprehensive 3D damage visualization in civil infrastructure digital twins.

Effect of concrete triaxial confinement on the nodal-zone efficiency of concrete deep beams reinforced with GFRP bars
abstract: This study examined the effect of concrete triaxial confinement on the nodal-zone efficiency of concrete deep beams reinforced with glass ﬁber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) bars. Eight large-scale GFRP-reinforced concrete deep beams and one steel-reinforced concrete deep beam (reference)—all with web reinforcement—were tested to failure under two-point loading. The only variation in the specimens was the dimensions of the loading and/or supporting plates relative to the concrete beam width. All other factors—such as the shear-span depth ratio, main reinforcement ratio, and specimen geometry—were kept constant. The failure mode of the tested specimens was identified as diagonal strut compression failure, except for the fully confined specimens that experienced diagonal shear failure. In addition, the results confirm the formation of arch action in the tested specimens, as evidenced by the cracking pattern and measured strain along the longitudinal reinforcement. On the other hand, the results reveal that both the flexural and diagonal crack widths remained below the limits specified in CSA and ACI standards governing GFRP-reinforced concrete structures. Additionally, the results confirm that triaxial concrete confinement is effective in GFRP-reinforced concrete deep beams, with the confinement efficiency increasing from 81% for the non-confined specimen to 119% for the fully confined specimen.

Simplified tying-bending model for robustness assessment of floor systems under corner column loss
abstract: In the context of structural robustness, floor systems subject to corner column loss have been perceived to be unable to offer resistance via tensile membrane action, due to the apparent lack of planar restraint to tying forces at the outer edges, relying instead on bending action. This paper challenges this perception and investigates the mobilisation of tensile membrane action in uniformly loaded floor systems under corner column loss, utilising in the first instance reinforcement that is diagonal to the edges of the corner floor system. A novel simplified analytical method is proposed, which captures the development of tensile membrane action with restrained inner edges of the corner floor system, considering the two dominant resistance mechanisms: i) tying and ii) bending. Following the exposition of its formulation, the proposed method is verified against nonlinear finite element analysis that is also validated against experimental results, demonstrating the effectiveness of the developed simplified model in predicting the tying response of floor systems under corner column loss. Importantly, the outcomes of this paper suggest that tying can be effective in corner floor systems, even those with the typical orthogonal reinforcement layout, provided that both the top and bottom reinforcements are continuous over the supports and within the floor slab. In this respect, the proposed simplified model offers for the first time the capability for considering tensile membrane action in the robustness assessment and design of floor systems under corner column loss.

Marker-free mobile inspection system for bridge apparent cracks: Fusing vision and low-cost triple-laser module for high-precision localization and quantification
Multi-objective optimization of seismic upgrading interventions in existing RC buildings
abstract: Existing reinforced concrete (RC) structures designed before the implementation of modern seismic codes often exhibit inadequate seismic performances and high vulnerability to earthquake-induced damage. Seismic retrofitting is therefore crucial for addressing construction deficiencies in non-conforming RC buildings, ensuring structural safety, and mitigating seismic risk. However, this task is not straightforward, owing to two key challenges. First, identifying the critical structural members that require retrofitting, along with determining the appropriate type and extent of retrofit, has a major impact on the overall effectiveness of the intervention. Second, conventional retrofitting design approaches often rely on subjective judgments only, typically resulting in non-optimal solutions that prioritize compliance with seismic safety standards while overlooking economic and environmental aspects. To overcome these challenges and support more informed decisions, this study introduces a novel computational framework for optimizing seismic retrofit interventions in RC buildings taking into account a wide range of potential strengthening techniques. It employs a multi-objective genetic algorithm to effectively manage conflicting design criteria, including cost minimization, safety improvement, and reduction of expected losses, with consideration of payback time and embodied carbon at the end of the optimization procedure to guide the selection of the final retrofitting scheme. Application to a case study highlights the capability of this approach to determine the optimal typology, location, and size of each retrofitting intervention by exploring common strengthening techniques, such as fiber-reinforced polymer wrapping, steel jacketing, steel braces, or combinations thereof. The seismic performance of the optimized retrofitted structure is finally evaluated via nonlinear dynamic analyses.

title: Experimental investigation of cross-laminated timber panels subjected to near-field blast loads
abstract: Research on the performance of structural timber elements subjected to near-field blast loads is lacking, with no known comprehensive experimental studies available to inform design standards and hazard mitigation strategies. This paper presents the results of an experimental test programme investigating the behaviour of cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels subjected to near-field blast loads. Full-scale specimens of varying panel depth were subjected to varying charge weights and standoff distances for the purpose of qualitative and quantitative characterization of behaviour at close-in ranges. Quasi-static three-point bending testing was conducted to establish a baseline in terms of mechanical properties and overall failure modes. When compared to far-field blast loads, the CLT panel specimens were found to be susceptible to localized damage and failure mechanisms, including as surface perpendicular-to-grain damage in compression, as well as delamination of outer laminates, accompanied by significant finger joint failures occurring within the outer laminates. In addition, by comparing quasi-static and dynamic strengths of the experimentally tested specimens, an average dynamic increase factor (DIF) of unity on the resistance was observed.

Fire tests on RC columns jacketed by FRP with a silicon-based matrix
abstract: This paper presents an experimental study conducted to investigate the feasibility of implementing an inorganic silicon-based matrix (SBM) as a matrix replacement for fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP) rehabilitation, aiming to address the dilemma of poor thermal performance associated with conventional FRP rehabilitation schemes. The presented work utilises typical carbon fibre sheets to demonstrate the feasibility of its implementation without the need for fibre mesh, unlike conventional approaches used with inorganic matrices (i.e., due to lower fibre-matrix compatibility) when replacing polymeric systems to enhance thermal response. Nine full-scale RC columns were tested under different conditions to validate the performance of SBM FRP and assess its practicality in fulfilling structural requirements at both ambient and fire conditions. The results revealed that the column with the SBM FRP scheme can match up to 84% of the capacity of a conventional epoxy-based FRP jacketed column at ambient conditions due to relatively lower matrix-to-fibre compatibility. The superior performance of the columns jacketed with SBM FRP, along with a relatively thin layer of insulation, was confirmed after surviving a 7-hour fire exposure at various load levels. The presented results are unprecedented, as no FRP system in the literature has been reported to withstand such exposure durations and load levels. Conversely, conventional FRP schemes typically fail prematurely due to their low glass transition temperature ( T g ) and the fact that they ignite in the presence of oxygen. The enhancement in the mechanical performance of the SBM FRP scheme for post-heating and fire conditions is primarily attributed to its high thermal stability and fibre-matrix compatibility. The results confirmed the promising potential of the proposed novel SBM FRP scheme as a viable alternative to traditional polymeric FRP schemes for practical use under ambient and fire conditions.

title: Editorial Board
Comparative evaluation of fan anchor and NSM–CFRP retrofits for slip mitigation in flexure–critical substandard RC columns
abstract: Substandard reinforced concrete (RC) columns constructed with plain round bars and low-strength concrete are highly susceptible to bond-slip degradation and rocking-dominated flexural failure under lateral loads. This study presents an experimental investigation on the cyclic performance of bond-critical RC columns retrofitted with Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) using two distinct anchorage strategies: fan anchors and near-surface-mounted (NSM) reinforcement. 12 full-scale cantilever specimens, representative of pre-1990s Mediterranean construction practice, were tested under lateral cyclic loading combined with constant axial compression. The test parameters included axial load ratio, longitudinal reinforcement end anchorage detailing, and the retrofit configuration. Experimental results revealed that reference specimens exhibited more pronounced pinching and limited energy dissipation compared to retrofitted ones. Experimental moment-curvature analysis confirmed severe curvature localization at the column base due to slip-dominated behavior in reference specimens. While the NSM retrofit yielded the highest increase in lateral strength, it was characterized by distinct post-peak strength deterioration triggered by epoxy–concrete interface failure. In contrast, the fan anchor retrofit significantly enhanced energy dissipation capacity and post-peak stability. Both retrofit strategies successfully reduced curvature localization, delaying damage localization and rocking-dominated response.

title: Performance evaluation of novel inerter-based vibrating barrier configurations
abstract: A vibrating barrier is a non-invasive approach for mitigating seismic effects on buildings. Recent developments have integrated inerter-based dampers, consisting of an inerter, a spring, and a dashpot arranged in various configurations, into vibrating barriers, leading to the concept of the inerter-based vibrating barrier (IViBa). Unlike conventional applications in which inerter-based dampers are embedded within the host structure where they modify the structural dynamic properties, their use as ground-installed barriers introduces a different interaction mechanism, altering wave propagation and soil–structure interaction, and consequently leading to distinct tuning and optimisation characteristics. This study addresses this gap through an investigation of IViBa configurations and their governing parameters. To date, only one IViBa configuration has been reported. This work introduces three alternative configurations derived from different arrangements of the inerter, spring, and dashpot. The influence of secondary mass and dashpot placement is examined, with performance optimised using H ∞ and H 2 criteria implemented via the Self-Adaptive Differential Evolution algorithm and the Kanai–Tajimi filter. The results show that the newly proposed IViBa configurations with parallel inerter–dashpot configuration achieve performance comparable to the existing IViBa while requiring approximately 96% lower damping. In the time-domain simulations, the proposed time-domain optimisation yields the best structural performance for the case considered, achieving about 27% reduction in both RMS and peak responses compared to the uncontrolled case. This is followed by the H ∞ and H 2 optimisation methods, which provide average response reductions of approximately 24% and 22%, respectively. These results define a clear design framework in which optimal inertance and configuration selection govern performance, enabling efficient and practically achievable IViBa solutions for seismic response mitigation.

title: Rubik’s cube inspired magnetic array with high-efficiency negative stiffness for space-constrained quasi-zero-stiffness vibration isolation
Staircase Cascaded Fusion of lightweight local pattern recognition and long-range dependencies for structural crack segmentation
abstract: Accurately segmenting structural cracks at the pixel level remains a major hurdle, as existing methods fail to integrate local textures with pixel dependencies, often leading to fragmented and incomplete predictions. Moreover, their high parameter counts and substantial computational demands hinder practical deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. To address these challenges, we propose CrackSCF, a Lightweight Cascaded Fusion Crack Segmentation Network designed to achieve robust crack segmentation with exceptional computational efficiency. We design a lightweight convolutional block (LRDS) to replace all standard convolutions. This approach efficiently captures local patterns while operating with a minimal computational footprint. For a holistic perception of crack structures, a lightweight Long-range Dependency Extractor (LDE) captures global dependencies. These are then intelligently unified with local patterns by our Staircase Cascaded Fusion Module (SCFM), ensuring the final segmentation maps are both seamless in continuity and rich in fine-grained detail. To comprehensively evaluate our method, this paper created the challenging TUT benchmark dataset and evaluated it alongside five other public datasets. The experimental results show that the CrackSCF method consistently outperforms the existing methods, and it demonstrates greater robustness in dealing with complex background noise. On the TUT dataset, CrackSCF achieved 0.8382 on F1 score and 0.8473 on mIoU, and it only required 4.79M parameters.

title: Data-driven prediction and interpretable analysis of shear capacity in PBL connectors
Dynamic reliability analysis of high earth-rockfill dams under non-stationary and non-Gaussian ground motions using an L-moment-based simplified quintic HPM
Finite element modeling of post-tensioned concrete beams with grout defects and evolution of strand corrosion in time
