Experimental validation and surrogate-assisted evolutionary optimization on polyline-based core sandwich structures
Moving mass-induced transient response of functionally graded and functionally graded graphene nanoplatelet-reinforced composite curved beams via quasi-3D finite element analysis
abstract: The transient response of functionally graded (FG) and graphene nanoplatelet-reinforced composite (GPLRC) curved beams under moving mass excitation is investigated using a quasi-3D finite element formulation. Such excitation is relevant to curved structural components carrying travelling vehicles, payloads, or mechanical devices, for which the inertia of the moving body interacts with the structure. The model extends a five-variable shear and normal deformation theory to the moving mass problem and incorporates the associated inertia, Coriolis, and centrifugal effects together with Newmark time integration. Parametric studies are conducted to evaluate the effects of speed ratio, beam curvature, slenderness ratio, material gradation, and graphene reinforcement on the dynamic amplification factor. The moving mass model consistently predicts higher amplification than the moving load idealisation, with differences of 2–5% due to inertia interaction between the travelling mass and the structure. The maximum response occurs when the moving mass travels at approximately half the critical speed. Curvature has a pronounced influence on the response, while increasing slenderness reduces the response. The power-law index significantly affects the response at low values, where rapid changes occur during the material transition. Among reinforcement patterns, the X-type distribution yields the lowest amplification, whereas the O-type produces the highest. These findings clarify the combined effects of beam curvature, material gradation, and moving mass inertia on the transient behaviour of advanced curved composite beams.

title: Brittle failure in steel-to-timber connections with rebar off-cuts: Experimental, analytical, and numerical assessment
abstract: This study investigates the use of steel rebars as mechanical fasteners in steel-to-timber connections. Specimens with five different configurations using rebars and smooth dowels were experimentally tested, with most configurations designed to promote brittle failure of the timber. Beyond the practical motivation of using controlled rebar off-cuts, the study aims to clarify how ribbed fastener geometry and the associated increase in fastener–timber friction influence stress redistribution and the transition between brittle failure mechanisms in multi-fastener connections. With the increasing number of fasteners, the corresponding failure modes shifted from ductile behavior, characterized by fastener bending and timber embedment, to brittle failure modes, including row shear, splitting, and block shear. For specimens with identical fastener arrangements, those using rebars generally resulted in higher load-carrying capacity and steeper initial load–slip responses than those using smooth dowels. The experimental observations indicate that ribbed rebars do not merely increase resistance, but also modify the governing brittle mechanism by promoting broader stress transfer and a greater tendency toward row-shear or block-shear failure. This observed difference in mechanical response is attributed to differences in friction coefficients between rebars and smooth dowels in the timber member, as reflected in the number of fracture planes observed in failed specimens. Analytical formulas from the new Eurocode 5 draft were also adopted to predict the capacities of failed specimens. In addition, a numerical model based on linear-elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) was employed to predict the capacity and interpret the friction-driven stress redistribution responsible for the different failure mechanisms between connections with smooth dowels and rebars.

title: Flexural behavior and stability of continuous composite beams using NSS and HSS castellated I-sections and slabs of NSC and UHPC
abstract: When steel castellated I-beams are connected to a concrete slab through shear connectors, resulting in steel-concrete composite alveolar beams, their flexural performance is significantly enhanced in terms of bending stiffness and ultimate moment. This performance can be further improved by using high-performance materials, such as high-strength steel (HSS) and ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC). In continuous composite beams, the advantages over simply supported beams include improved deflection control and a reduced maximum sagging moment. At the same time, the support regions of continuous composite beams are subjected to hogging moments, where the steel profile is under compression and the concrete slab is under tension. In these regions, the concrete slab may experience severe cracking, and the steel I-beams may reach lateral-distortional buckling (LDB). This paper examines the flexural behavior and stability of continuous steel-concrete composite beams with normal-strength steel (NSS) and (HSS) castellated I-sections and slabs of normal-strength (NSC) and (UHPC), with a focus on the occurrence of LDB and its coupling with local instability modes. Additionally, some possibilities for reducing the steel and concrete consumption in composite beams are verified, including the replacement of conventional NSS solid I-sections and NSC slabs with NSS or HSS castellated I-sections and UHPC slabs, respectively. Numerical models considering linear buckling analyses and geometrically and materially nonlinear analyses with imperfections are used in this study. The results showed that the gains in bearing capacity, resulting from increasing the steel yield strength, are more pronounced for I-sections with higher dimensions. Another observation is that the expansion rate of 1.6 for the castellated beams presented these elements as more susceptible to Web-Post Buckling (WPB) occurrence, which reduced their bearing capacity compared to the expansion rates of 1.4 and 1.5. Replacing the NSC slab (height of 100 mm) with a thinner UHPC slab (height of 75 mm) did not produce significant changes in the load-deflection curves, suggesting that concrete consumption can be reduced when using UHPC without compromising structural response. Finally, the updates in the European and Brazilian standards for LDB resistance prediction were assessed. The Brazilian code showed higher accuracy than Eurocode 4, without significantly overestimating the ultimate moment of the beams, with a maximum overestimation of 2.9%.

title: Wind-induced coupled lateral-torsional response of tall buildings using bidirectional tuned mass damper inerter
Seismic retrofit of corroded RC columns using textile reinforced UHTCC jackets and near-surface-mounted BFRP bars
abstract: Corroded reinforced concrete (RC) columns usually require retrofitting to ensure the seismic safety of engineering structures. This study employs an innovative combined strengthening system, comprising textile-reinforced ultra-high toughness cementitious composite (UHTCC) jackets and near-surface-mounted (NSM) BFRP (basalt fiber reinforced polymer) reinforcement, referred to as the TRU-NSM system. In this study, the seismic behavior of six corroded RC columns strengthened with the TRU-NSM system was investigated through cyclic lateral loading tests. The test variables included corrosion ratios, stirrup ratios, and axial load ratios. The experimental results indicated that the TRU jacket can effectively restrain shear deformation and concrete cracking in the plastic hinge zone, and all the strengthened specimens showed ductile flexural failure. When the corrosion ratio was below 13.59%, the seismic resistance of corroded columns can be effectively restored. Despite severe corrosion damage to the stirrups, the TRU jacket can still provide sufficient transverse confinement. With an increase in axial load ratio from 0.25 to 0.4, the ultimate load-bearing capacity of the strengthened columns increased by 1.12 times, but its deformation capacity was reduced apparently. Although the NSM reinforcement could enhance the peak load to some extent, early failure of the BFRP bars at a drift ratio of 3% to 5% resulted in a limited effect on their deformation and ductility. Furthermore, a numerical model that accounts for the slip effects of corroded reinforcement and BFRP bars was proposed to predict the hysteretic curves of TRU-NSM-strengthened corroded RC columns.

title: Shear capacity prediction and influence of a/d ratio, horizontal web reinforcement ratio and size of openings in RC deep beams
A TCN-PatchTST framework for efficient reconstruction of missing acceleration data in bridge structural health monitoring
Experimental study of size effect on shear-controlled hollow clay brick unreinforced masonry walls under in-plane shear-compression loading
abstract: Drift capacity of unreinforced masonry walls (URM) is a key parameter for seismic assessment and design. Although previous studies have established its dependence on wall size for flexural and hybrid failure modes, this relationship remains unclear for walls failing in shear. This study investigates how wall size influences the in-plane drift capacity of hollow clay brick URM walls in walls with shear-controlled behaviour. Six quasi-static shear-compression tests were conducted on walls of three heights (1.4 m, 2.0 m and 2.8 m), with the same aspect ratio, material properties and boundary conditions, and with two levels of compression load. Results show that small walls exhibit significantly higher drift capacity than medium and large walls, supporting previous recommendations to adopt a minimum testing height of 1.5 m when deriving drift capacities from experiments. From a mechanical perspective, the ratio of shear-to-flexural displacement was found similar across the wall sizes, indicating it is not responsible for the observed drift differences. Digital Image Correlation measurements revealed that at a given drift, crack widths were smaller in small walls, while at a given limit state, crack widths were similar across all sizes. This suggests that crack width could be used as a size-independent indicator of limit state attainment, despite the challenges associated with quantifying this parameter in certain numerical models. Future research should examine the applicability of these findings to other masonry typologies.

title: Performance analysis of long-span arch bridges against transversal fault rupture within fault-dislocation influence zones using multi-scale modeling
Seismic retrofit of masonry walls using engineered cementitious composites: Experimental insights, numerical modeling, and design recommendations
abstract: Masonry structures typically exhibit limited seismic resilience and a pronounced tendency toward brittle failure. While engineered cementitious composites (ECC) have shown promise as effective materials for seismic retrofitting, comparative studies examining different ECC reinforcement layouts and their mechanistic foundations remain scarce. To bridge this knowledge gap, this research systematically evaluates the seismic performance of full-scale masonry walls strengthened with three ECC configurations: full-surface overlay, cross-strip, and beam-column strip. The investigation employs quasi-static testing, detailed numerical simulations, and theoretical analysis. Results reveal that ECC overlays markedly affect failure modes, transitioning the brittle shear–compression response into more ductile, composite failure mechanisms. The double-sided full-surface overlay proved most effective, enhancing cumulative energy dissipation by up to 407% and ultimate load capacity by 57%. Single-sided full-surface overlays and cross-strip reinforcement also improved ultimate load capacity, by 42% and 24%, respectively. Key influencing parameters, such as vertical stress and ECC tensile strength, were identified, and corresponding shear capacity calculation methods were developed. Finite element analysis confirmed strong agreement between predicted and experimental results, with mean ratios ranging from 0.89 to 1.17 across the three reinforcement strategies, underscoring the reliability of the proposed models. This study clarifies the underlying mechanisms and performance variations among different ECC retrofit configurations, offering validated theoretical frameworks and actionable design recommendations for engineering practice.

title: Vibroacoustic analysis of graphene platelet–reinforced metal foams cylindrical shells coupled with annular plates
Nonlinear vibration suppression of elastically restrained GPL-reinforced porous nanocomposite beams using an inertial nonlinear energy sink
Residual stress model for hot-rolled steel I-sections
abstract: Residual stresses are self-equilibrating internal stresses that exist within structural members in the absence of external loads. In hot-rolled steel I-sections, these stresses develop primarily during manufacturing due to uneven cooling. Their distribution and amplitude can significantly influence the stability and ultimate strength of steel members; however, existing predictive models often fall short in terms of their accuracy. This limitation is addressed in the current paper by first reviewing existing models and compiling the most extensive residual stress database to date, comprising measurements on over 190 cross-sections from the global literature, and then proposing a new predictive model. Analysis of the collected residual stress measurements reveals several critical insights. The data show that (1) a bi-linear distribution best describes the residual stress pattern within the flanges, while the web stress distribution is most accurately represented by a parabolic distribution, (2) there is net tension in the flanges, balanced by net compression in the web in deeper I-sections, (3) the residual stress amplitudes are not dependent on the material yield strength and (4) in contrast to the existing ECCS model, there is a gradual variation in residual stress amplitude with cross-section height-to-width ( h / b ) ratio. Based on these findings, refined and experimentally validated predictive models in which the key stress amplitudes are a continuous function of h / b are proposed. Overall, the proposed model enhances the consistency, range of applicability and accuracy of the prediction of residual stresses in hot-rolled steel I-sections, which is essential for facilitating the growing use of advanced computational methods in the analysis and design of steel structures.

title: Simplified modeling of inter-module connections with combined load interactions in modular steel construction
Free vibration of rotating origami-inspired folded graphene-reinforced copper twisted cylindrical curved plate
Continuous quantum-inspired multi-objective optimization for robust structural damage identification under temperature variations
Experimental and analytical investigation of 6-panel frameless cold-formed steel corrugated wall system subjected to in-plane loads
The ellipsoidal head of a multi-bubble pressure tank: Concept and principles
From uniform reliability to uniform failure risk in seismic design: A framework consistent with EN 1998–1-1:2024
Hysteretic behavior of InorgBam-steel composite columns under cyclic loading
Design scheme for high-performance and environment-oriented composite beams with puzzle-shaped shear connectors under cyclic loading
Accuracy analysis of membrane antennas considering prestress and structural clearance
Experimental investigation on precast spiral reinforcement lightweight aggregate concrete confined normal concrete columns under eccentric compression
Seismic performance of modular steel buildings with a composite strengthening system incorporating grouted connections and modular composite columns
Anti-progressive collapse performance analysis and enhancement of cold-formed steel framed substructure
abstract: Cold-formed steel framed (CSF) structures are widely used due to their high strength-to-weight ratio and construction efficiency. However, their thin-walled members and open cross-sections increase susceptibility to local failure, rendering them more vulnerable to progressive collapse than conventional hot-rolled steel frame structures following the loss of a critical member. This study investigates the anti-progressive collapse behavior of a CSF substructure under a middle column removal scenario through quasi-static testing and numerical simulation analysis, focusing on failure mechanisms, internal force redistribution, and resistance evolution. The findings reveal that the collapse resistance of the substructure is critically governed by the performance of beam–column connections; adequately robust connections facilitate the development of catenary action, thereby enhancing the load-carrying capacity. The entire load-bearing process can be characterized by four sequential stages: elastic, elastic-plastic, transitional, and failure fluctuation. The predominant failure modes involve fracture of angle steels and bolts at the middle column connection. To address the limited collapse resistance of the CSF connection, an improved connection is proposed, resulting in increases of approximately 171.3% in peak load and 91.5% in deformation capacity. A corresponding design method is subsequently developed.

title: Experimental study on mechanical properties of Q690 high-strength steel T-stub joints in coastal atmospheric environment
Study on surface morphology characteristics and tensile properties of non-uniformly corroded stud connectors
abstract: In complex environments, stud connectors are prone to corrosion, which reduces the cross-sectional area and forms surface rust pits, thereby deteriorating their tensile properties. To investigate the surface morphology characteristics and tensile property degradation mechanism of non-uniformly corroded studs, this study adopts an electrification method to accelerate stud corrosion, employs three-dimensional scanning technology and a self-developed MATLAB program to obtain the geometric characteristics of corrosion morphology, and conducts tensile tests based on digital image correlation (DIC) technology. The results indicate that stud corrosion is relatively uniform in radial distribution but significantly non-uniform along the longitudinal direction, with the degree of non-uniformity increasing as corrosion intensifies. Corrosion degrades the tensile properties of studs: yield strength and ultimate strength decrease linearly with the average corrosion rate, ultimate strain decreases exponentially, while the yield ratio and elastic modulus change slightly. The load-bearing capacity of studs is mainly determined by the minimum residual cross-sectional area; stress concentration caused by corrosion increases the non-uniformity of cross-sectional stress distribution, promotes the directional propagation of internal cracks, and ultimately reduces their deformation capacity.

title: Cable vibration measurement based on UAV and improved Lucas-Kanade optical flow method
Fatigue performance of electrical insulator bolted connection with an unintended gap
abstract: The bolted connections are important components in overhead power distribution network systems, fixing the insulator to the cross-arm. This connection is subjected to various loads, such as the self-weight of the conductor, wind, and thermal, which induce cyclic stresses that can lead to fatigue failure. The presence of separation gaps, resulting from non-compliances with dimensional tolerances in insulator connections, increases stress concentrations at the thread roots and promotes the initiation of cracks. Therefore, the role of gap size in the fatigue performance of the insulator connection is investigated in this study. The fatigue performance of a commonly used bolted connection (i.e., M24x3.0p stud) in a distribution power network having controlled gap sizes was experimentally tested under reverse cyclic flexural load using a test rig specifically developed for this purpose. The experimental results were used to develop a probabilistic fatigue life model for bolted connections with gaps. Furthermore, the probability of failure was estimated considering the effect of both gap size and load level of the connection. Also, the Miner's linear cumulative damage theory was employed, together with Monte Carlo simulation, to enable the inclusion of wind load variation to describe variable in-service loading and used for life expectancy estimation of the in-service connection. It was observed that fatigue life is reduced by approximately 80% as the gap distance increases from 1 mm to 3 mm. Finally, probabilistic life expectancy curves were developed to provide a quantitative assessment tool to assist the asset owners, in performing risk-based asset management.

title: Corrosion-triggered response transition in impact-loaded RC beams: SPH-FEM modeling with corrosion expansion pre-damage
Operational Modal Analysis from multi-setup measurements with roving references and Stochastic Subspace Identification
abstract: Accurate characterization of the modal parameters of existing structures from ambient vibration data within the field of operational modal analysis requires, in general, the collection of synchronous measurements at multiple points of the structure. However, when an insufficient number of sensors is available, the experimental campaign must be organized by dividing the measurements into subsets. In these situations, approaches like the reference-based Stochastic Subspace Identification method allows for full structural output-only identification with fixed reference sensors. Nevertheless, having common reference sensors for the whole campaign is not always feasible. Thus, this paper proposes a method to merge measurements from different ambient vibration data collection times and locations without a common reference sensor across all sets. To do so, the approach relies on roving references that are common only between successive groups of simultaneously measured positions. The algorithm’s operation is tested and analysed for two different case studies: a first one that uses synthetic data from a numerical model for the dynamic response of a simply supported beam subjected to ambient vibrations, and a second case that employs experimental measurements at an elevated pedestrian crossing. The results show that, in general, the proposed method is able to identify natural frequencies and mode shapes from ambient vibration measurements even with significant noise levels. Thus, this method can serve as a viable and straightforward alternative in situations where maintaining common reference sensor locations through the whole measurement campaign is not possible.

title: Lateral torsional buckling analysis of strengthened timber beams
A unified rate-dependent rheological model for high damping rubber bearings: Seismic performance assessment in cold climates
Experimental investigation of passive gyro stabilizers for pitch motion control of a 15-MW spar floating offshore wind turbine
Vulnerability assessment of high-rise glass curtain walls under wind loads with building interference effects
abstract: This paper investigates the wind-induced vulnerability of glass curtain wall systems in high-rise buildings emphasizing aerodynamic interference effects from neighboring structures. Two building configurations, namely tandem and staggered arrangements, are examined across six interference scenarios. Deflection-controlled failure is identified as the primary failure mode for glass curtain walls. A structural performance function is developed to model failure under wind loading, and Monte Carlo simulations are employed to account for spatial correlations of wind pressures. For the tandem arrangement, interference effects generally reduce the damage ratio, with the most favorable condition occurring at x/B = 1.5, y/D = 0, where the average damage ratio of the glass curtain wall is reduced to approximately 5% of that observed for the isolated building. Although the initial failure wind speed is consistently reduced by 1–4 m/s, the glass panels located along the crosswind-side edges are the most vulnerable to damage. For staggered arrangements, the interference effect exhibits both favorable and unfavorable characteristics. Despite this variability, the initial failure wind speed consistently decreases by 1–5 m/s. The most adverse condition is observed at a wind speed of approximately 35 m/s for the interfering building position at x/B = 3, y/D = 3, where the average damage ratio reaches 2.8 times that of the isolated building. Furthermore, as the wind direction angle increases from 0° to 45°, the interference effect progressively transitions from unfavorable to favorable.

title: Probabilistic modeling of extraordinary loads in buildings using big data-driven stochastic simulation: Methodology, applications, and extreme value analysis
Fatigue assessment of heavy-thick welded T-joint improved by portable pneumatic needle-peening treatment
abstract: In this study, fatigue strength of heavy-thick T-joints (50 and 80 mm) improved by portable pneumatic needle-peening (PPP) treatment is assessed through nominal and local stress approaches. Fatigue tests of T-joint specimens are carried out under as-welded and as-peened conditions. The IIW design curves for welded joints improved by high frequency mechanical impact (HFMI) treatment are compared and validated against the experimental data. A numerical framework, integrating welding, peening, and cyclic loading analyses, is refined to obtain local stress histories. The local approaches of fatigue assessment with local stress ratio correction are applied to establish master SN curves involving the combined effects of toe profile, residual stress (as-welded and as-peened residual stresses), thickness (9, 50, and 80 mm), joint type (out-of-plane gusset joint and T-joint), and stress ratio ( R = 0 and 0.2). The results show that PPP treatment exhibits a fatigue strength improvement of more than four FAT classes under the IIW HFMI recommendation, even for heavy thickness. Both the Smith-Watson-Topper parameter and Local MIL-HDBK-5 equivalent stress method prove strong capabilities for the local fatigue assessment of heavy-thick T-joints improved by PPP treatment.

title: Axial compressive performance of thin-walled T-shaped concrete-filled steel tubular stub with angle stiffeners
Seismic rehabilitation of severely earthquake-damaged ductile RC T-shaped beams using mechanically anchored CFRP strips: Anchorage requirements and experimental validation
Experimental and numerical investigation of axial hysteretic performance in corroded T-joints
Seismic resilience mechanism of rocking piers: Theoretical derivation and probabilistic-based failure control
Inverse design of multi-frequency bandgaps for multi-modal vibration control in long-span bridge cables
Generalizable structural behavior modeling with synthetic pretrained tabular transformer network for dam health monitoring
Estimation of wind-induced nonstationary buffeting loads and states for long-span bridges
Vertical failure modes and residual vertical load-carrying capacity of post-earthquake RC bridge piers
Structural behavior of steel-timber composite beams with mass plywood panels and self-tapping screw shear connections
abstract: Steel-timber composite floor systems consisting of steel beams and a mass timber floor slab represents an efficient and sustainable alternative to traditional steel-concrete composite systems. As use of steel-timber composite floors increases, so too does the potential to use novel engineered wood products in this application. Massive plywood panels (MPP) are one example, which offer higher strength and stiffness when compared to an equivalent volume of cross laminated timber (CLT) while also addressing material shortage and quality challenges. This paper presents experimental results on the structural behavior of steel-timber composite beams fabricated using MPP. The influence of shear connection method, panel segmentation, and gaps between panels on the stiffness, strength, and failure modes of the composite beams are examined. The studied shear connection methods include self-tapping screws as well as a novel end-bearing steel angle. Experimental results show that the elastic stiffness of the composite section is 1.24 times that of an equivalent non-composite section and that up to 62% of the stiffness of the full composite section can be achieved. The end-bearing steel angle connection was found to be as effective as a screw-only connection. The presence of gaps between timber panels was found to have a significant impact on initial stiffness of the composite beams but had minimal impact on ultimate capacity. Existing theoretical models in the literature were found to be able to predict the stiffness and strength of the tested beams within 5% of the experimental result on average. Finally, the behavior of the steel-MPP composite beams are compared with experimental data on steel-CLT composite beams in the literature.

title: Seismic performance test and numerical analysis of a full-scale historic timber frame reinforced with viscoelastic dampers
Seismic modeling of GFRP-reinforced concrete members including strain penetration effects
abstract: Reliable nonlinear modeling capable of capturing the seismic responses of glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP)-reinforced concrete (GFRP-RC) structural elements is essential for advanced seismic analysis that promotes the real-world applications of such structures. This study develops an integrated and practical seismic modeling framework for GFRP-RC members, including detailed considerations for element formulation, GFRP-confined concrete, reinforcement constitutive models, joint distortion, and a newly developed strain penetration modeling procedure. Validation of the proposed framework against experimental results from representative columns and beam-column connections showed its capability to accurately reproduce hysteretic response, strain development, damage progression, and failure modes. In particular, for the specimens included in the validation database, the average prediction errors are below 3% for key performance indices, including peak load, drift capacity, residual drift, and energy dissipation. Parametric studies further demonstrated the robustness of the proposed approach and highlighted the critical role of strain penetration, as neglecting this mechanism leads to overestimation of peak load by up to 29% and underestimation of drift capacity by up to 51% among the investigated cases. Overall, the developed modeling strategies provide a reliable foundation for system-level seismic assessment and the derivation of seismic performance factors with reduced modeling uncertainty.

title: Identification of nonlinear aerodynamic damping based on LSTM-modified unscented Kalman filter
Unified bending analysis of plates via a data-free physics-informed neural network
Flexural performance and calculations of concrete-encased square concrete-filled steel tubular (CFST) hybrid structures
Field blast testing of reinforced concrete column prototype based on the existing overpass design
abstract: Controlled field‑blast tests were conducted on scaled reinforced‑concrete overpass column prototypes representative of existing highway bridges without explicit seismic or blast detailing. A vulnerable cross‑section was identified through preliminary numerical analysis and constructed with materials and reinforcement consistent with the available technical documentation. Specimens were tested under constant axial preload with fixed base and pinned top boundary conditions. Spherical plastic explosive charges were detonated at close‑in standoff and in contact at the same height. High‑rate instrumentation recorded incident and reflected pressures, which were benchmarked against commonly used predictive models. Peak incident overpressures were repeatable and broadly aligned with analytical estimates, whereas positive‑phase durations and Friedlander decay coefficients showed greater scatter. Reflected pressures differed substantially from predictions, influenced by near‑field effects and secondary reflections from the crossbeam. Damage progressed from superficial cracking to heavy, hazardous states governed by flexure–shear interaction, with pronounced spalling at the charge height; the contact detonation produced severe local damage without global instability. Dense transverse reinforcement, limited core breaching, debris projection, and pressure–impulse diagrams tended to overpredict damage for this configuration. The findings underscore the need to calibrate near‑field blast models and highlight the requirement to implement retrofit strategies for existing reinforced‑concrete bridge columns.

title: Experimental behaviour of steel-timber composite (STC) stub columns with cruciform steel core under axial compression
A dual mechanical tuning framework for rigid pillared elastic metamaterials: Geometric reconfiguration and controllable prestress
Cracking risk assessment of high arch dam under abnormal abutment deformation during long-term operation
Cross-section behaviour and CSM based design of stainless steel I-sections in fire
abstract: In this paper, a comprehensive investigation into the cross-section behaviour and design of stainless steel I-sections in fire is carried out. Shell finite element (FE) models able to mimic the cross-section response of stainless steel I-sections at elevated temperatures are developed and validated. An extensive numerical parametric study is then conducted using the validated shell FE models to comprehensively investigate the behaviour of stainless steel I-sections in fire, taking into account 12825 stainless steel I-sections and covering a very broad range of cross-section slendernesses, cross-section geometries, elevated temperature levels and stainless steel grades. Based on the results from the parametric studies, a new version of the deformation based cross-section design approach Continuous Strength Method (CSM) is proposed for the fire design of stainless steel cross-sections. The proposed new version of the CSM is assessed against (i) the stainless steel cross-section design provisions of the European structural steel fire design standard EN 1993-1-2 and (ii) the existing versions of the CSM. The results demonstrate that the proposed version of the CSM offers a very reliable approach to predict the ultimate resistances of stainless steel I-sections at elevated temperatures, leading to more consistent ultimate resistance predictions relative to EN 1993-1-2 and the existing versions of the CSM.

title: Dynamic graph learning for forecasting coupled winds in twin tower structures during typhoons
abstract: During typhoons, dynamic wind loading can induce pronounced aerodynamic interference between closely spaced supertall buildings, yet most existing prediction approaches still rely on simplified interference-factor models, which are unable to capture the interactions between adjacent towers and their complex spatiotemporal evolution. This study proposes a dynamic graph learning framework for short-term forecasting of typhoon winds in a twin tower system. The framework is built upon a spatiotemporal graph neural network (GNN), in which an Adaptive Dynamic Graph Module (ADGM) updates inter-tower connectivity according to large-scale flow indicators such as shared mean wind direction and tower-top mean wind speed. By exploiting these direction-aware graphs, the network maps recent tower-top measurements to near-future statistics of along-wind, cross-wind, and vertical turbulence intensities, together with mean wind speeds at both towers. The proposed model is validated using multi-typhoon field measurements from a pair of closely spaced supertall towers. Compared with a static-graph model and GRU/LSTM sequence baselines that treat the towers as independent channels, the ADGM model improves turbulence prediction, increasing R2 by up to 27.6% and reducing RMSE by up to 26.4% (relative to the static-graph baseline), while delivering comparable accuracy for mean-wind statistics. Analysis of the learned edge weights reveals a clear, physically interpretable dependence of aerodynamic coupling strength on incident wind direction, without prescribing interference patterns a priori. These results demonstrate that dynamic graph learning provides an effective and physics-consistent tool for forecasting coupled typhoon winds in twin tower structures, thereby supporting condition-based operation, early warning, and resilience assessment of supertall building clusters.

title: Temperature effects on probabilistic seismic fragility of isolated bridges with high damping rubber bearings under mainshock-aftershock sequences: Intensity measure optimization
abstract: The Cascadia subduction zone poses significant seismic hazards to western Canada, capable of generating megathrust earthquakes followed by prolonged aftershock (AS) sequences. These sequential ground motions can exacerbate structural damage, particularly to critical infrastructure like highway bridges. Furthermore, in regions such as British Columbia (BC), Canada, low ambient temperatures can significantly alter the mechanical properties of seismic isolation systems, such as high damping rubber (HDR) bearings, potentially compromising bridge seismic performance. Current design codes lack explicit guidelines for assessing the combined effects of mainshock-aftershock (MS-AS) sequences and temperature variations. This study investigates the seismic fragility of an isolated bridge equipped with HDR bearings under MS-AS sequences, accounting for temperature-dependent material and isolator behavior. A refined finite element model incorporating a thermo-coupled restoring force model for the HDR bearing is developed and validated. The applicability of various intensity measures ( IMs ) is evaluated through regression analysis to establish probabilistic seismic demand models. Results indicate that low temperatures significantly amplify pier damage potential while reducing bearing displacement demands due to isolation stiffening, which is most pronounced under crustal and interface earthquakes. While peak ground velocity ( PGV ) emerges as the most reliable IM across diverse seismic scenarios, the inclusion of AS is found to increase response variability and weaken correlations. These findings provide a solid basis for the seismic fragility assessment of isolated bridges in cold regions under multi-event sequences.

title: A general time-domain framework described by time-varying impulse response functions for modeling 3-DOF coupled nonlinear self-excited forces on bridge decks
Corrigendum to “Experimental investigation on prevalent local failure mechanisms in hard rock tunnel linings using distributed optical fibre sensors” [Eng Struct 333 (2025) 120185]
In-plane buckling and strength of pined-end steel arches with local corrosion
Experimental investigation on aerodynamic optimization for a square-cylinder structure using passive-rotating vertical axis wind turbines
Out-of-plane bending behavior of SHS-to-CHS and H-to-CHS X-joints
Bending behaviour of cementitious composite beams reinforced with 3D-printed TPMS geometries
Research on design and applications of multistable mechanical metamaterial structures with high fatigue resistance
A novel hierarchical importance sampling method guided by bidirectional hybrid sampling for efficient failure probability function estimation
Deep learning-based temperature-induced bearing displacement prediction and anomaly warning for a high-speed railway cable-stayed bridge
Fire behavior and high-temperature vertical load-bearing capacity of cold-formed steel center-sheathed shear walls
Hybrid pseudo-force method for the stochastic analysis of fractional-damper-connected structures subjected to non-stationary random excitations
abstract: This paper presents a novel procedure for evaluating the stochastic response of adjacent multi-degree-of-freedom linear frame structures interconnected by fractional Kelvin–Voigt viscoelastic dampers and subjected to non-stationary seismic excitation. The main novelty lies in extending the hybrid pseudo-force formulation to multi-degree-of-freedom adjacent structures by treating the fractional viscoelastic contribution as an equivalent pseudo-force within a convolution integral framework. Compared with the traditional pseudo-force method, the proposed formulation expresses the convolution integral as the sum of two contributions: one related to the modulating function, which can be evaluated in closed form for functions commonly used in the literature, and one accounting for the pseudo-force associated with the fractional viscoelastic component. The use of a time- and frequency-dependent input model allows the influence of non-stationary seismic excitation on the time evolution of the displacement variance to be assessed. The stability, accuracy, and practical applicability of the proposed procedure are evaluated through numerical examples and validated by comparison with Monte Carlo simulations.

title: Numerical prediction of debris loads on underground structures following progressive collapse of multi-story buildings
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive methodology for analyzing static loads acting on underground structures due to debris accumulation following the progressive collapse of above-ground, multi-story, reinforced concrete buildings. A large set of frame-slab type structures was parametrically generated and numerically collapsed using custom Python scripting integrated with Abaqus/Explicit. The debris characteristics, such as surface footprint, height, and volume, were calibrated based on empirical data from recent war-related building collapses in Ukraine. The simulations accurately reflected real-world rubble behavior by selecting optimal debris parts (elements) sizes and credible distributions. A novel numerical fitting method for three-dimensional debris fields was developed, enabling virtual validation of load conditions that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive to test experimentally. The results provide a robust foundation for ongoing updates of the international guidelines addressing rubble-induced static loads on buried structures, especially in the context of warfare or progressive collapse scenarios.

Deep learning-based metamodeling of nonlinear stochastic dynamic systems under parametric and predictive uncertainty
abstract: Modeling high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamic structural systems under natural hazards presents formidable computational challenges, especially when simultaneously accounting for uncertainties in external loads and structural parameters. Studies have successfully incorporated uncertainties related to external loads from natural hazards, but few have simultaneously addressed loading and parameter uncertainties within structural systems while accounting for prediction uncertainty of neural networks. To address these gaps, three metamodeling frameworks were formulated, each coupling a feature-extraction module implemented through a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), a message-passing neural network (MPNN), or an autoencoder (AE) with a long short-term memory (LSTM) network using Monte Carlo dropout and a negative log-likelihood loss. The resulting architectures (MLP-LSTM, MPNN-LSTM, and AE-LSTM) were validated on two case studies: a multi-degree-of-freedom Bouc-Wen system and a 37-story fiber-discretized nonlinear steel moment-resisting frame, both subjected to stochastic seismic excitation and structural parameter uncertainty. All three approaches achieved low prediction errors: the MLP-LSTM yielded the most accurate results for the lower-dimensional Bouc-Wen system, whereas the MPNN-LSTM and AE-LSTM provided superior performance on the more complex steel-frame model. Moreover, a consistent correlation between predictive variance and actual error confirms the suitability of these frameworks for active-learning strategies and for assessing model confidence in structural response predictions.

Shutdown orientation induced load transfer and risk redistribution in a floating vertical-axis wind turbine under extreme wind and wave conditions
abstract: The survivability of floating vertical axis wind turbines (VAWTs) under extreme parked conditions is strongly affected by the transfer of aerodynamic loads through the rotor, floating platform, mooring system, and critical structural regions. However, the role of rotor shutdown orientation in this system-level load transfer process remains insufficiently understood. In this study, a high-fidelity CFD method coupled with a third-party CAE implicit solver is used to establish a two-way fluid structure interaction framework, in which the rotor, platform, and mooring lines are treated as flexible structures. A two-bladed H type floating VAWT mounted on a semi-submersible platform is investigated. Under the 50-year extreme wind speed and a representative severe sea condition, the fully coupled dynamic responses are compared for three shutdown orientations, namely 0°, 45°, and 90°. The results show that the 0° orientation produces the strongest flow separation and vortex shedding, together with the largest rotor thrust, platform pitch, and ML2 peak tension. The maximum rotor stress is concentrated at the blade support arm connection. The 45° orientation reduces the mean thrust but introduces stronger asymmetric loading, leading to larger sway, roll, yaw, mooring tension redistribution, and twisting of the side mooring lines. The 90° orientation shows the lowest aerodynamic loads, platform motion, blade deformation, and overall mooring tension, but shifts the local mooring risk toward the seabed contact region. This study provides guidance for shutdown orientation selection and future degradation driven survivability assessment of floating wind systems.

Aerostatic stability-driven aero-structural optimization of bridges
abstract: The burgeoning growth of main span lengths reached by modern long-span bridges is progressively drawing attention to aerostatic stability-resistant design to guarantee bridge safety throughout its lifespan. However, design frameworks focusing on aerostatic stability must address the nonlinear structural behavior that inherently drives this aeroelastic phenomenon. Nonlinear behavior of stays, large displacement effects, beam–column effects, the interdependence of lateral and torsional deck displacements, and nonlinear aerodynamics, among other factors, certainly increase the modeling and computational demands throughout the wind-resistant design process. This study proposes an aero-structural optimization framework to automatically mitigate the occurrence of aerostatic instability, incorporating all these factors in the design process. The aerostatic stability of each candidate design is analyzed using a nonlinear finite element model and an efficient modal-based method, leveraged by a root-finding algorithm, which enables the rapid identification of the critical wind velocity. Bridge deck aerodynamics as a function of the angle of attack and all deck shape design variables are obtained by wind tunnel tests-validated CFD simulations to train a multi-directional aerodynamic surrogate that predicts the force coefficients along the optimization process. The aerostatic critical velocity, along with a comprehensive set of structural responses, such as stresses and displacements under dead and live loads, is used to tailor the full bridge design according to prescribed specifications while targeting material savings. The inclusion of nonlinear aerostatic stability into aero-structural optimization frameworks is a pivotal step for the effective implementation of multi-hazard design optimization of long-span bridges.

A two-tier SHM framework for nonlinear identification of friction pendulum isolators in base-isolated buildings
abstract: This paper presents a structural health monitoring (SHM)–oriented framework for the nonlinear identification of friction pendulum isolators in a real base isolated school building. Based on a parametric investigation carried out for this study, which identifies the high-speed friction coefficient and the stiffness parameter as the most influential variables governing isolator deformations and base shear, the proposed identification strategy focuses on the high-speed friction coefficient while assuming the linear stiffness properties to be known from independent calibration using ambient vibration data. A detailed three-dimensional finite element model is paired with a condensed representation characterized by a limited number of degrees of freedom, where the isolation system is replaced by a single equivalent FP isolator. A genetic algorithm–based identification procedure is first applied to the full finite element model, accurately recovering the family-wise high-speed friction coefficients and reproducing target accelerations and isolator deformations with very small discrepancies, even in the presence of realistic Gaussian noise. The same optimization framework is then applied to a condensed model with only few degrees of freedom, where the isolation system is represented by a single equivalent FP isolator and the search space is reduced to two decision variables, one for each horizontal direction. The results show that the simplified model retains sufficient accuracy, yielding response histories comparable to those of the full model while requiring only about 6% of the corresponding computational time. This makes the condensed model suitable for rapid event-by-event updating, whereas the detailed FE model is reserved for less frequent in-depth analyses when significant changes are detected.

title: Deep learning based reconstruction of particle reinforced materials from wave measurements
abstract: Accurate characterization of particle distributions in particle-reinforced materials is important for understanding their mechanical performance. However, estimating internal particle configurations from boundary wave measurements remains a challenging inverse problem due to complex wave–particle interactions, multiple scattering effects, and the high dimensionality of the unknown microstructure. In this study, a data-driven framework is proposed to investigate the feasibility of estimating particle distributions from boundary-measured wave signals. A synthetic dataset is generated using numerical simulations of wave propagation in two-dimensional heterogeneous plates containing randomly distributed particles under controlled geometric constraints. A temporal convolutional neural network is developed to learn the nonlinear relationship between multi-sensor wave responses and particle center coordinates. The reconstruction problem is formulated as a point-set prediction task, and a permutation-invariant Chamfer distance is employed to account for the unordered nature of particle distributions. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework is capable of recovering the major spatial characteristics of particle distributions across a wide range of configurations. Systematic parametric studies further reveal that reconstruction performance is influenced by particle size, particle number, inter-particle spacing, excitation frequency, and sensor configuration. In addition, the results provide insights into how wave–particle interactions affect the identifiability and learnability of the inverse problem. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of combining wave-based measurements with deep learning for particle-distribution estimation and provides a foundation for future research toward data-driven material characterization and nondestructive evaluation.

Experimental dynamic progressive collapse assessment of post-and-beam mass timber substructures with two-bay cross-laminated timber floors under interior column removal
abstract: Mass timber buildings are emerging construction systems that present distinct design challenges, one of which is progressive collapse. Current design guidelines are largely based on studies conducted on steel and concrete structures, whereas experimental research on the progressive collapse behaviour of mass timber buildings has been predominantly limited to quasi-static testing. However, progressive collapse is a dynamic and nonlinear phenomenon that can lead to severe social and economic repercussions. This paper provides new insights into the progressive collapse behaviour of three-dimensional post-and-beam mass timber buildings with cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels spanning two-bays. Two scaled substructures were subjected to both quasi-static and dynamic testing under an interior column removal scenario. The load was incrementally increased until collapse. The structural responses, load redistribution mechanisms, dynamic increase factors (DIFs), failure modes, and associated collapse mechanisms are analysed and discussed. The findings highlighted that the substructures exhibited fewer alternative load paths and a less uniform load‑redistribution pattern compared with conventional concrete systems. The CLT panels spanning two-bays provided the primary alternate load path, only compressive arch action was observed, not catenary action. It is critical that the elements along the primary alternate load path are designed to sustain most of the redistributed load. The observed average DIF value was 1.69 and was 15.5% lower than the theoretical DIF value of 2.0 proposed in the DoD and Eurocode. The observed collapse mechanisms were characterised by the successive shear failure of the beam-to-column connectors, with those along the primary alternate load path failing first.

title: Surrogate assisted optimization of S-type shape memory polymer lattice metastructures for enhanced energy absorption and recovery
abstract: Shape memory polymers have attracted growing attention in recent years due to their unique capability of combining high energy absorption with reversible deformation. These characteristics make them promising candidates for lightweight, multifunctional structures in aerospace, automotive, and biomedical applications. In this study, a lattice structure with S-type unit cells (a geometry known for its curved, arc-shaped configuration) is fabricated from polylactic acid (PLA) shape-memory polymer. The thermo-mechanical cycle of deformation, cooling, unloading, and reheating was simulated and experimentally validated to characterize the time-dependent shape-memory behavior. Data extracted from finite element simulations were employed to train an artificial neural network (ANN) surrogate model, which provided accurate predictions of mechanical performance. Subsequently, a genetic algorithm (GA) was applied to optimize lattice geometry with the dual objectives of maximizing energy absorption and enhancing recovery efficiency. Results demonstrated approximately 80% shape recovery upon reheating above T g . The proposed integrated numerical-machine learning-optimization framework highlights the potential of combining high-fidelity physics-based modeling with data-driven surrogate models for the efficient design of advanced energy-absorbing metastructures with excellent recoverability. The novelty of this study does not lie in the geometric shape of the structure itself, but rather in the first-time combination of: (i) experimental and numerical characterization of its full thermo-visco- hyper-elastic shape memory behavior, (ii) development of an ANN surrogate trained on high-fidelity finite element data, and (iii) multi-objective GA optimization specifically targeting the concurrent maximization of energy absorption and shape recovery.

title: Service-life extension of cantilevered traffic signal structures with aerodynamic damping retrofit
Design and performance evaluation of a bio-inspired multilayer helmet liner for rotational impact mitigation
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of a novel multi-layered bio-inspired structured helmet liner designed to reduce rotational acceleration during bicycle helmet impacts. Recognising the critical role of angular kinematics in traumatic brain injury, the liner was evaluated under oblique impact conditions using a biofidelic 3D-printed head surrogate developed from a validated anatomical model. The surrogate incorporated detailed skull and soft tissue structures and was refined to resolve mesh irregularities, integrate sensors, and ensure compatibility with a drop-tower setup. Drop tests were performed on helmets fitted with either a conventional expanded polystyrene liner or the proposed bio-inspired liner, and the surrogate’s measured response was used to validate corresponding finite element simulations. Results demonstrate that the proposed liner substantially reduces peak angular acceleration by up to 44% compared to the conventional expanded polystyrene liners, demonstrating its potential to enhance helmet safety. This work underscores the value of combining advanced surrogate modelling with innovative liner architectures to improve head injury mitigation in cycling impact.

title: Programmable nonlinear response in spatially varying continuous-fibre lattices: Experimental and numerical investigations
abstract: Continuous fibre-reinforced lattice structures have emerged as a promising class of architected materials for lightweight applications, offering exceptional stiffness-to-weight ratios and energy absorption capacity through the strategic placement of fibres within cellular geometries. While extensive research has focused on their linear elastic behaviour and stiffness optimisation, the nonlinear deformation mechanisms and failure responses of spatially graded continuous fibre lattices remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a comprehensive experimental and numerical investigation of the flexural behaviour of additively manufactured graded lattice beams across the full deformation range, from initial elasticity to post-peak collapse. The lattice architectures are generated through an optimised graded lattice procedure that distributes five geometrically compatible star-hourglass re-entrant unit cells across a simply supported beam domain, with spatial variation enabling distinct mechanical roles within a single monolithic structure. Beams fabricated from pure PLA and continuous glass-fibre-reinforced PLA using fused deposition modelling are tested under three-point bending and analysed through nonlinear finite element simulations in Abaqus. The results demonstrate that structural-scale grading activates deformation mechanisms inaccessible to uniform architectures. Notably, graded Configs exhibit geometric stiffening, characterised by an increase in tangent stiffness with progressive deformation due to the sequential engagement and compaction of successive cell layers, thereby counteracting conventional softening behaviour. Furthermore, by varying unit-cell geometry and fibre reinforcement distribution, the global failure mode can be deliberately shifted between brittle localised fracture and quasi-ductile progressive collapse without altering the base material. Systematic comparison of six optimised Configs reveals a quantifiable stiffness-strength trade-off, with architectural variation enabling movement along this design frontier. The key novelties of this work include: (i) experimental demonstration of geometric stiffening in graded continuous fibre lattices, (ii) architecture-driven programmability of failure behaviour through spatial cell distribution, and (iii) validated nonlinear FE analysis capturing the observed deformation sequencing and collapse mechanisms. These findings establish spatially varying continuous fibre lattices as programmable mechanical systems in which stiffness distribution, nonlinear engagement, and failure progression can be tailored through coordinated multiscale design, expanding the attainable design space beyond conventional lightweight structures.

Quasi-static flow-type loading tests for the out of plane performance assessment of full-scale masonry infill walls in reinforced concrete frames
abstract: Existing performance assessment methods for structures subjected to flow-type loading (i.e., flood, tsunami) rely on assumptions and previous knowledge derived from other hazards, such as earthquakes. However, flow-type induced loads on structures are fundamentally different in nature from seismic action, inducing long-duration non-uniform pressures on inundated components. Flume or wave basin tests on large-scale structural components under fluid loading are limited due to the difficulties in scaling. The present paper proposes a novel quasi-static testing method for performing full-scale tests on masonry infill walls in reinforced concrete (RC) frames subjected to simulated flow-type loading in a structural laboratory setting. The innovative test set up involves the use of an array of 28 pneumatic actuators and a novel testing procedure (i.e. test set-up and load protocols) is developed for simulating quasi-statically flow-type induced loads with increasing flow depth on full-scale building components. The feasibility of the proposed testing method is herein demonstrated on four full-scale masonry infill walls (dimensions 4.2 m x 2.3 m) in RC frames. The tests allow for the out of plane (OOP) performance of masonry infill walls to be assessed under flow-type loading conditions with increasing flow depth. Masonry walls are tested with and without plaster to point out the effect of the latter on the overall capacity of the wall. Original experimental data from flow-type testing are presented and discussed to provide insights into the OOP capacity of infill walls under flow-type loading. Finally, the OOP performance of infill walls under flow-type loading is compared with that of the same specimen previously tested under seismic loading conditions. Results attest the feasibility of the proposed testing method to characterise the structural response of full-scale building components under flow-type loading.

title: Moment capacity of back-to-back cold-formed steel channel bolted joints: An experimentally validated design approach
abstract: Cold-formed steel (CFS) bolted joints formed with back-to-back channel sections are widely used in portal frame construction due to their efficiency and ease of fabrication. However, the discrete force transfer between individual channels produces non-uniform stress distributions within the joint region, leading to localised stress concentrations, shear lag effects, bimoment-induced stresses due to restrained warping, and premature web buckling. These effects can reduce the moment capacity of typical joints by up to 40% compared with the nominal capacity of the connected members; however, this reduction is not explicitly addressed in current CFS design standards, including AISI S100, AS/NZS 4600, and EN 1993–1–3, which treat member and joint capacities independently. To address this gap, this paper presents a comprehensive experimental and parametric investigation to quantify the capacity reduction in CFS bolted joints and provide a reliable design method for practical applications. A detailed finite element (FE) model was first developed and validated against experimental results from CFS portal frame joint tests. Subsequently, an extensive parametric study comprising over 3400 FE simulations was performed to capture the influence of cross-sectional non-dimensional slenderness, as well as a wide range of geometric, material, and joint parameters. Based on these findings, a simplified design equation is proposed to enable reliable prediction of the reduced moment capacity of back-to-back channel bolted joints. The application of the proposed design equation is then verified against both numerical and experimental results of CFS frames, demonstrating excellent accuracy, with predictions within 1–3% of the actual capacities on average and coefficients of variation ranging from 0.06 to 0.09.

Flexural behaviour of glulam panels under sequential fire and blast loading
abstract: This study presents an experimental investigation of glued-laminated timber (GLT) panels subjected to a real fire followed by far-field blast-type loading. Seven GLT panels extracted from the Mass Timber Demonstration Fire Test Program were exposed to one-sided fire until self-extinguishment and then tested under four-point bending with simply supported boundary conditions, statically as well as dynamically using the University of Ottawa Shock Tube testing facility. Failure modes in charred panels were characterized by flexural failure, consistent with uncharred panels' failure modes, with some charred panels exhibiting visible glue line separation. Static and dynamic resistance curves were characterized as linear elastic up to maximum resistance in panels. The average strength increase factor (SIF) obtained for the charred panels was 1.8. No statistically significant dynamic strength increase in flexural strength or stiffness was observed. The findings demonstrated that a single-degree-of-freedom model, used together with the Reduced Cross-Section Method, can be a reliable predictive tool with proper inputs to simulate the dynamic response of structural elements for fire-followed-by-blast loading scenario; a methodology which can be extended to other timber structural elements.

title: Energy-absorption performance of M300 chiral topologies under quasi-static and blast-induced compression
abstract: This study evaluates the energy absorption of high-strength M300 maraging steel chiral cellular lattices, fabricated via selective laser melting, for blast-protection systems. Thin-walled (0.15 mm) hexachiral (HX) structures were tested under quasi-static (QS) compression and blast-induced dynamic loading using an explosive-driven shock tube (EDST). Experimental data validated an LS-DYNA numerical model employing a Tabulated Johnson-Cook constitutive relation calibrated via split Hopkinson pressure bar tests. Discrepancies between numerical and experimental quantitative parameters remained below 8%, with HX energy absorption matching within + 1.3% (QS) and −7.9% (blast). The validated model assessed five additional topologies—trichiral (TRC), tetrachiral (TC), anti-tetrachiral (AT), hybrid (HCC), and re-entrant chiral auxetic (RCA)—to compare deformation mechanisms. Results show HX maintains a stable, rotation-dominated collapse across regimes, yielding superior plateau stress and specific energy absorption (SEA) of 686.0 J/kg (QS) and 660.0 J/kg (EDST). Conversely, transient blast loading significantly altered the performance of other geometries: RCA can be highly competitive demonstrating a 42% increase in energy absorption (34.12 J to 48.33 J) and a strong negative Poisson’s ratio (-1.08), whereas AT energy absorption decreased by nearly 50% (49.35 J to 24.83 J). The study confirms that additively manufactured M300 chiral structures possess significant potential for modern protective systems, offering an efficient means of mitigating high-intensity blast energy.

title: Behaviour of welded lean duplex stainless steel T-stub components under varying loading rates
abstract: This study presents the first systematic investigation of the strain rate dependent response of welded lean duplex stainless steel T-stub components through an integrated experimental and numerical modelling programme. Twenty-four T-stub specimens incorporating M16 and M20 fully threaded A4–70 and DX109 bolts were tested under quasi-static loading and loading rates varying from 10 mm/s to 75mm/s. Coupon and bolt-nut assembly tests were conducted to quantify material strain rate sensitivity. The results demonstrate clear positive strain rate effects on strength for both flange plates and bolts, leading to increases of up to 15% in equivalent yield resistance at the T-stub component level, while deformation capacity and energy dissipation decrease. Bolt spacing governs stiffness, resistance and prying action, while loading rate has limited influence on prying development prior to peak load. A finite element model was developed and validated against the experimental tests; it was used to reproduce the full range response including fracture with high degree of accuracy. An improved method for predicting the moment capacity of the flange consistent with the plastic resistance of the T-stub based on a strain limit approach, incorporating the effects of strain hardening and loading rate, is proposed. The method provides a rational basis for predicting the plastic resistance of stainless steel T-stub connections under both static and elevated loading rate tensile actions, enabling more reliable assessment of connection robustness under extreme loading conditions.

Experimental study on improving the fire and post-fire performance of the concrete columns with Fe-SMA spiral stirrups
abstract: This paper innovatively proposed a novel method for achieving quickly active confinement of spiral reinforced concrete column using iron-based shape memory alloy (Fe-SMA). In this method, Fe-SMA spiral stirrups were employed to partially replace conventional stirrups in the mid-span region. By utilizing the shape memory effect (SME) of Fe-SMA, active circumferential confinement was provided to the core concrete, thereby overcoming the stress hysteresis and inherent thermal degradation issues of ordinary steel spirals, while also improving structural performance. A total of 8 spiral reinforced concrete circular columns were designed and tested under three conditions: fire resistance under an axial load ratio of 0.3, axial compression and post-fire axial compression (after 60 min and 90 min of fire exposure). The aim was to investigate the feasibility of performance enhancement by Fe-SMA at three stages: during fire, at room temperature and after fire. Experimental results showed that the Fe-SMA used in this study exhibited a higher recovery stress plateau, indicating great potential for improving both fire resistance and post-fire mechanical performance of concrete columns. Under a load ratio of 0.3, the Fe-SMA spiral reinforced column achieved a 39.84% increase in fire resistance compared to the conventional columns, demonstrating effective active confinement during fire and suppression of fire-induced damage. Axial compression tests confirmed that Fe-SMA spiral enhanced the axial compression capacity through their super elasticity (SE) and improved both post-fire load capacity and toughness through their SME. Furthermore, the compressive Toughness Index (T.I.) was employed to quantify the enhancement in post-fire toughness of columns with Fe-SMA spiral, and a modified calculation model for post-fire circumferential confinement stress was proposed. This study revealed for the first time the active circumferential confinement mechanism of Fe-SMA spiral stirrup for column, providing a basis for designing high-toughness fire-resistant structures.

Elastic buckling analysis of platings with torsionally and warping restrained supports by truncated series expansion applied to a hierarchical trigonometric function set
abstract: The paper provides a new framework for the elastic buckling analysis of platings under linearly varying uniaxial loads, with torsionally and warping restrained longitudinal supports. The new method, based on the employment of a hierarchical trigonometric function set, allows analysing any type of boundary conditions at the plate long edges, ranging from the simple support to the clamped ones. In order to make the calculations viable for practical design purposes, an analytical formulation, based on the 3rd order truncated series expansion of the vertical displacement field, is developed. The effectiveness of the new analytical solution is investigated, focusing on several values of the torsional stiffness of longitudinal supporting members, in order to cover various types of boundary conditions at the plate long edges. Particularly, the new analytical formulation is checked by a comparative analysis against the asymptotic values, the relevant results obtained by the eigenvalue buckling analysis, carried out by Ansys Mechanical APDL, as well as current Rule formulas. Based on current results, the new method not only provides a more rational approach for the elastic buckling analysis of ship platings, but it also allows improving the accuracy in determining the buckling capacity in the entire design range typical of ship platings.

Experimental investigation and strength prediction of concrete-encased square CFST structures under axial tension
abstract: Concrete-encased concrete-filled steel tubular (CFST) structures consist of an inner CFST component and an outer reinforced concrete (RC) component. Although their compressive behaviour has been extensively studied, the axial tensile behaviour of concrete-encased square CFST structures remains insufficiently understood, particularly regarding failure mode, hybrid effects, and strength prediction. This study experimentally investigates the axial tensile behaviour of this hybrid structure and develops an improved strength prediction method. Twelve specimens were tested under monotonic axial tension, including eight concrete-encased square CFST specimens, one concrete-encased circular CFST specimen, two square CFST specimens, and one RC specimen. The effects of steel tube strength, steel tube thickness, fabrication process and cross-sectional configuration were examined. Two typical failure modes were identified according to crack distribution: the uniform cracking mode and the end cracking mode. The uniform cracking mode allowed more distributed strain development and greater participation of the outer RC component, whereas the end cracking mode was associated with localized end damage and premature fracture of rebars. Increasing the steel ratio significantly improved tensile strength and deformation capacity, while simply increasing the steel tube strength did not lead to a proportional improvement in tensile strength. The effects of fabrication process and cross-sectional configuration were reflected mainly in the strain distribution and failure localization. Based on the observed load-transfer mechanisms, an improved strength prediction method was proposed by considering the biaxial stress enhancement of the steel tube, limited utilization of high-strength steel, and different RC contributions in the two failure modes. The proposed method showed improved accuracy and lower dispersion for this type of hybrid structure.

abstract: Earth masonry has attracted renewed interest as a low-emission construction system, yet its in-plane shear resistance at structural scale remains insufficiently quantified for design. This study addresses this gap through an experimental and analytical investigation of unstabilised load-bearing earth masonry walls. Nine full-scale shear wall tests were carried out under controlled combinations of vertical precompression and horizontal loading using an ESECMaSE-type setup (Enhanced Safety and Efficient Construction of Masonry Structures in Europe). Complementary material tests were conducted under laboratory climate, allowing moisture effects to be explicitly considered in the interpretation of the results. Shear failure was successfully induced in all tests. Depending on vertical precompression and overlap, the walls exhibited frictional joint failure, tensile block failure, and shear-compression failure. The results establish a characteristic shear resistance envelope where capacity initially scales with normal stress - governed by bed joint sliding - reaches a peak limited by the tensile strength of the units, and subsequently declines as compressive masonry crushing becomes dominant. Moisture-dependent changes in compressive and tensile strength were found to be essential for consistent interpretation of the results. The experimental peak loads and governing failure modes were compared with mechanically based analytical models according to Mann/Müller (1978) and subsequent extensions. Good overall agreement was obtained, with a mean ratio of experimental-to-calculated resistance of 1.05 when moisture effects were included. The results indicate that mechanically based shear design approaches developed for conventional masonry can, in principle, be transferred to earth masonry, provided that moisture-sensitive material properties are adequately accounted for.

Numerical analysis and experimental verification of a locally resonant interlocking brick assembly
abstract: The recent global housing affordability crisis has heightened the demand for more efficient and cost-effective construction methods. Within these solutions, mortarless interlocking bricks have gained attention because they are self-aligning and mortar-free, reducing construction costs and easing reliance on skilled labour. Studies have shown that interlocking bricks exhibit significant energy dissipation due to inter-brick friction; however, this capability diminishes rapidly with repeated loading because of brick surface abrasion. This study proposes a novel meta-block, designed to provide a durable enhancement of the dynamic response of interlocking bricks. The meta-block comprises locally resonant elements (LREs) embedded within interlocking bricks. A stochastic analysis, calibrated against experimental tests, studied meta-blocks including the randomness introduced by inter-brick gaps due to brick imperfections and lack of mortar. A novel LRE was designed using this framework, achieving a displacement attenuation of 35%. Stochastic parametric analyses revealed that the effectiveness of LREs increased progressively with each unit of the chain. Subsequently, experimental validation examined the dynamic response of meta-blocks. Results confirmed that the band gap formation and attenuation levels were within the range of numerical predictions. The study establishes a robust design methodology for meta-blocks and highlights their potential for mitigating dynamic responses in modular systems.
