Multi-directional shake table real-time hybrid simulation of rolling pendulum isolation systems using nonlinear kinematic transformations
abstract: A real-time hybrid simulation (RTHS) framework is developed for in-plane, multi-directional evaluation of rolling pendulum (RP) seismic isolation systems residing within structural systems and designed to protect acceleration-sensitive nonstructural components in mission-critical facilities and data centers. The framework couples a full-scale RP bearing assembly, serving as the experimental substructure, with a three-dimensional nonlinear finite-element model of a building–server–cabinet system representing the analytical substructure. A nonlinear kinematic transformation is formulated to map multi-directional, large-deformation motions between the analytical and experimental coordinate systems, and the explicit dissipative MKR- 𝛼 integration algorithm is used to ensure unconditional stability during real-time execution. Accurate real-time coupling between the analytical and experimental substructures is achieved using a third-order Adaptive Time Series (ATS) compensator, which mitigates actuator-control dynamics and delay and enables precise tracking of the commanded multi-directional shake-table motions. The nonlinear and rate-dependent behavior of the RP isolation system is characterized to determine the equivalent stiffness and damping parameters required by the integration scheme, and actuator dynamics are quantified to assess displacement tracking accuracy under multi-axis loading. Bi-directional earthquake simulations demonstrate stable real-time execution, synchronized numerical-experimental coupling, and robust multi-directional shake table control. The results establish the framework as a reliable platform for full-scale experimental evaluation of multi-directional RP isolation systems embedded within structural systems and for performance-based evaluation of seismically isolated nonstructural components.

Drive-by batch estimation method for girder deflections of bridge section based on the difference between loaded and unloaded track geometries
abstract: This study develops a drive-by batch estimation method for quasistatic girder deflections in consecutive simply supported spans using the difference between loaded and unloaded track geometries (DLU). The use of DLU improves sensitivity to girder deflection and enables implementation on track-inspection vehicles equipped with only one onboard track-geometry device. A novel reference-waveform-based linear regression formulation accounts for the influence of longitudinally adjacent spans introduced by track-geometry processing, including band-pass filtering. For the examined 12.3-m span, the DLU sensitivity was 0.45, approximately twice the maximum value reported for the previous method. Numerical validation was conducted for seven consecutive spans with alternating relative flexural stiffnesses of 0.90 and 1.00. The maximum deflection-estimation error was 1.3% under ideal conditions. Robustness was further examined by introducing 10-m chord-versine noise with standard deviations of 0.2 and 0.3 mm and positional offsets of up to ±0.50 m. The method was also applied to field measurements from an actual steel bridge comprising five consecutive 12.3-m simply supported spans with direct-fixation track, obtained at approximately 50 km/h. The estimated relative girder deflections agreed with ground-based measurements within 10%. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method for the examined bridge system and measurement conditions.

title: Shear behavior of 3D-printed concrete beams with CFRP reinforcement: An experimental parametric analysis
abstract: The shear behavior of reinforced 3D-printed concrete (3DPC) members remains insufficiently understood, particularly due to the layered material structure, interlayer interfaces and reinforcement integration challenges. This study experimentally investigates the shear behavior of CFRP-reinforced 3DPC beams through 16 three-point bending tests, including both printed and conventionally cast reference specimens. The investigated parameters comprise fabrication method, shear slenderness, longitudinal and transverse reinforcement ratios, member size and printing interval time. The results show that several shear mechanisms known from conventional reinforced concrete (RC) remain relevant for 3DPC members at a global level. However, printing-induced interfaces and bond-dependent reinforcement interaction influenced crack development and failure mechanisms. Compared with the cast reference specimens, the printed beam without shear reinforcement showed a similar shear capacity, whereas the printed beam with textile shear reinforcement exhibited a 48% lower capacity, indicating the critical role of shear reinforcement integration. Printing pause time also had a pronounced effect: a 15-minute pause increased the shear capacity by 48%, while a 60-minute pause caused interlayer delamination and reduced the capacity by 28%. The influence of shear slenderness followed established RC trends, with non-slender specimens reaching substantially higher capacities than slender ones. A comparison with current FRP design provisions showed that ACI 440.11-22, CSA S806-12 and the DAfStb Guideline predominantly overestimated the experimentally determined shear capacities, indicating that existing design approaches cannot be directly transferred to reinforced extrusion-based 3DPC without appropriate modification and validation.

title: Numerical parametric investigation on the compression and shear-compression response of masonry panels strengthened by CRM
abstract: In recent years, strengthening techniques based on externally bonded composite materials have been increasingly adopted to improve the structural performance of masonry structures. Among these, Composite Reinforced Mortar (CRM) systems have proven effective for both compression and shear-compression retrofitting. Despite their growing use in engineering practice, research on CRM-strengthened masonry remains limited, particularly about in-plane flexural capacity, drift performance, and the contribution of CRM layers to out-of-plane stability. Moreover, comprehensive analytical models capable of explicitly quantifying the mechanical contribution of CRM reinforcement are still lacking, with current design guidelines mainly relying on simplified amplification factors applied to masonry mechanical properties. This study presents the development of a finite-element model capable of reproducing both the shear-compression response and the out-of-plane buckling behavior of masonry walls under compression strengthened with CRM systems. A parametric numerical investigation is carried out to analyze the in-plane shear response and out-of-plane buckling behavior of CRM-retrofitted panels. The numerical models are calibrated using experimental results from previous tests conducted by the authors and validated against additional data available in the literature. The results identify the key parameters governing the CRM–masonry interaction and enable the proposal of an analytical approach for estimating the effective mechanical properties of retrofitted masonry panels.

abstract: This paper presents the first Lumped Damage Mechanics (LDM) framework for the seismic reliability assessment of timber-frame structures. The proposed model explicitly represents elastic behavior, plastic rotations, and fracture-driven damage through internal state variables, allowing localized stiffness degradation and energy dissipation to be captured within a computationally efficient formulation. The LDM model is implemented in a user-defined finite element and coupled with incremental dynamic analysis to perform probabilistic seismic assessment. Model parameters are calibrated and validated using experimental monotonic bending and cyclic timber frame tests. Seismic fragility curves are derived directly from internal damage variables, which are adopted as engineering demand parameters within a performance-based earthquake engineering framework. A parametric study on one and two-story timber frames subjected to earthquake excitation demonstrates the scalability of the approach and its ability to identify governing collapse mechanisms. Results show that damage-based fragilities provide a physically meaningful alternative to conventional drift-based metrics and enable direct identification of soft-story failure modes. The proposed framework offers an efficient and mechanically consistent tool for seismic reliability analysis and collapse assessment of timber structures.

Diamond-shaped lattice steel structural elements realized with Wire-Arc Additive Manufacturing: Fabrication, testing and strength calibration
abstract: Lattice steel elements produced by Wire-Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) are emerging as promising candidates for lightweight, architected structural members, yet their structural-scale behaviour remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates the structural response of WAAM-produced diamond-shaped lattice steel elements (D-Poles) under axial compression, providing the first comprehensive experimental dataset for this new class of components. D-Poles are formed by repetition of diamond-shaped units (D-Chips) along the height and around a polygonal cross-section, resulting in continuous lattice members without discrete mechanical connections. A fabrication campaign was carried out using a robotic WAAM setup with Cold Metal Transfer, producing three-, four- and six-faced D-Poles in three different heights (0.30 m, 0.60 m and 0.90 m). The specimens were characterized by industrial computed tomography to quantify porosity and thickness distribution, followed by monotonic compression tests on short and tall D-Poles. The global response is found to be governed by flexural behaviour of the D-Chips rather than by global buckling. An analytical model is adopted to interpret yielding and ultimate capacities and to develop a Eurocode-consistent calibration of characteristic and design strength values.

Rapid identification based data-driven topology design independent from high-information entropy initial dataset
abstract: Topology optimization (TO) has been widely adopted in engineering design; however, it is prone to being trapped in local optima, particularly in strongly nonlinear problems. Sensitivity-free data-driven topology design (DDTD) offers a promising alternative. Nevertheless, existing DDTD-based methods still depend heavily on prior information or sensitivity-based TO methods for initialization, limiting their generality and independence in engineering applications. In this study, an efficient DDTD-based framework capable of being driven from low information-entropy initial datasets is proposed while improving computational efficiency. To reduce the dependence on high information-entropy initial datasets, a mesh-independent mutation module is introduced as a supplementary source of geometric features, enabling stable exploration under low information-entropy initialization. To alleviate the computational bottleneck in DDTD, where all candidate structures require numerical evaluations, a non-AI-based rapid identification algorithm is developed to efficiently identify potential high-performance structures, thereby significantly reducing the number of expensive high-fidelity simulations. The framework generates material distributions on body-fitted meshes to maintain consistency between numerical simulations and physical manufacturing. A signed distance field-based minimum length constraint is further incorporated to ensure reliable mesh generation. Numerical experiments on strongly nonlinear stress-related problems, together with comparisons with sensitivity-based TO methods, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. In microfluidic reactor and shell design problems involving non-differentiable constraints, the proposed method successfully addresses scenarios that remain challenging for both sensitivity-based TO and conventional DDTD-based methods.

title: High fidelity acoustic distributed fiber optic approach for prestressed concrete cylinder pipe prestressing wire break detection
In-service vibration performance of an engineered bamboo floor system: Dynamic properties and serviceability assessment
abstract: Engineered bamboo is emerging as a sustainable alternative to timber in multi-storey construction, yet its in-service vibration performance remains uncharacterised. This paper presents the first comprehensive experimental investigation into the dynamic properties and vibration serviceability of an engineered bamboo floor system in a full-scale, occupied building. Four modal test configurations and a series of controlled walking tests were conducted under in-service conditions. Five vibration modes were identified in the frequency range of 16–29 Hz, with a fundamental frequency of approximately 16 Hz. The floor exhibited damping ratios of 5.1–5.3% for the fundamental mode and 2–4% for the higher-order modes, notably higher than the 1–2.5% typically reported for bare mass timber floors. A comparison of test configurations showed that an optimised measurement grid avoiding potential nodal regions along beam lines, combined with multiple accelerometers, provided the most complete and reliable modal identification. Vibration serviceability was assessed against ISO 10137 and AIJES-V0001–2018. At normal step frequencies, response factors remained around 4 and the AIJ rating was hardly annoyed, satisfying the requirements for general office environments. The findings are specific to the tested floor configuration; further field measurements across a range of engineered bamboo floor systems are needed to establish bamboo-specific design recommendations.

Engineered wood beams with curved corrugated core: Experimental verification of design methodology
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive design and structural performance evaluation of novel engineered wood beams incorporating curved corrugated panels. To gain a deeper understanding of the assembly of corrugated panels, the direction of the corrugation axis, and the orientations of wood fibers, two configurations, namely concave and convex, were simulated using the Abaqus finite element (FE) software. A geometric parametric study was also conducted using the FE model to reveal the influence of corrugation geometry on the bending stiffness (BS) of the engineered wood beams. Based on the FE results and considering several parameter combinations, a unit cell geometry for the curved corrugated panel was designed, and the core configuration and fiber orientation were specified. Curved corrugated panels were manufactured from southern yellow pine strands bonded with phenol-formaldehyde (PF) adhesive and formed using an aluminum matched-die mold. Engineered beams with both concave and convex core configurations were assembled and subsequently subjected to compression and four-point bending tests to evaluate their structural performance and validate finite element model (FEM) predictions. Experimental validation showed close agreement with the FE simulations. The convex configuration exhibited bending stiffness values up to 3.3% higher than the FEM predictions, whereas the concave configuration showed values up to 7.7% lower. The convex configuration demonstrated improved mechanical performance in bending, whereas the concave configuration showed better compressive strength. Both configurations surpassed the specific bending stiffness of glulam, demonstrating their potential as lightweight, high-performance alternatives for structural applications using curved corrugated panels.

Dry and wet strengthening techniques for timber frames with various infills
abstract: Paianta houses belong to the traditional vernacular typology in Romania and have, as a main feature, the presence of the timber frame (posts, beams, and diagonals) infilled with several types of materials, such as fired earth brick masonry, earth and straw mix, wattle and daub, or timber logs. Although generally proved to behave well in earthquakes, they may exhibit large deformations of the frame, infill collapse and various other minor to moderate damage. Most of them are quite old and owned by lower income people, but recently, especially after the pandemic and energy crisis, people became more aware of resources’ economy and the demand to just improve the existing buildings, rather than to demolish and build new, slowly increased. The StrongPa project investigates for the first time in Romania the influence of various strengthening techniques on such houses and aims to provide the owners with easy to apply and low-cost solutions to improve their houses in terms of both seismic resistance and thermal comfort. The novelty of the paper is approaching the vernacular (paianta) house interventions with scientific validating methods (in-plane static cyclic experiments on walls). The results indicate low-cost, compatible and locally applicable strengthening techniques, covering a gap between vernacular practice and structural engineering while enabling performance-based retrofit selection.

title: Fatigue life assessment of corrosion-damaged weathering steel bridge girders
abstract: Owing to its superior atmospheric corrosion resistance and low maintenance requirements, weathering steel is widely used in steel bridges and is often preferred by bridge owners over painted steel. However, recent studies have reported localized metal loss and perforation in weathering steel bridge members, raising concerns about the structural integrity, durability, and overall service life of these systems. These concerns are further amplified when corrosion damage coupled with fatigue is considered in the assessment of the service durability of steel bridges. At present, design guidelines do not provide an explicit approach for predicting the service life of steel structures in general, and weathering steel members in particular, that accounts for corrosion damage. In this study, we propose a practical framework that can be readily implemented to estimate the reduction in fatigue life of weathering steel girders due to corrosion damage. Since direct assessment of corrosion-induced damage in steel girders is cumbersome, the corrosion product mass ratio, α / γ ∗ , is used to correlate the corrosion rate of weathering steel with patina mineralogy, providing a framework for estimating fatigue life without reliance on long-term environmental monitoring. The estimated corrosion rate is then used to predict the corresponding reduction in fatigue life due to uniform corrosion and the effects of pitting corrosion. The proposed framework provides a simple and practical approach for evaluating the remaining fatigue performance of weathering steel bridge girders and serves as a useful tool for bridge inspection, maintenance planning, and life-cycle assessment.

Trackside-measurement-based railway track irregularity estimation using a vehicle-track model and extended Kalman filtering strategy
abstract: Track vertical irregularity is a key indicator of railway track geometry condition. However, frequent monitoring remains difficult using conventional inspection methods. For critical sections, fixed rail and sleeper sensors provide an alternative way to record trackside responses during train passage. These responses can be used to estimate track irregularity, but its systematic capacity has not yet been fully explored. Therefore, this study proposes an extended Kalman filter (EKF) framework for estimating track irregularity using fixed trackside dynamic responses. A reduced-order nonlinear vehicle-track model that retains nonlinear Hertzian wheel-rail contact is used as the observation model in the EKF. The unknown irregularity is treated as an augmented state in the EKF formulation and recursively updated based on sleeper acceleration, rail acceleration, and rail displacement measurements. Numerical results show that the proposed method can reconstruct the vertical irregularity profile under different trackside observation types effectively. The effects of sensor spacing and measurement noise are examined to evaluate the stability of the proposed method. Sensor spacing denotes the distance between two adjacent instrumented track locations, which varies from 0.6 m to 2.4 m. Increasing the sensor spacing reduces the spatial density of available trackside measurements and degrades the reconstructed irregularity profile, especially for sleeper acceleration. At a sensor spacing of 0.6 m, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) is approximately 0.15 mm. When the spacing increases to 2.4 m, the RMSE increases to approximately 0.39 mm. The wavelength-band error further shows that sparse measurements mainly increase the estimation error in the long-wavelength range. Measurement noise has a stronger influence on acceleration-based observations. Rail displacement provides the most stable noise performance, with RMSE values ranging from 0.141 mm to 0.146 mm under 5%–20% root-mean-square (RMS) noise.

Mechanics-guided sparse identification of hysteretic restoring force equations for reinforced concrete columns
abstract: Nonlinear time history analysis of reinforced concrete (RC) columns requires restoring force equations that remain accurate and numerically stable when coupled to the equation of motion. Conventional hysteretic models fix a complete model before calibration, whereas many data-driven approaches encode the restoring force relation in trained parameters. This study presents a mechanics-guided sparse identification framework that identifies an explicit equation for each response from a shared library of twelve operators. A bounded cumulative energy state allows selected contributions to evolve with loading history. The framework was evaluated using 75 finite element (FEM) earthquake cases, 5 cyclic specimens, and 230 external RC column records. The FEM equations retained a median of four operators. With 40% identification coverage, OURS-sparse completed all 75 closed-loop analyses without divergence and achieved mean normalised root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) of 4.91% for displacement and 5.63% for restoring force, close to the corresponding values at full coverage. Across the external records, the mean restoring force NRMSE was 6.79%, and 96.1% of records had NRMSE below 10%. The contribution of the state-modulated terms increased with ductility demand in the FEM analyses. The resulting compact equations remained stable in closed-loop FEM analysis and captured degradation trends across the evaluated cyclic records, providing an interpretable basis at the structural response level for future seismic degradation modelling.

title: Aqua-thermally treated high-strength rubberized concrete railway sleepers reinforced with recycled tire steel fibers: Mechanical performance assessment and structural viability for modern railway systems
abstract: Railway sleepers are subjected to quasi-static, dynamic, and impact loading, which can accelerate cracking and premature deterioration due to the inherent brittleness and low energy absorption capacity of conventional concrete. This study proposes a high-performance rubberized concrete composite incorporating aqua-thermally treated rubber aggregates and recycled tire steel fibers to enhance the structural resilience of prestressed concrete railway sleepers. Material-level investigations revealed that high-strength concrete incorporating 10% treated rubber aggregates and 0.5% recycled tire steel fibers fully restores the compressive strength to the level of control concrete, eliminating the inherent strength losses typically associated with rubberized concrete. Furthermore, the modified composite exhibited approximately 11% and 18% higher tensile and flexural strengths, respectively, together with a 7.3-fold increase in impact resistance compared with the control concrete. Microstructural analyses using scanning electron microscopy, micro-CT, and nanoindentation confirmed improved stress-transfer mechanisms and a 2.62-fold increase in plastic energy-dissipation capacity. The proposed material was subsequently implemented in full-scale railway sleepers and evaluated under static and impact loading conditions. Modified sleepers exceeded the designed first-crack load by more than 25% at both the rail-seat and midspan regions, while exhibiting nearly 4.8-fold greater impact energy-dissipation capacity than conventional sleepers. Enhanced resistance to crack initiation and propagation was also observed under service-representative loading conditions. Additionally, RTSF-RuC sleepers sustained more than 99% of the field-based induced wheel-rail interaction repeated impact loading without forming cracks. These findings identify the proposed dual-recycled composite as a sustainable alternative for modern rail infrastructure, with significantly improved load-bearing performance, toughness, and crack resistance.

Wind-induced response of tall mass timber buildings using an efficient fluid–structure interaction framework
abstract: Sustainable mass timber systems are increasingly adopted in tall buildings. However, their lightweight, relatively low lateral stiffness, and inherent damping make them sensitive to wind-induced vibrations. Although fluid-structure interaction (FSI) provides a rigorous framework for wind assessment, its application to tall mass timber structures has been limited in practice by high computational costs and the difficulty of accurately characterising the dynamic properties of timber lateral force-resisting systems. This study proposes an efficient one-way FSI framework with high-fidelity pressure mapping based on Large Eddy Simulation for mass timber structures. Three load mapping strategies with different spatial resolutions, namely façade-resolved, distributed, and lumped-force, are systematically evaluated. The framework is validated against wind engineering benchmarks and applied to a 30-story case-study building. While global responses (e.g., roof displacement and base shear) show close agreement across all methods, significant differences arise at the local level. The proposed distributed mapping approach captures peak Von Mises stresses at critical wall connections up to 18% higher than those predicted by the lumped-force approach, highlighting the importance of preserving the spatial non-synchronicity of wind pressures. In addition, the proposed approach reduces computational time by approximately 79% relative to conventional FSI, while maintaining comparable accuracy to the façade-resolved approach. A parametric study on structural damping shows that the serviceability performance of the case-study tall mass timber building is highly sensitive to damping assumptions. According to ISO 10137, a damping ratio of 3% satisfies the acceleration limit for office occupancy, whereas residential comfort requires a damping ratio exceeding 5%. These findings emphasize the importance of high-resolution pressure mapping and accurate damping characterization for reliable serviceability assessment and connection-level design of tall mass timber buildings.

title: Bayesian model uncertainty analysis of fluid viscous dampers and its influence on retrofitted reinforced-concrete frame fragility
Simultaneous seismic mitigation and harvesting performance of an electromagnetic energy-harvesting nonlinear energy sink
abstract: A novel electromagnetic energy-harvesting nonlinear energy sink (EH-NES) is proposed for simultaneous vibration mitigation and energy harvesting. Considering parasitic effects, shaking table tests are conducted to examine the device performance, followed by parameter identification. Numerical models are validated in terms of both mechanical and electrical responses, followed by parametric studies to quantify the impact of critical parameters on the dual-functional performance. Moreover, seismic robustness analyses evaluate the potential of the EH-NES for synchronized vibration mitigation and energy harvesting across various seismic scenarios. Experimental results indicate that the EH-NES reduces structural displacement by over 20%, while harvesting a peak voltage and power of 376 mV and 83.22 mW, respectively, at a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of 0.25g. Parametric studies identify the optimal EH-NES mass ratio between 7.5% and 10%. The EH-NES performance degrades markedly with increasing inertance ratio, whereas an inertance ratio below 10% is an acceptable limit. In addition, increasing load resistance enhances vibration mitigation by 5%-8%, whereas output voltage approaches saturation as harvested power continuously decreases. Seismic robustness analyses reveal that the EH-NES performance is highly sensitive to PGAs, exhibiting a marked improvement with increasing seismic intensity. Across diverse seismic scenarios, the EH-NES yields an average reduction ratio, output voltage, and power of 21.29%, 289 mV, and 109.3 mW, respectively. These findings confirm the spectral robustness of the EH-NES for simultaneous vibration mitigation and energy harvesting under seismic excitations.

title: GCDO-Net: Differential operator graph network for gradient computation on unstructured meshes
Progressive collapse behaviour of end-plate beam-to-column connections with austenitic stainless steel bolts
abstract: This paper presents an integrated experimental and numerical study into the application of austenitic stainless steel bolts to enhance the progressive collapse performance of end-plate beam-to-column connections. Four substructure specimens, designed with flush and extended end-plate connections, were tested to simulate a middle-column-removal scenario in a steel frame structure. To isolate the effect of using austenitic stainless steel bolts, two comparative tests were performed for each connection type: one featuring conventional carbon steel (G8.8) bolts and the other featuring austenitic stainless steel (A4–80) bolts. The test results clearly demonstrated that the use of A4–80 bolts instead of G8.8 bolts greatly enhanced the ultimate resistance of the connections. The enhancement in dynamic load resistance (a key performance index of progressive collapse resistance) was 94% and 56% for the flush and extended end-plate connections, respectively. Subsequently, an advanced finite element (FE) model capable of simulating fracture in steel components was developed to further investigate the behaviour of the connections under column removal. The validated FE model was employed to perform a comprehensive parametric study to examine the effects of different design parameters on the connection behaviour. It was found that the end-plate thickness and the number of bolt rows are the most critical parameters influencing the behaviour of the connections under column removal. Finally, a limit value for end-plate thickness was proposed to efficiently utilise austenitic stainless steel bolts for enhanced progressive collapse resistance.

title: Mechanical performance of 4D-printed honeycombs with various Poisson’s ratios under quasi-static and low-velocity compression
abstract: Four-dimensional (4D) printing provides a promising route for prototyping reusable energy-absorbing metamaterials that can recover their geometry after large deformation. However, the cyclic performance of 4D-printed shape-memory honeycombs remains governed by topology, loading direction, loading rate, and cold programming history. This study investigates the rate-dependent compressive response and cyclic reusability of 4D-printed polylactic acid honeycomb metamaterials with positive, negative, and zero Poisson’s ratios. The as-printed specimens were tested along two orthogonal directions at crosshead velocities of 0.025 and 25 mm/s. The X-direction specimens were then subjected to six severe deformation–recovery cycles to evaluate cyclic mechanical retention and shape-memory recovery. The results show mechanical anisotropy, with compression along the principal cell-alignment direction yielding higher structural stiffness, plateau force, and specific energy absorption. Increasing the loading velocity enhances plateau force and energy absorption, whereas the structural-stiffness response depends on topology and loading direction. By Cycle 6, SEA retention remained at least 69.60% across all tested conditions, with the zero-Poisson’s-ratio honeycomb showing the most balanced retention across the quantified cyclic mechanical metrics. These findings provide design guidance for additively manufactured reusable shape-memory metamaterials for impact mitigation and protective applications.

title: A novel dynamic analytical method for seismic response of rocking steel piers
abstract: Abstract The prestressed self-centering rocking steel bridge pier with external energy-dissipating devices has excellent seismic and economic performance and broad application prospects. This paper establishes a prediction model for the height of the compression zone at the pier bottom based on the existing statics analytical model of the rocking steel bridge piers under the horizontal cyclic load. Furthermore, based on the dynamics Lagrange’s equation and the conservation theorem of angular momentum before and after the impact, a dynamics analytical calculation method for the rocking steel pier structural system is proposed, which considers the energy dissipation in the plastic hinge zone at the pier bottom and the collaborative work of multiple components under horizontal ground motions. Compared with the calculation results of the static and dynamic refined finite element models, for rocking steel piers with different structural parameters, the statics analytical method can obtain accurate load–displacement hysteresis curves. Moreover, the displacement time history results and restoring force–displacement curves of the proposed dynamics analytical model are quite accurate. The dynamics analytical calculation method proposed in this paper can provide an important support for the establishment of seismic design method of the rocking steel pier.

title: A numerical study of multi-story light-frame timber modular towers with rubber based inter-modular connections using substructure method
abstract: With the growing interest in timber building technologies and the pursuit of efficient modular construction, light-frame timber modules are gaining increasing popularity across the globe. Most residential buildings using such modules in Nordic countries are built up to a maximum six stories and are typically designed for the racking strength using the simplified analysis of wall diaphragms prescribed in Eurocode 5. Recent studies in light-frame timber shear walls present detailed finite element (FE) models that are better than simplified analysis. However, for modular systems, apart from the shear walls, the influence of transverse walls, floor diaphragms and inter-modular connections plays a crucial role in accurately predicting the global response of multi-story buildings. Although creating a detailed FE model of multiple modules can be computationally demanding, excessive simplification may lead to loss of essential structural behavior. To address this, the present study proposes an adaptive modeling strategy that offers a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. The approach combines a non-linear standard FE-formulation for a representative module with a linear substructure formulation for stacked modules, which may have identical or varying designs. The substructure modules are connected to nonlinear inter-modular connections via nodal points where the degrees of freedom are retained. Consequently, the limitation of the substructure formulation, namely, the continuation of linear behavior beyond plastic deformation of the module, is confined to the substructure models meanwhile, the nonlinear effects are captured in the critical bottom module and at the inter-modular connections. A tower is analyzed with an adaptive model of a typical asymmetric module to evaluate both the global racking stiffness and racking strength, as well as the local sheathing-to-framing connection and axial compression in studs of the most heavily loaded bottom module. Story drift of only the bottom module of the six story tower is found to be within the recommended serviceability limit. For the modules above, around 40% contribution to the total horizontal displacement was due to the rigid body rotation, or rocking, of the module while using friction based inter-modular connections. An additional 35% contribution was from shear displacement of the modules while the remaining 25% was caused by slip displacement. Stiffer design of inter-modular connections is crucial and therefore, is recommended in design practice to reduce the story drift, thus upgrading the design to reach the recommended serviceability limit criteria.

title: Topology optimization for modular construction with multi-material, periodic, and demoldable units

Mechanical behavior of a 9-story timber building with clt rocking wall-columns in structural core base on seismic response analysis
abstract: In recent years, the use of wood in buildings has become widespread worldwide because of social factors such as the realization of carbon neutrality and the sustainable development of forestry. Given the widespread adoption of cross-laminated timber (CLT), CLT rocking wall columns have attracted increasing attention. CLT rocking wall columns are characterized by low slippage and high origin-oriented performance owing to vertical prestress introduced by prestressed concrete steel bars. The deformation of each story can be ensured to remain uniform by using the rocking wall columns as through-wall columns in mid- to high-rise wooden buildings. The performance of buildings can be maintained by introducing CLT rocking wall columns in mid- to high-rise wooden buildings, which have a large slip property; however, few such cases exist. In this study, the mechanical behavior of a nine-floor wooden building with CLT rocking wall columns as part of its undamped frame was investigated through a seismic response analysis using a frame model, and the differences in behavior with and without CLT rocking wall columns were confirmed. To obtain all the necessary parameters to model building structures under horizontal loads, we performed tests on frames as well as on CLT rocking wall columns with different parameters, and finally with beam-to-column joints.

title: The minimal thickness of masonry pavilion vaults
abstract: The aim of this study was to determine the minimally necessary uniform thickness of cloister vaults to carry their selfweight. First, preliminary virtual experiments (using well-calibrated DEM models to simulate strong limestone masonry with dry contacts) were done on the simplest geometries, to gain a first insight into the failure modes and into the internal stress states. By applying the experiences gained this way, analytical predictions were then derived for the minimum thickness in two alternative ways, i.e., using the two theorems of Limit State Analysis, for the full range of reasonable opening angles. After this, virtual experiments were done on various opening angles again, determining the minimal thickness for each. The comparison of the results from the three approaches revealed that while the predictions provided by the Kinematic Theorem were in excellent agreement with the virtual experimental results, the Static Theorem yielded overly conservative predictions, due to the inevitable oversimplification of the internal stress system. For a 2x90 degrees opening angle, the minimal thickness is 4,28% of the radius of the middle barrel surface, decreases with decreasing opening angle, and becomes zero at 2x54 degrees.

title: An identification and classification framework for bridge cracks using transposed convolution-CBAM-Segformer with transfer learning

An inerter-based lumped-parameter model using improved legendre polynomials for time-domain analysis of soil-structure interaction
Climate-informed assessment of long-term buffeting performance of suspension bridges
abstract: Due to the continuous rise in greenhouse gas emissions, the global climate system is becoming increasingly unpredictable. For wind-sensitive structures, such as cable-supported bridges, a higher frequency of intense windstorms and increased extreme wind speeds can lead to serviceability problems, including more frequent operational closures and long-term structural issues related to material fatigue. This study presents a framework for integrating high-resolution climate projection data into the assessment of changes in extreme wind events. The approach employs a convection-permitting climate model (CPCM), which explicitly resolves convective processes at a 3 km grid spacing. Projections are considered for two Representative Concentration Pathway scenarios, RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5. Analysis of the climate projections indicates that wind speeds are not expected to change substantially across much of Fennoscandia. However, considering the overwhelming uncertainty in the projections, the bridge performance is assessed under additional synthetic scenarios to explore its vulnerability. The framework is demonstrated using the Hardanger Bridge in Norway, which combines site-specific wind and turbulence models with performance assessment metrics that account for both buffeting-induced serviceability exceedance, operational downtime, and wind-induced fatigue demand under climate-projected and synthetic wind scenarios

title: An automated scan-to-FE model workflow for steel box girder exterior surfaces based on in-situ point clouds
Long-term hygro-viscoelastic creep and stress redistribution in a flax-fiber-reinforced polymer bridge: Field monitoring and numerical investigation
abstract: The long-term structural performance of bio-based composite bridges under varying environmental conditions remains insufficiently understood, particularly the influence of humidity-dependent creep on stress evolution and serviceability at the structural scale. This study investigates the hygro-viscoelastic creep behavior of a full-scale flax fiber-reinforced polymer (FFRP) pedestrian bridge through a combined experimental and numerical approach. A three-dimensional orthotropic viscoelastic model based on a generalized Kelvin–Voigt formulation is developed and implemented in Abaqus via user-defined material subroutine (UMAT) to capture humidity-dependent anisotropic creep behavior. Model parameters are calibrated using humidity-controlled creep tests on FFRP laminates and validated against long-term in situ monitoring data, showing good agreement. Parametric simulations over a 10-year service period show that environmental humidity significantly accelerates creep deformation, with a pronounced nonlinear increase above approximately 75% relative humidity. While global deflection and laminate strain increase monotonically with humidity, internal stress exhibits a non-monotonic trend. Ply-level analysis shows that different fiber orientations respond differently to humidity-dependent stiffness degradation, leading to stress redistribution within the laminate. This behavior is quantified using a load redistribution indicator, highlighting a soft redundancy mechanism associated with time-dependent stiffness contrasts among plies. The results demonstrate that long-term structural performance cannot be assessed based on deformation alone, as humidity-induced stress redistribution plays a critical role. These findings provide insights for serviceability assessment and durability-oriented design of bio-based composite bridge structures.

Orthotropic plate buckling method for the design of stainless steel structures manufactured by wire-arc directed energy deposition
abstract: Wire-arc directed energy deposition (DED-Arc) offers significant advantages for manufacturing stainless steel plates, but the inherent material anisotropy of DED-Arc stainless steel challenges the isotropic assumptions underlying current design standards (e.g., AISC 360, EN 1993-1-4, GB 50017). This paper proposes an Orthotropic Plate Buckling Method (OPBM) for predicting the local buckling resistance of DED-Arc stainless steel plate elements in compression. Analytical solutions for the elastic critical buckling stress of orthotropic plates were first derived for simply-supported (SS) and simply-supported–free (SF) boundary conditions. A comprehensive experimental database comprising 595 tensile coupon test results was established to characterise the anisotropic material properties of common DED-Arc stainless steel grades. Based on this database, empirical correlations for estimating directional Young’s moduli and Poisson’s ratios were proposed and used to determine the orthotropic material properties for stub column tests for which a full set of material test data was unavailable. Using 101 collated stub column test results, new local buckling design curves were developed for SS and SF plates, with the plate slenderness determined based on the orthotropic material assumption. Comparative assessments demonstrate that the OPBM significantly improves accuracy over the conventional isotropic design rules in EN 1993-1-4, with the mean test-to-predicted resistance ratio decreasing from 1.30 to 1.10 for SS plates and from 1.47 to 1.17 for SF plates. Two worked examples are provided to illustrate the practical implementation of the OPBM. The proposed OPBM provides a mechanics-based design framework for DED-Arc stainless steel plate elements and can be extended to other AM metallic materials exhibiting anisotropy, supporting their safe and efficient application in structural engineering.
